focus_areas.name: Gig Rider Safety
focus_areas.relevance: Delhi-NCR is one of India's largest gig/quick-commerce delivery hubs, and the national trend Crashfree India cites -- two-wheeler riders now forming close to half of all road-crash fatalities, up from about 30% in 2014 to roughly 45% by 2023 (per MoRTH data reported by Newslaundry, 10 Nov 2025, which also notes India loses nine two-wheeler riders an hour) -- plays out acutely on Delhi's high-speed corridors such as Outer Ring Road and the Delhi-Meerut Expressway. Delhi's own 2022 accident data showed two-wheeler riders (510 male, 41 female) among those killed, within a year that also recorded 648 deaths from 2,144 overspeeding-related accidents (per The Tribune). Crashfree India's own Gig Rider Safety work (300+ two-wheeler gig riders surveyed nationally, 15 in-depth interviews, per the organisation's own site) remains thematic and national rather than tied to a named state pilot, but Delhi is a natural fit given rider density and given that Delhi's government has, unusually among Indian states, taken direct executive action on gig-worker conditions. In January 2026 the Centre pushed food and quick-commerce platforms to drop explicit '10-minute delivery' guarantees after nationwide rider protests, a move reported (Al Jazeera, 28 Jan 2026) as a direct response to road-safety and worker-fatigue concerns; and Delhi's own FY2026-27 budget created a dedicated Gig Workers Welfare Board and funded rest infrastructure explicitly linked in coverage to reducing fatigue-driven road accidents among riders. This combination of national delivery-pressure reform and Delhi-specific welfare/rest-stop policy makes Delhi one of the more policy-active geographies for this focus area, even though Crashfree India has not yet named a state-specific pilot for Gig Rider Safety.
focus_areas.progress: Several concrete, dated developments touch gig-rider road safety in Delhi/NCR. A nationwide flash strike by delivery workers on New Year's Eve 2025 protested the '10-minute delivery' model, explicitly citing traffic accidents, injuries and mental stress as drivers of the protest. In response, government pressure led platforms to scale back explicit '10-minute' delivery branding by late January 2026 (Al Jazeera, 28 Jan 2026; British Safety Council India), though researchers note the underlying algorithmic time pressure on riders persists even without that label. Delhi CM Rekha Gupta held pre-budget consultations directly with gig workers (per The Daily Pioneer) ahead of the March 2026 budget, where workers raised safe-parking, EV-infrastructure, and job-security demands. The Delhi Budget 2026-27, presented 24 Mar 2026, announced formation of a Gig Workers Welfare Board and an Auto-Taxi Driver Welfare Board, plus rest stops attached to Atal Canteens intended to let delivery workers eat, charge phones and recover -- explicitly framed in coverage as addressing fatigue-related road accidents (Newsgram, 24 Mar 2026; Daily Pioneer). However, a civil-society reaction (Counterview.net, 25 Mar 2026) reported that the Gig & Platform Service Workers Union welcomed the budget as 'a step forward' but flagged missing implementation detail ('what, when, how much') and noted that roughly 45 of the proposed Atal Canteen rest-stop locations may sit far from actual high-demand delivery/pickup zones, limiting real-world safety benefit. No evidence was found that the Welfare Board has since been formally constituted, funded, or made operational, and no Delhi-government helmet or safety-kit distribution program (as distinct from Crashfree India's own 120+ kits distributed nationally) was located.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: Delhi shows more visible, dated policy willpower on gig-worker conditions than it does on the hit-and-run claims-processing gap. The government held direct pre-budget consultations with gig workers, announced a dedicated Gig Workers Welfare Board and Auto-Taxi Driver Welfare Board in the FY2026-27 budget, and funded rest-stop infrastructure explicitly framed around reducing fatigue-driven accidents -- all within the past year. This aligns with a broader national policy shift (an anticipated Labour Code extending social-security coverage to gig/platform workers, partly funded by a 1-2% levy on aggregator turnover) that Delhi's steps track. That said, the signal is qualified by two findings: first, the union's own reaction (Counterview.net) that budget language lacks implementation specifics and legislative backing; second, no evidence was found of a Delhi-specific target, KPI, or timeline for reducing gig-rider road fatalities specifically, as distinct from general worker welfare, nor evidence that the Welfare Board is operational as of September 2026. Overall assessment: real, recent, budget-backed willpower exists at the 'worker welfare' framing level, but a road-safety-specific mandate, target, or enforcement mechanism for gig riders has not yet been clearly and separately articulated by the Delhi government in the sources reviewed.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Crashfree India's Gig Rider Safety program is currently national/thematic in scope -- the organisation's own site describes an ongoing 300+-rider survey and 15 in-depth interviews with no state-specific pilot yet named -- so Delhi is not currently a named CFI engagement geography for this program, though its status as a top gig-economy hub and its recent welfare-board/rest-stop policy activity make it a plausible expansion candidate worth CFI's attention.

focus_areas.name: Project Rakshak
focus_areas.relevance: Project Rakshak turns youth-led corridor audits into government-approved infrastructure fixes -- Cohort 1 (2025) audited 31 high-risk locations across 18 cities and secured 23+ approvals; Cohort 2 (2026) has scaled to 95 teams across 34 cities and 32 institutions. Delhi matters to this program in a narrower, specific way rather than as a confirmed audited city: Delhi hosts several of the institutions and mentors that anchor Rakshak nationally. Crashfree India's own Project Rakshak page names IIT Delhi among the academic institutions tied to the program (alongside IIT Kharagpur, IIT Madras, IIT BHU, IIT Indore and others), and two IIT Delhi-affiliated experts are associated with the program's mentorship/evaluation structure. This makes Delhi institutionally significant to Rakshak's mentor and evaluation ecosystem even though I could not confirm Delhi is one of the cities where a student team actually audited a local crash corridor. Given Delhi's own severe two-wheeler and overspeeding-crash profile -- hundreds of fatalities annually, concentrated on corridors like Outer Ring Road -- it would be a natural candidate city for a future Rakshak cohort, and its unusually high concentration of engineering colleges (IIT Delhi, DTU, Jamia Millia and others) gives it a strong potential bench of student teams and mentors compared with most Indian cities. Whether Crashfree India intends to extend Rakshak's audit-to-fix model into Delhi itself, as opposed to using it only as a mentor/host hub, is not established in the organisation's own published materials or in independent reporting located during this research.
focus_areas.progress: The concrete, dated Delhi-linked activity that could be triangulated is Delhi's role as a mentor/institutional hub: Crashfree India's own Project Rakshak page lists IIT Delhi among the program's academic institutions, and names Delhi-based experts among the program's mentors, while listing confirmed city-level participating locations as Vijayawada, Indore, Chennai, Mumbai, Varanasi, Guntur and Chandigarh -- without listing Delhi as a city where a local team audited a corridor in Cohort 1. Separately, Crashfree India's own social-media channel describes a Cohort 1 'National Road Safety Forum' finale held at IIT Delhi, at which a subset of the 31 finalist student teams presented corridor-fix proposals; because this detail is sourced only to the organisation's own social-media post rather than an independently verifiable article, it is reported here descriptively rather than as a confirmed, citable fact (see research gaps). Cohort 2 (2026), whose orientation completed 3 September 2026, is reported in program materials to span 95 teams across 34 cities in 19 states/UTs -- but Crashfree India's own brief is explicit that the full 34-city list is not published, and no independent, dated source (news article or official list) confirming or ruling out Delhi's inclusion as an audited city in Cohort 2 could be found. This is a genuine, unresolved research gap rather than a negative finding either way.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: Project Rakshak's 'policy willpower' signal in Delhi is really a question of whether Delhi's own civic agencies (PWD, Delhi Traffic Police, DDA) engage with student-led audit recommendations, since the program's model depends on local-authority buy-in rather than state legislative action. Evidence was found of Delhi Traffic Police acting on infrastructure in a Rakshak-adjacent way through a separate channel: at the State Road Safety Council meeting reported by The Tribune (11 Dec 2025), 18 accident hotspots were described as undergoing 'active remediation' with completed work at Delhi Gate and ISBT Kashmere Gate, and a partnership between Delhi Traffic Police and IIT-Delhi was announced to identify further high-risk locations for camera surveillance. This shows the same audit-to-fix logic Rakshak uses is already operating in Delhi through a parallel Traffic Police-IIT Delhi channel, independent of Crashfree India. Whether Crashfree India's own Rakshak teams or mentors have any formal link to, or influence on, this existing Delhi Traffic Police-IIT Delhi hotspot program is not established by this research and would be a valuable connection for CFI to clarify or pursue -- it represents a potential channel through which Rakshak's methodology could gain direct government traction in Delhi specifically.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Delhi's confirmed CFI/Project Rakshak engagement is currently limited to serving as an institutional/mentor hub via IIT Delhi-affiliated experts and (per Crashfree India's own social media, not independently verified) as the host venue for Cohort 1's finale forum; Delhi could not be confirmed as one of the cities where a Rakshak student team actually audited a local crash corridor in either the 18 cities of Cohort 1 or the still-unlisted 34 cities of Cohort 2.

focus_areas.name: SATARK (ANPR Enforcement Technology)
focus_areas.relevance: SATARK's Bengaluru pilot (Trinity Circle, live since Sept 2025) established a model -- ANPR scanning, real-time compliance lookup, a public 'AI Challan Billboard,' and on-ground officer alerts -- that has since gone live in Gurugram and Jaipur, with four more installations underway in Pune, Rajkot, Gandhinagar and Thiruvananthapuram. Delhi's relevance to SATARK is as a comparator rather than an expansion target in the pipeline: Delhi already runs substantial independent ANPR/AI camera enforcement of its own, through Delhi Traffic Police in partnership with Delhi International Airport Ltd (DIAL)/GMR and the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), separate from anything branded Crashfree India or SATARK. This matters for Crashfree India's strategy because it suggests Delhi is not a blank-slate city waiting for enforcement technology -- it already has camera-based automated challan infrastructure -- but it does not appear to have replicated SATARK's specific innovations: a public-facing real-time violator billboard for citizen-facing transparency, and a described workflow for alerting on-ground officers to priority non-compliance in real time. A future SATARK conversation with Delhi authorities would therefore likely need to be framed around adding this transparency/alert layer onto existing infrastructure, rather than proposing camera enforcement as a new concept.
focus_areas.progress: Delhi is confirmed NOT to be a current or announced SATARK location: SATARK's live sites remain Bengaluru (Trinity Circle, since Sept 2025, per Deccan Herald), Gurugram and Jaipur, with Pune, Rajkot, Gandhinagar and Thiruvananthapuram underway; no Delhi mention was found in Crashfree India's own materials or in independent search results. Delhi does have substantial independent ANPR/AI enforcement activity of its own: (1) Delhi Traffic Police, in partnership with DIAL/GMR, has installed ANPR cameras on approach roads to Indira Gandhi International Airport -- 14 cameras as of a reported installation, with 35 more planned -- covering violations including overspeeding, illegal parking, wrong-side driving, triple-riding, and helmet non-compliance (The Daily Pioneer); (2) Delhi Traffic Police has integrated NHAI's ANPR cameras on the Delhi-Dehradun Expressway with its e-challan system, issuing 1,000+ speeding challans/notices (Delhi News Live); and (3) at the December 2025 State Road Safety Council meeting, the Transport Minister cited 47 AI-powered cameras already operational citywide, with plans -- via a stated Delhi Traffic Police-IIT Delhi partnership -- to expand coverage and designate 'zero-tolerance' enforcement zones on Ring Road, Outer Ring Road and NDMC areas (The Tribune). None of these initiatives, as reported, include a public-facing real-time violator billboard comparable to SATARK's signature feature, nor a described real-time on-ground-officer-alert workflow; they function as automated challan-issuance systems rather than SATARK's 'detect, publicly display, and alert police for priority action' model.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: Delhi's political and administrative willpower on ANPR/AI enforcement technology broadly looks comparatively strong and well-resourced: multiple parallel initiatives (airport-area cameras with DIAL/GMR, expressway cameras with NHAI, a Delhi Traffic Police-IIT Delhi partnership for hotspot identification, and a stated citywide camera network) were underway or announced across 2025-2026, backed by explicit ministerial statements at a State Road Safety Council meeting reported in December 2025. This suggests Delhi's government does not lack willpower on enforcement technology generally -- it has instead built its own multi-agency ANPR ecosystem (Delhi Police plus DIAL/GMR plus NHAI plus IIT Delhi) rather than adopting or requesting a SATARK-branded deployment from Crashfree India/Cars24. Whether this reflects a considered institutional choice, a lack of awareness of SATARK specifically, or simply that SATARK (launched September 2025, still only 3 live cities per Crashfree India's own brief) is too new and small to have reached Delhi's decision-makers yet, could not be established from public sources: no Delhi government statement mentioning Crashfree India, Cars24, or SATARK by name was found in this research.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Delhi is explicitly NOT named as a current or planned SATARK location in Crashfree India's own materials, and this was independently corroborated by search: no Delhi mention appears alongside SATARK's confirmed live (Bengaluru, Gurugram, Jaipur) or underway (Pune, Rajkot, Gandhinagar, Thiruvananthapuram) sites. Delhi instead runs its own, separately-administered ANPR/AI-challan enforcement initiatives (Delhi Traffic Police with DIAL/GMR, NHAI, and IIT Delhi), meaning any future CFI engagement in Delhi on this focus area would need to be framed as a complementary transparency/alert layer or a comparator relationship rather than a green-field deployment.

madhya_pradesh.political_context: Madhya Pradesh has been governed since 13 December 2023 by a Bharatiya Janata Party ministry headed by Chief Minister Dr. Mohan Yadav, formed after the BJP's decisive win in the November 2023 Assembly election (163 of 230 seats). Yadav, a first-time CM from Ujjain, retained the Home, General Administration, Public Relations, Jail, Mining, Aviation and Industrial Policy portfolios for himself and appointed two Deputy Chief Ministers -- Jagdish Devda (Finance, Commercial Tax, Planning) and Rajendra Shukla (Public Health and Medical Education) -- with a roughly 25-member Council of Ministers operating out of Vallabh Bhawan, Bhopal (newsdarpan.in, 12-19 Aug 2026, https://newsdarpan.in/en/article/madhya-pradesh-cabinet-ministers-list-2026-contact-numbers-portfolios). Cross-checking this Aug 2026 portfolio list against the original December 2023 allocation (Zee News, 30 Dec 2023) and against February-September 2026 event coverage confirms the road-safety-relevant portfolio holders have been stable for the government's full term to date: Uday Pratap Singh (Transport and School Education), Rakesh Singh (Public Works Department), Kailash Vijayvargiya (Urban Development and Housing, Parliamentary Affairs) and Prahlad Singh Patel (Panchayat and Rural Development, Labour) all still held their respective portfolios as of August-September 2026 (starsamachar.com, 12 Feb 2026; indianmasterminds.com, 11 Sep 2026). What has changed constantly is the administrative/bureaucratic layer beneath these ministers. Madhya Pradesh's civil service has seen an unusually rapid churn: a new Chief Secretary, Ashok Barnwal (1991-batch IAS), took charge on 23 July 2026 after predecessor Anurag Jain was elevated to CEO of the central NITI Aayog (indianmasterminds.com, 23 Jul 2026); the Transport Commissioner's post changed hands four times in about two years (Sanjay Jha, DP Gupta, Vivek Sharma and, most recently, Umesh Joga from 29 January 2026), a volatility directly traceable to the 'Saurabh Sharma' transport check-post corruption scandal (a former transport constable allegedly amassing assets worth several hundred crore rupees via bribery at check-posts), which also triggered a restructuring of the State Transport Authority so that an IAS-rank Additional Chief Secretary/Principal Secretary now chairs it rather than the Transport Commissioner alone. The Public Works Department was the subject of a critical CAG Performance Audit (Report No. 7 of 2025, tabled in the Assembly around January 2026) finding minimal road-network growth despite heavy investment, maintenance-fund yardstick rates unrevised since 1997, and works executed without proper technical sanction -- a direct institutional vulnerability and opportunity for road-safety advocacy given PWD's roughly 80,000 km road network. On the enforcement side, DGP Kailash Makwana (1988-batch IPS, in charge since 1 December 2024) had his tenure extended to December 2026 under Supreme Court minimum-tenure norms (Free Press Journal, 24 Nov 2024), but no single, clearly-named state-level ADG (Traffic) could be confirmed in this research; the most recent identifiable traffic-enforcement leadership figure is Jitendra Singh Panwar as DCP (Traffic) for the Bhopal Police Commissionerate (Aug 2025). Overall, the government is politically stable with no coalition risk and no scheduled election before 2028, but the frequent IAS/IPS reshuffles (26-42 officers moved in single orders roughly every few months through 2025-2026) mean CFI outreach should treat named bureaucratic contacts as provisional and re-verify shortly before any engagement, while treating the ministerial layer (Yadav, Devda, Shukla, Singh, Singh, Vijayvargiya, Patel) as the more durable point of entry.

governance_bodies.name: Madhya Pradesh Transport Department (Office of the Transport Commissioner)
governance_bodies.mandate: Enforcement of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988, the Madhya Pradesh Motor Vehicles Taxation Act 1924 (amended 1993), and rules framed under both — i.e. vehicle registration, driving-licence issuance, permits, fitness certification, tax/toll collection at check-posts, and (jointly with Police) enforcement of traffic rules on the road network.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None directly — it is a regulatory/enforcement and revenue body, not a road-owning agency. It licenses/regulates vehicles and operators that use roads owned by PWD, MPRDC, NHAI, MPRRDA and urban local bodies.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Minister for Transport (currently Uday Pratap Singh, who also holds School Education) -> Additional Chief Secretary/Principal Secretary, Transport Department (Home Dept cadre officers have also held transport charge) -> Transport Commissioner (an IPS/ADG-rank officer, headquartered at Moti Mahal, Gwalior) -> Regional Transport Officers (RTOs) and District Transport Officers across Madhya Pradesh's districts -> Assistant RTOs, transport inspectors and check-post staff.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Regional Transport Authorities (RTAs) at division/district level; a state Transport Authority (recently reconstituted so that an Additional Chief Secretary/Principal Secretary chairs it, with the Transport Commissioner reduced to a member, following High Court scrutiny of one officer holding multiple concurrent posts); the transport check-post network (47 check posts across the state); Madhya Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation-linked contract-carriage administration for the new 'Mukhyamantri Sugam Parivahan Seva' city bus scheme.

Policy changes (tax rates, permit quotas, new transport schemes), major procurement (e.g. bus fleets) and reorganisation of the Transport Authority require Cabinet/Finance Department and, per recent restructuring, a senior IAS chair's sign-off rather than the Commissioner's alone.
governance_bodies.data_role: Maintains the state vehicle registration (VAHAN) and driving-licence (SARATHI) databases, fitness/permit records, and check-post transaction data; feeds vehicle-population and licensing data used in NCRB/MoRTH road-accident statistical compilations.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: Subject of a major corruption scandal (the 'Saurabh Sharma' case) in which a former transport constable allegedly amassed assets worth Rs 500-700 crore, largely via bribery at the department's check-posts (23 of 47 check-posts implicated); this directly triggered the removal of the sitting Transport Commissioner in January 2025 and a restructuring of the state Transport Authority's chairmanship after High Court scrutiny of conflicts of interest.

governance_bodies.name: Madhya Pradesh Public Works Department (PWD), Building & Roads (B&R) wing
governance_bodies.mandate: Planning, designing, construction and maintenance of government-owned roads, bridges, Railway Over Bridges (ROBs)/flyovers and buildings; the principal agency for National Highways (where PWD executes on NHAI's behalf), State Highways, Major District Roads, Other District Roads and some village roads outside PMGSY's ambit.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Approximately 80,775 km of road network under PWD (B&R), per the department's own figures — covering national highway stretches built/maintained on NHAI's behalf, all state highways, major district roads, other district roads and connecting village roads, plus bridges, ROBs and flyovers.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Minister, PWD (Rakesh Singh, as of the most recent confirmed reshuffle) -> Principal Secretary, PWD (Sukhveer Singh, IAS 1997 batch, appointed 18 July 2025, succeeding Neeraj Mandloi who held additional charge and DP Ahuja before him) -> Engineer-in-Chief -> Chief Engineers (zone-wise) -> Superintending Engineers (Circles) -> Executive Engineers (Divisions — 56 B&R divisions statewide per CAG's audit sample) -> Assistant/Sub-Engineers at sub-division and site level.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: PWD Project Implementation Unit (PIU) for externally-funded projects (e.g. New Development Bank/NDB-financed roads); Bridge Corporation-linked works; district PWD divisions that provide the ex-officio Member Secretary (Superintending Engineer) to District Road Safety Committees.

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Can technically sanction and execute works within delegated financial limits at each engineering tier; major schemes, budget allocation and externally-funded (NABARD/NDB/CRIF) projects require State Finance Department and sometimes Union MoRTH/NABARD approval. CAG found many works proceeding without proper technical sanction at all — see performance_issues.
governance_bodies.data_role: Maintains road-asset inventory, works-execution and maintenance-expenditure records feeding the state's budget/works-monitoring systems; is a primary source of infrastructure-condition data relevant to blackspot and safety-audit exercises.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: CAG Performance Audit Report No. 7 of 2025 ('Development of Roads in Madhya Pradesh by MP Public Works Department', for the period 2018-2023, tabled/dated 20 Jan 2026) found: minimal road-network growth despite substantial investment from the State Budget, Central Road Fund/CRIF, NABARD and NDB; maintenance-fund allocation based on yardstick rates unrevised since June 1997, causing chronic underfunding versus real material/labour costs; roads executed without technical sanction; poor contract management and inadequate monitoring leading to sub-standard road works, completion delays and subsequent road damage. A separate, earlier CAG performance audit specifically on Construction of Major Bridges in Madhya Pradesh by PWD also exists (2023 report series) but its detailed findings could not be extracted as readable text in this research (binary PDF).

governance_bodies.name: Madhya Pradesh Road Development Corporation Limited (MPRDC)
governance_bodies.mandate: A wholly state-government-owned undertaking (incorporated 2004) declared successor/assignee of the erstwhile Madhya Pradesh Rajya Setu Nirman Nigam Limited (MPRSNN), entrusted with implementation of State Highway, National Highway and Major District Road projects in Madhya Pradesh, principally through BOT/PPP/annuity/DBFOT financing models rather than direct budgetary works.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Manages/oversees a network of over 22,000 km of National Highways, State Highways and Major District Roads in Madhya Pradesh, largely the higher-value/PPP-financed corridors.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Chaired by a senior state government nominee (Board of Directors, government-owned) -> Managing Director (Bharat Yadav, IAS, 2008 batch, appointed January 2025, previously Secretary to the Chief Minister) -> functional Divisions (project, technical, finance, and a dedicated Road Safety Cell) -> Project Directors/General Managers for individual BOT/annuity road projects across the state.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: A Road Safety Cell has been set up within MPRDC (per World Bank-documented program reporting) to run safety-audit and blackspot-improvement work on MPRDC-managed corridors; project-specific Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) are typically created for individual BOT concessions.

governance_bodies.name: Urban Administration & Development Department, Madhya Pradesh (Directorate of Urban Administration & Development) and Urban Local Bodies (Nagar Nigam/Nagar Palika/Nagar Parishad)
governance_bodies.mandate: State-level department overseeing Madhya Pradesh's 378 Urban Local Bodies (16 Municipal Corporations/Nagar Nigams including Bhopal, Indore, Jabalpur and Gwalior; 98 Municipal Councils; 264 Nagar Parishads), which are the constitutional (74th Amendment) custodians of municipal roads, streetlighting, drainage and urban infrastructure within their limits, including schemes such as the Chief Minister Urban Infrastructure Development Scheme (CMUIDS).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Municipal/urban roads within the limits of each Nagar Nigam/Nagar Palika/Nagar Parishad — i.e. city streets, ward roads and local drainage-linked infrastructure, as distinct from state highways (PWD/MPRDC) and National Highways (NHAI) that may also pass through city limits.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Minister, Urban Administration & Development -> Principal Secretary (Sanjay Shukla, per a November 2024 reshuffle) -> Commissioner, Directorate of Urban Administration & Development (based at Palika Bhawan, Shivaji Nagar, Bhopal) -> Municipal Commissioners (IAS/state civil service, one per Nagar Nigam, e.g. Bhopal, Indore, Jabalpur, Gwalior Municipal Corporations) -> City Engineers and ward-level junior engineers.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Individual Nagar Nigams (Bhopal, Indore, Jabalpur, Gwalior, Ujjain, Sagar, etc.), Nagar Palika Parishads, and Development Authorities (e.g. Ujjain Development Authority) that also undertake road-linked infrastructure in their planning areas; a 24/7 citizen helpline (18002335522) is run centrally.

key_positions.title: Principal Secretary, Urban Development Dept.
key_positions.name: Sanjay Shukla
key_positions.confidence: tier-4 sourcing (Elets eGov, a specialist e-governance/bureaucracy outlet explicitly permitted as tier-4 under this research's source policy), dateline November 2024 — nearly two years old versus the Sept 2026 reference date; flagged for re-verification.

citation.label: Elets eGov — '26 IAS transferred in Madhya Pradesh, Sanjay Shukla made Principal Secretary Urban Development Dept.' (tier-4)

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Municipal Corporations can sanction and execute local road/drainage works within their own budget and byelaw powers (including permitting/rejecting speed-breaker requests, subject to District Road Safety Committee clearance per Indore precedent); larger capital schemes (CMUIDS, smart-city works) require state-level scheme approval and funding release.
governance_bodies.data_role: Local bodies maintain municipal asset registers (roads, streetlights, drains) but no centralised, publicly documented urban road-safety database was identified in this research.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: The Gwalior Bench of the Madhya Pradesh High Court (in a public-interest matter over the 2015 State Road Safety Policy) directly criticised the 'responsibility-shifting' between the Gwalior Municipal Corporation and the State Government/PWD over who was responsible for maintaining specific poorly-lit, poorly-maintained roads — the Corporation argued five of six roads named were PWD's responsibility while the state pushed responsibility back onto the Corporation, illustrating a documented jurisdictional/accountability gap. A cited IIT Delhi Transportation Research & Injury Prevention Programme study (2020, referencing 2018 data) found Gwalior's road-fatality rate to be 50% higher per 100,000 persons than the average of other Indian cities studied.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not established from available sources; research gap.

governance_bodies.name: Madhya Pradesh Police — Traffic Enforcement Wing (under the Home Department)
governance_bodies.mandate: Enforcement of traffic rules under the Motor Vehicles Act 1988 and Madhya Pradesh Police Act provisions: challans/e-challans, speed enforcement, drunk-driving checks, traffic-signal and junction management, and accident-scene first response/FIR registration on all road categories within a district's jurisdiction.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None — an enforcement body operating across all road types (NH, SH, MDR, rural, urban) within its jurisdiction, not a road-owning agency.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Home Minister (Home Department, GoMP) -> Director General of Police (DGP) (Kailash Makwana, IPS 1988 batch, took charge 1 December 2024, tenure extended by the state to 1 December 2026 to comply with Supreme Court service-tenure directives) -> Additional Director General (Traffic), Police Headquarters Bhopal -> in the two Police Commissionerate cities (Bhopal and Indore) a Deputy Commissioner of Police (Traffic) commands city traffic enforcement (Jitendra Singh Panwar was named DCP Traffic, Bhopal, in an August 2025 reshuffle) -> in all other (SP-led) districts, a Superintendent of Police oversees a District Traffic-in-charge/Traffic Sub-Division -> Traffic Inspectors, Sub-Inspectors and constabulary at police-station/chowki level.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: City traffic police units (Bhopal, Indore, Jabalpur, Gwalior); district traffic police sub-divisions; the DCP/SP-level traffic wing that acts as a standing member of the respective District/City Road Safety Committee.

key_positions.title: Director General of Police, Madhya Pradesh
key_positions.name: Kailash Makwana
key_positions.confidence: Well corroborated across multiple tier-4 outlets (Deccan Herald is tier (c) and also covered his appointment) — took over 1 December 2024, tenure extended to December 2026 per Supreme Court mandate; considered current as of the Sept 2026 reference date but nearing the end of the extended tenure, so a successor announcement may be imminent.

key_positions.title: Deputy Commissioner of Police (Traffic), Bhopal
key_positions.name: Jitendra Singh Panwar (IPS, 2016 batch)
key_positions.confidence: tier-4 sourcing (Elets eGov, dateline August 2025) — a lateral move from DCP Zone-4, Bhopal, to DCP Traffic; roughly 13 months old as of the reference date.

citation.label: Elets eGov — 'Madhya Pradesh Govt Transfers Nine IPS Officers, Jitendra Singh Panwar made DCP Traffic' (tier-4)

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Can unilaterally enforce, challan, impound vehicles and register FIRs; cannot unilaterally redesign junctions, install signage or build infrastructure (that requires PWD/Nagar Nigam/MPRDC/NHAI action) — enforcement and engineering are institutionally separated, a structural bottleneck frequently noted in road-safety practice.
governance_bodies.data_role: Primary source of accident FIR/e-challan data that feeds state and NCRB road-accident statistics; also runs local 'black-spot' identification jointly with PWD/MPRDC/NHAI as a District Road Safety Committee member.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: A specific, dateline-confirmed report found the DCP (Traffic) post in Bhopal had been left vacant for several months prior to the August 2025 appointment, according to Free Press Journal reporting on pending police postings — indicating staffing gaps in traffic enforcement leadership even in the state's capital.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Attends District/City Road Safety Committee meetings, which in Indore, for example, were documented as having met five times between April and August 2023 (roughly monthly to bimonthly).

governance_bodies.name: Madhya Pradesh Rural Road Development Authority (MPRRDA)
governance_bodies.mandate: A society registered under the Societies Registration Act, created specifically as the state's nodal implementing agency for the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) — providing all-weather road connectivity to unconnected rural habitations — as well as other state-funded rural road schemes.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: 78,094 km of PMGSY roads sanctioned in Madhya Pradesh to date, with a further ~12,000 km proposed under PMGSY-III and 15,846 km being constructed under other state-funded rural road schemes, per MPRRDA/PMGSY programme documentation.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: General Body chaired by the Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh (policy-setting and programme monitoring) -> Chief Executive Officer (a serving IAS-cadre officer) -> 100 Project Implementation Units (PIUs) covering the state's (then) 50 districts, each headed by a General Manager of Superintending/Executive Engineer rank -> field engineering staff supervising contractors and independent quality-monitoring consultants.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: 100 district/sub-district Project Implementation Units (PIUs); an online Works Management System ('SAMVEG') for programme monitoring.

key_positions.title: Chief Executive Officer, MPRRDA
key_positions.name: Not established — official MPRRDA site (mprrda.org) and its works-management portal (samveg.mp.gov.in) were unreachable during this research (DNS/HTTP failures), and no press report naming the current CEO was found via allowed sources.
key_positions.confidence: Research gap — could not identify current incumbent; flagged rather than guessed.

citation.label: MPRRDA official portal (unreachable during research)

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: PIUs can supervise and certify contractor work within sanctioned PMGSY project scope; new road sanctions, phase (PMGSY-I/II/III) allocations and funding releases require Union Ministry of Rural Development approval jointly with the State Panchayat & Rural Development Department.
governance_bodies.data_role: Maintains the PMGSY project-wise physical/financial progress database for Madhya Pradesh (feeding the national PMGSY online monitoring system) and, per World Bank-documented programme reporting, has had over 300 of its staff trained in road-safety-conscious design as part of a pilot road-safety programme.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: No MPRRDA-specific CAG or gazette-sourced audit finding was identified in this research (distinct from the PWD audits above); this is a research gap, not a clean bill of health.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: General Body (chaired by the CM) sets policy and monitors the programme; specific meeting frequency not established from available sources.

governance_bodies.name: Madhya Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority (MPSDMA)
governance_bodies.mandate: Constituted under the Disaster Management Act, 2005 (a central Act under which every state must set up a State Disaster Management Authority, statutorily chaired by the Chief Minister) to lay down disaster-management policy, plans and guidelines for the state, spanning both natural disasters and, in practice, mass-casualty road-accident emergency response coordination.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None — a coordinating/policy authority, not a road-owning agency.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Chaired by the Chief Minister (per the Disaster Management Act 2005's standard state-authority structure) -> Vice-Chairperson/CEO (typically a senior IAS officer) -> State Executive Committee -> District Disaster Management Authorities chaired by the District Collector.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: District Disaster Management Authorities (one per district, chaired by the Collector); operational linkage to the state's 108 Emergency Ambulance and fire/rescue response networks for accident response.

key_positions.title: Chairperson, MPSDMA
key_positions.name: Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh (Mohan Yadav), ex officio per the Disaster Management Act 2005's standard structure
key_positions.confidence: Structural/statutory inference from the Disaster Management Act 2005's uniform national template for State Disaster Management Authorities, cross-checked against Madhya Pradesh's own disaster-management planning documents; the MPSDMA's own web portal (mpsdma.mponline.gov.in) could not be reached during this research (DNS failure) to directly confirm current office-holder listings.

citation.label: Madhya Pradesh State Disaster Management Plan document (state government)

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Sets state disaster-management policy/plans and can direct resource mobilisation across departments during a declared disaster; day-to-day road-accident emergency response is operationally executed by Police, 108 ambulance operators and district administration rather than by MPSDMA directly.
governance_bodies.data_role: Coordinates disaster-related data/reporting including, in principle, mass-casualty road-accident events, but no MP-specific road-accident-focused MPSDMA dataset was identified in this research.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: Not established from available sources in this research; research gap.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not established from available sources; research gap.

governance_bodies.name: Madhya Pradesh 'Dial 108' Emergency Ambulance Service
governance_bodies.mandate: State emergency medical response service (operating under the National Health Mission umbrella, with MP's service contracted to a private operator, Ziqitza Health Care Ltd, per available reporting) aimed at reaching accident and disaster victims within the 'golden hour' to improve survival odds — the direct emergency-response arm relevant to road-crash outcomes.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None — a mobile emergency-response service, not a road-owning agency.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: National Health Mission, Madhya Pradesh (state health department) contracts and oversees the service -> operator (Ziqitza Health Care Ltd, per available reporting) -> district-level ambulance fleets and call-centre dispatch.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Over 606 '108' ambulances and 839 'Janani' (maternal) ambulances reported operational across the state's 52 districts, per operator-side reporting.

key_positions.title: Operator
key_positions.name: Ziqitza Health Care Ltd (Dial 108, run in partnership with the State Government and National Health Mission)
key_positions.confidence: tier-4 sourcing (operator's own public materials, cross-checked against NHM references); no single named state government official identified as the direct programme head in this research — research gap.

citation.label: Ziqitza Health Care Ltd — '108 Emergency Ambulance Number for India' (operator materials, tier-4)

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Can dispatch and operationally manage ambulance response; fleet-size, contract-renewal and funding decisions rest with the State Health Department/National Health Mission, not the operator alone.
governance_bodies.data_role: Holds response-time and call-volume data for emergency dispatches, a key metric for road-safety 'golden hour' outcomes, though no publicly available MP-specific response-time dataset was located via allowed sources in this research.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: Not established from available sources in this research; research gap (no CAG/PIB/mainstream-press audit of 108 service performance in MP specifically was found).
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not applicable/not established.

governance_bodies.name: District Road Safety Committees (DRSCs), Madhya Pradesh
governance_bodies.mandate: Constituted under Section 215(3) of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988 (as amended by the Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act 2019) and by state government order (in Madhya Pradesh's case an order dated 5 July 2022, later gazette-notified) to review road-safety measures, accident data, and infrastructure deficiencies at district level, and to approve/clear local safety interventions (e.g. speed-breaker installation, per Indore precedent).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None — a coordinating/oversight committee, not a road-owning body; it sits above the PWD, MPRDC, Nagar Nigam, NHAI and Police representatives who each own/execute within their own jurisdiction.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Chaired by the District Collector -> Superintendent of Police (or DCP Traffic, in Commissionerate cities) as a core member -> Superintending Engineer, PWD as ex-officio Member Secretary -> RTO, Municipal Commissioner/City Engineer, NHAI/MPRDC Project Director (where applicable), and health-department (108/trauma-care) representatives as members.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: None below it at district level, though it is itself supervised by state-level Road Safety oversight (and, per Supreme Court directions, subject to review by the apex Supreme Court Committee on Road Safety, which has directly reviewed traffic measures in Jabalpur).

key_positions.title: Chairman, District Road Safety Committee (district-by-district, e.g. Indore, Jabalpur, Agar Malwa, Gwalior)
key_positions.name: The respective District Collector (rotates by district and by transfer; no single statewide name)
key_positions.confidence: Structural fact confirmed via district government portals (Indore, Agar Malwa) and press coverage of the Supreme Court Committee on Road Safety's review of Jabalpur; individual Collectors' names are subject to frequent IAS transfers and are not centrally tracked in this research.

citation.label: District Indore — Road Safety Committee (official district portal)

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Can approve/reject local traffic-calming measures (e.g. speed breakers, per Indore's documented requirement that these need DRSC permission) and direct local departments to act on identified blackspots; cannot override state-level budget allocation or force PWD/MPRDC/NHAI capital works without those agencies' own sanction.
governance_bodies.data_role: Reviews district accident-statistics reports (Indore's committee page links to accident-statistics documents from its meetings) and tracks local blackspot-rectification progress.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: The Madhya Pradesh High Court's Gwalior Bench PIL directly evidences a breakdown in inter-agency accountability at this level — with the Municipal Corporation and State Government/PWD each blaming the other for un-repaired, poorly-lit roads named in the petition, rather than the DRSC mechanism resolving it before litigation.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Indore's DRSC held 5 recorded meetings between April and August 2023 (roughly monthly-to-bimonthly); frequency likely varies by district and is not centrally mandated at a fixed interval in the sources reviewed.

governance_bodies.name: Madhya Pradesh State Road Safety Policy (2015) framework / State-level Road Safety Council
governance_bodies.mandate: The Madhya Pradesh State Road Safety Policy 2015 (Gazette Notification No. 100, dated 3 March 2016) is the state's foundational road-safety policy document, intended to set overarching direction for engineering, enforcement, education and emergency-care ('4 E's') interventions statewide, and (per the standard national template that most states follow, and consistent with MoRTH's push for State Road Safety Councils/Funds) is understood to anchor a State Road Safety Council structure, though this research could not directly access or fully verify the operative council's current composition, meeting cadence or fund corpus via allowed sources.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None — a policy-and-coordination framework, not a road-owning body.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Believed to be chaired at Chief Secretary or Minister (Transport/Home) level per the national template for State Road Safety Councils, with the Transport Commissioner, PWD Engineer-in-Chief, ADG (Traffic), MPRDC MD and Health Department representatives as members — but this exact composition for Madhya Pradesh specifically was NOT independently confirmed in this research and should be treated as indicative rather than verified.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: District Road Safety Committees (see separate entry) are the operative district-level arm of this policy framework.

key_positions.title: Chair (indicative, not independently confirmed for MP)
key_positions.name: Not established — the substantive text of the 2015 Policy and any current State Road Safety Council order were not accessible via allowed sources in this research (the indexing site found only carried the gazette's metadata, not its full text)
key_positions.confidence: Explicit research gap — do not treat as confirmed.

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Not established with confidence from available sources; research gap.
governance_bodies.data_role: Not established with confidence from available sources; research gap.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: The Madhya Pradesh High Court (Gwalior Bench) has directed the State Government and a Municipal Corporation to file compliance reports specifically on implementation of the 2015 Road Safety Policy, after a citizen's petition alleged poor road maintenance and insufficient street lighting — direct judicial evidence that the Policy's on-the-ground compliance is contested and under active court scrutiny as of the petition (matter listed for further hearing).
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not established from available sources; research gap.

governance_bodies.name: Madhya Pradesh Home Department
governance_bodies.mandate: The cabinet department with overall administrative control of the Police Department (including its traffic wing), Home Guards, and — as evidenced during the transport-scandal fallout — the power to issue transfer/appointment orders even for Transport Commissioner-rank postings when police officers are deputed to that role.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None — a policy/administrative-control department, not a road-owning agency.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Home Minister (portfolio holder not independently confirmed in this research beyond the fact that the Chief Minister has historically retained or closely overseen Home in Madhya Pradesh — research gap) -> Additional Chief Secretary/Principal Secretary, Home -> Director General of Police (see MP Traffic Police entry) and Director General, Home Guards/Civil Defence.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Madhya Pradesh Police (all wings including Traffic), Home Guards, and administrative oversight of the Transport Commissioner's post when filled by a police (IPS) officer, as is presently the case.

key_positions.title: Home Minister
key_positions.name: Not independently confirmed in this research — the Home Department's own portal (home.mp.gov.in) returned repeated HTTP 503 errors during this research session, preventing direct verification.
key_positions.confidence: Explicit research gap.

citation.label: Home Department, Government of Madhya Pradesh (official portal, unreachable during research)

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Issues transfer/appointment orders for police officers including those deputed to run the Transport Department (as happened in the January 2025 Transport Commissioner change); sets overall policing policy and resource allocation to the Traffic wing.
governance_bodies.data_role: Aggregates policing and law-and-order data, including traffic-enforcement statistics reported up from district SPs/DCPs.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: Directly implicated in the transport check-post corruption fallout in that it was the Home Department which issued the order removing the Transport Commissioner in January 2025 amid the Saurabh Sharma scandal — evidencing that transport-sector integrity failures escalated to Home Department-level intervention.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not established from available sources; research gap.

road_ownership_matrix.Owner/custodian: NHAI (for NHAI-declared stretches) or State PWD acting as executing agency for NHAI on other NH stretches
road_ownership_matrix.Construction: NHAI-appointed EPC/HAM/BOT contractors via NHAI Regional Office Bhopal/PIUs, or PWD (B&R) divisions where PWD executes on NHAI's behalf
road_ownership_matrix.Maintenance: NHAI (through its concessionaire/O&M contractor) or PWD, depending on the stretch
road_ownership_matrix.Enforcement: MP Police Traffic wing (district SP/DCP) with RTO/Transport Dept for vehicle-side violations
road_ownership_matrix.Safety audit: NHAI's own road-safety audit process (national mandate); District Road Safety Committee also reviews NH blackspots within its district
road_ownership_matrix.Funding: Union Budget via Ministry of Road Transport & Highways (MoRTH), Central Road & Infrastructure Fund (CRIF), NHAI market borrowing, and toll revenue
road_ownership_matrix.Local body role: Minimal — urban local bodies coordinate on NH stretches passing through city limits (e.g. service roads, drainage tie-ins) but do not own them

road_ownership_matrix.Owner/custodian: Madhya Pradesh PWD (B&R) and/or MPRDC (for BOT/PPP-financed State Highway stretches)
road_ownership_matrix.Construction: PWD divisions (budget-financed works) or MPRDC-appointed BOT/DBFOT concessionaires (PPP-financed corridors)
road_ownership_matrix.Maintenance: PWD divisions, or the BOT concessionaire during the concession period for MPRDC corridors
road_ownership_matrix.Enforcement: MP Police Traffic wing; RTO for vehicle/permit compliance
road_ownership_matrix.Safety audit: PWD's own engineering review and, on MPRDC corridors, MPRDC's Road Safety Cell; District Road Safety Committee oversight
road_ownership_matrix.Funding: State Budget, Central Road Fund/CRIF, NABARD and New Development Bank (NDB) loans (per CAG's audit sample), and MPRDC's toll/annuity/VGF-financed PPP structure
road_ownership_matrix.Local body role: Limited — mainly coordination where a State Highway passes through a Nagar Nigam's urban limits

road_ownership_matrix.Construction: PWD divisions, sometimes MPRDC for select MDR stretches bundled into larger PPP packages
road_ownership_matrix.Safety audit: PWD engineering review; District Road Safety Committee
road_ownership_matrix.Local body role: Coordination role only, no ownership

road_ownership_matrix.Road type: Rural Road (PMGSY / Other District & Village Roads)
road_ownership_matrix.Owner/custodian: Madhya Pradesh Rural Road Development Authority (MPRRDA), under the Panchayat & Rural Development Department
road_ownership_matrix.Construction: Contractors supervised by MPRRDA's ~100 Project Implementation Units (PIUs), one set per district, with independent quality-monitoring consultants
road_ownership_matrix.Maintenance: MPRRDA (PMGSY roads carry mandated multi-year maintenance contracts bundled with construction contracts) and, for some village link roads, the Panchayat & Rural Development Department/Gram Panchayats
road_ownership_matrix.Enforcement: MP Police (district SP) with limited RTO presence on rural stretches
road_ownership_matrix.Safety audit: MPRRDA-trained staff (300+ trained under a World Bank-documented pilot programme) and District Road Safety Committee review
road_ownership_matrix.Funding: Union Ministry of Rural Development (PMGSY Centre-State cost-sharing) plus State-funded rural road schemes
road_ownership_matrix.Local body role: Gram Panchayats provide local oversight/maintenance input but MPRRDA remains the executing authority

road_ownership_matrix.Owner/custodian: The relevant Urban Local Body — Nagar Nigam (Municipal Corporation, e.g. Bhopal, Indore, Jabalpur, Gwalior), Nagar Palika, or Nagar Parishad, under the Urban Administration & Development Department
road_ownership_matrix.Construction: Municipal Corporation's own City Engineering wing, or contractors engaged under state urban schemes (e.g. CMUIDS) or Smart City project structures
road_ownership_matrix.Maintenance: The Urban Local Body's City Engineering wing
road_ownership_matrix.Enforcement: MP Police Traffic wing (in Bhopal/Indore, the Police Commissionerate's DCP Traffic; elsewhere, SP-led traffic units) and municipal traffic-management byelaws
road_ownership_matrix.Safety audit: Not centrally documented in this research — no dedicated urban-road safety-audit body was confirmed; District/City Road Safety Committee is the de facto review forum
road_ownership_matrix.Funding: Municipal own-revenue, state grants (CMUIDS and similar schemes), and central urban-mission funding where applicable
road_ownership_matrix.Local body role: Primary owner, builder and maintainer — the Nagar Nigam/Palika/Parishad itself, not a delegated role

road_lifecycle.Who is responsible (urban roads): Municipal Corporation's own quality checks — no independent third-party mechanism was confirmed in this research

road_lifecycle.Who is responsible (NH): NHAI/concessionaire, per concession-period obligations

road_lifecycle.Who is responsible (NH): NHAI's national road-safety-audit mandate
road_lifecycle.Who is responsible (urban roads): Not centrally confirmed — District/City Road Safety Committee is the de facto review forum, not a dedicated urban audit body

road_lifecycle.Who is responsible (state/rural roads): District Road Safety Committee (Collector-chaired), with PWD/MPRDC and Police Traffic wing input
road_lifecycle.Who is responsible (NH): NHAI, feeding MoRTH's national blackspot list, with District Road Safety Committee also reviewing NH blackspots locally
road_lifecycle.Who is responsible (urban roads): District/City Road Safety Committee with Municipal Corporation and Police Traffic wing input

road_lifecycle.Who is responsible (state/rural roads): PWD or MPRDC executes engineering fixes once identified and approved
road_lifecycle.Who is responsible (NH): NHAI/concessionaire executes fixes
road_lifecycle.Who is responsible (urban roads): Municipal Corporation executes fixes, subject to DRSC clearance for measures like speed breakers (per Indore's documented rule)

road_lifecycle.Who is responsible (state/rural roads): PWD divisions / MPRRDA PIUs as part of routine maintenance
road_lifecycle.Who is responsible (NH): NHAI/concessionaire
road_lifecycle.Who is responsible (urban roads): Municipal Corporation's City Engineering wing

road_lifecycle.Who is responsible (state/rural roads): District administration (Collector's revenue machinery) jointly with PWD/MPRRDA
road_lifecycle.Who is responsible (NH): District administration jointly with NHAI (under the National Highways Act's right-of-way provisions)
road_lifecycle.Who is responsible (urban roads): Municipal Corporation jointly with district administration/police for enforcement

district_level_actors.Role: Chairs the District Road Safety Committee; heads the District Disaster Management Authority (emergency-response coordination for mass-casualty accidents); controls the land-acquisition machinery for road projects; is the ultimate district-level convening authority when PWD, Municipal Corporation, Police and RTO fail to coordinate (as evidenced by the Gwalior High Court case's inter-agency blame-shifting).

district_level_actors.Actor: Superintendent of Police (SP) / Deputy Commissioner of Police-Traffic (in Bhopal & Indore Commissionerates)
district_level_actors.Role: Commands district/city traffic enforcement — challans, speed enforcement, drunk-driving checks, accident FIR registration; sits on the District/City Road Safety Committee as a core member; cannot independently commission engineering fixes (signage, junction redesign) — must refer these to PWD/Nagar Nigam/MPRDC/NHAI.

district_level_actors.Actor: Regional Transport Officer (RTO) / District Transport Officer
district_level_actors.Role: Local face of the state Transport Department — vehicle registration, licensing, permits, fitness certificates, and check-post enforcement within the district; reports up to the Transport Commissioner at Moti Mahal, Gwalior; historically a locus of the corruption concerns exposed by the Saurabh Sharma case (which involved 23 of the state's 47 transport check-posts).

Executes and maintains State Highway/MDR/other district roads within the division; provides the ex-officio Member Secretary function (at Superintending Engineer level) to the District Road Safety Committee; responsible for technical sanction and quality control of works within the division — the CAG audit found systemic weaknesses here (works without technical sanction, sub-standard quality, unrevised maintenance-rate yardsticks).

district_level_actors.Actor: General Manager, MPRRDA Project Implementation Unit (PIU)
district_level_actors.Role: Supervises PMGSY rural-road contractors and consultants within the district/PIU jurisdiction (of ~100 PIUs covering the state's districts); reports to the MPRRDA Chief Executive Officer; a key channel for rural-road safety-design training under the World Bank-documented pilot programme.

district_level_actors.Actor: Municipal Commissioner / City Engineer (within Nagar Nigam limits)
district_level_actors.Role: Owns, builds and maintains municipal roads, streetlighting and drainage within city limits; a District/City Road Safety Committee member; the entity whose maintenance failures were specifically litigated in the Gwalior High Court road-safety case.

district_level_actors.Actor: District Road Safety Committee (as a body, chaired by the Collector)
district_level_actors.Role: The formal district-level coordination mechanism under Section 215(3) of the Motor Vehicles Act — reviews accident data, approves/clears local safety interventions (e.g. Indore's speed-breaker permission rule), and is meant to resolve the very inter-agency responsibility disputes that, per the Gwalior case, can otherwise end up in the High Court.

Coordinates emergency medical response and trauma-care linkage for road-accident victims within the 'golden hour', operationally distinct from but reporting into the District Disaster Management Authority/District Collector's overall coordination during major incidents.

quick_reference_matrix.Problem: Dangerous intersection (urban, e.g. within Bhopal/Indore city limits)
quick_reference_matrix.Primary institution: Municipal Corporation (Nagar Nigam) City Engineering wing
quick_reference_matrix.Supporting institutions: MP Police Traffic wing (DCP Traffic in Commissionerate cities), District/City Road Safety Committee
quick_reference_matrix.Decision-maker: Municipal Commissioner, subject to DRSC clearance for traffic-calming measures
quick_reference_matrix.Implementer: Municipal Corporation's own works wing or contracted agency
quick_reference_matrix.Likely bottleneck: Jurisdictional overlap/responsibility-shifting between Corporation and State PWD when the intersection sits on a State Highway passing through city limits (as litigated in the Gwalior case)

quick_reference_matrix.Problem: Dangerous intersection / junction (on a highway, outside city limits)
quick_reference_matrix.Supporting institutions: MPRDC (if a BOT corridor), District Road Safety Committee, MP Police Traffic wing
quick_reference_matrix.Decision-maker: PWD Executive Engineer or NHAI Project Director
quick_reference_matrix.Likely bottleneck: CAG-documented technical-sanction and quality-control weaknesses in PWD execution; funding-approval delays for capital fixes

quick_reference_matrix.Primary institution: Municipal Corporation (urban) or PWD (where a state road lacks one)
quick_reference_matrix.Supporting institutions: Urban Administration & Development Dept (for scheme funding, e.g. CMUIDS)
quick_reference_matrix.Likely bottleneck: No dedicated urban road-safety-audit body confirmed in this research to systematically flag footpath gaps; relies on ad hoc citizen petitions or DRSC review

quick_reference_matrix.Primary institution: Municipal Corporation (urban) or PWD (state highway stretches)
quick_reference_matrix.Implementer: Municipal Corporation's electrical wing or PWD division
quick_reference_matrix.Likely bottleneck: Exactly the issue litigated in the Gwalior High Court case — Corporation and State/PWD blaming each other for unlit, poorly-maintained stretches

quick_reference_matrix.Primary institution: NHAI Regional Office Bhopal / relevant PIU
quick_reference_matrix.Supporting institutions: MoRTH's national blackspot programme, District Road Safety Committee, MP Police Traffic wing
quick_reference_matrix.Decision-maker: NHAI Project Director, subject to MoRTH funding sanction for larger fixes
quick_reference_matrix.Likely bottleneck: Central-level sanction delays for capital-intensive fixes (flyovers, underpasses) versus quicker signage/marking fixes

quick_reference_matrix.Primary institution: PWD (B&R) or MPRDC (on BOT corridors, via its Road Safety Cell)
quick_reference_matrix.Supporting institutions: District Road Safety Committee, MP Police Traffic wing
quick_reference_matrix.Likely bottleneck: State-budget allocation constraints and the CAG-flagged unrevised (since 1997) maintenance-funding yardstick, which the audit found insufficient for real costs

quick_reference_matrix.Primary institution: Transport Department (RTO enforcement of permits/fitness) and MP Police Traffic wing
quick_reference_matrix.Supporting institutions: State Transport Authority (now chaired by an ACS/Principal Secretary, with the Transport Commissioner as a member)
quick_reference_matrix.Decision-maker: Transport Commissioner / RTO for permit action; State Transport Authority for policy
quick_reference_matrix.Implementer: RTO enforcement staff and Police at check-posts/on-road
quick_reference_matrix.Likely bottleneck: Documented check-post corruption (Saurabh Sharma case) undermining enforcement credibility; the January 2025 leadership change and August 2025 structural reform of the Transport Authority both stemmed directly from this bottleneck

quick_reference_matrix.Primary institution: 108 Ambulance Service (Ziqitza Health Care Ltd, under National Health Mission MP)
quick_reference_matrix.Supporting institutions: MP State Disaster Management Authority, District Collector/District Disaster Management Authority, District Hospital trauma-care network
quick_reference_matrix.Decision-maker: State Health Department / National Health Mission (for fleet size, contract terms)
quick_reference_matrix.Implementer: 108 operator's district ambulance fleet and call-centre dispatch
quick_reference_matrix.Likely bottleneck: No publicly available MP-specific response-time performance data was located via allowed sources in this research — a transparency gap in itself

quick_reference_matrix.Primary institution: MP Police Traffic wing (district SP or DCP Traffic)
quick_reference_matrix.Supporting institutions: Transport Department (RTO, for vehicle-fitness-linked speed-governor compliance)
quick_reference_matrix.Implementer: Traffic Police field staff, increasingly via e-challan/camera systems
quick_reference_matrix.Likely bottleneck: Reported staffing gaps (e.g. Bhopal's DCP Traffic post left vacant for months before the August 2025 appointment)

quick_reference_matrix.Primary institution: Road-owning agency for that stretch — PWD, MPRDC, NHAI, or Municipal Corporation
quick_reference_matrix.Supporting institutions: District Road Safety Committee (flags the deficiency)
quick_reference_matrix.Decision-maker: The relevant Executive Engineer/Project Director/City Engineer
quick_reference_matrix.Implementer: The owning agency's maintenance wing or contractor
quick_reference_matrix.Likely bottleneck: Fragmented ownership across five+ agencies for different road types means signage standards/quality are inconsistently applied statewide

quick_reference_matrix.Problem: Encroachment on carriageway/footpath narrowing effective road width
quick_reference_matrix.Primary institution: District Collector's revenue/enforcement machinery, jointly with the road-owning agency
quick_reference_matrix.Decision-maker: District Collector (for eviction orders) jointly with the road-owning agency
quick_reference_matrix.Implementer: District administration enforcement squads, Municipal Corporation anti-encroachment wing
quick_reference_matrix.Likely bottleneck: Politically sensitive evictions and slow revenue-court processes typically delay right-of-way restoration (a pattern documented nationally, though a Madhya Pradesh-specific case study was not located via allowed sources in this research)

quick_reference_matrix.Problem: School-zone road safety (speed, crossings near schools)
quick_reference_matrix.Primary institution: District Road Safety Committee jointly with the road-owning agency and Police Traffic wing
quick_reference_matrix.Supporting institutions: School Education Department (relevant since the Transport Minister also holds School Education in the current MP Cabinet)
quick_reference_matrix.Decision-maker: District Collector (via DRSC) for approving zone-specific measures
quick_reference_matrix.Implementer: PWD/Municipal Corporation for physical measures (signage, speed breakers, zebra crossings); Police for enforcement
quick_reference_matrix.Likely bottleneck: No dedicated statewide school-zone road-safety programme or budget line was confirmed in this research — treated as a research gap

funding_architecture.Implementer: Not established from available sources — research gap
