haryana.political_context:
Nayab Singh Saini (BJP) has served as Chief Minister of Haryana since 12 March 2024 and was returned to office after the October 2024 Haryana Legislative Assembly election, with cabinet portfolios allocated on 21 October 2024. CM Saini personally holds roughly a dozen portfolios, including Home, Finance, Planning, Excise & Taxation, Town & Country Planning, Urban Estates, Housing, Criminal Investigation, and Law & Legislative -- a centralisation pattern seen in several other states in this research series -- though PWD and Transport sit with separate ministers. Haryana's Saini ministry has no Deputy Chief Minister (a structural difference from Bihar, Rajasthan and several other states researched in this series, all of which have one or more Deputy CMs); no source found in this pass names a Haryana Deputy CM for the 2024-2029 term. No cabinet reshuffle since October 2024 was found across this pass's searches (re-checked through September 2026), so the ministerial line-up first verified in the prior research pass -- Anil Vij (Transport, Energy, Labour), Ranbir Singh Gangwa (PWD Buildings & Roads, and Public Health Engineering), Vipul Goel (Revenue & Disaster Management, Urban Local Bodies), Krishan Lal Panwar (Development & Panchayats), and Arti Singh Rao (Health) -- is treated as still current, subject to the caveats noted on each minister's entry.

On the bureaucratic side, Anurag Rastogi, IAS continues as Chief Secretary and chairs the state's Fund Management Committee (FMC) on road safety; the state government sought (per The Print, 25 June 2026) a second one-year extension for him beyond his original 30 June 2025 retirement, through June 2027, citing administrative continuity. Sudhir Rajpal, IAS holds the Additional Chief Secretary, Home Department post and is the official who actually signs Haryana Police's transfer and reshuffle orders (confirmed as recently as an 11 July 2026 IPS reshuffle and referenced again around the 3 September 2026 reshuffle), since the Home Minister portfolio itself sits with the Chief Minister personally. The administrative bureaucracy is also under visible strain: as of the date of this research (25 September 2026), Haryana was reported running roughly 44 IAS officers short of its sanctioned strength, with several more retirements due before the end of 2026, including Arun Kumar Gupta -- who holds the dual charge of Principal Secretary to the Chief Minister and Finance Secretary -- due to retire on 30 September 2026 with no successor confirmed in this pass.

On policing, Ajay Singhal, IPS (1992-batch, an IIT Delhi mechanical-engineering graduate from Rewari) took charge as Haryana DGP on 1 January 2026, with a guaranteed minimum two-year tenure under the 2006 Prakash Singh Supreme Court judgment and a natural retirement date of 31 October 2028; he succeeded O.P. Singh, who had held interim charge after predecessor Shatrujeet Singh Kapur went on leave while named as an accused in an IPS officer's suicide case. Re-verification through the most recent Haryana IPS reshuffles found in this pass (11 July 2026 and 3 September 2026, the latter affecting 29 IPS and one HPS officer) confirmed Singhal remains DGP. Singhal has built a genuine, dated road-safety record distinct from routine departmental duty: on taking charge he set out a four-pillar strategy (engineering, enforcement, emergency medical response, awareness) and, by mid-January 2026, had launched an IIT-Madras-built 'Sanjaya' accident-mapping platform alongside a 'Baseline Survey' app tracking roughly 1,009 hospitals' trauma-care readiness, with a linked hospital performance-rating system tied to patient survival outcomes. His immediate predecessor as (interim) DGP, O.P. Singh, had separately written to the Union Ministry of Road Transport and Highways in November 2025 over 136 unaddressed black spots (of 474 identified statewide since 2019-20, with 223 rectified and 251 still pending), citing over 4,000 road-accident deaths in 2025 against roughly 800 homicides -- Singh's own words were that 'roads are now bigger killers.' Haryana's ADG, Traffic and Highways is currently Amitabh Singh Dhillon, IPS (1997-batch, Haryana cadre), who received the portfolio only as an additional charge (alongside ADGP Modernisation & Welfare and ADGP, Emergency Response Support System/112) in the 3 September 2026 reshuffle, succeeding Vikas Arora; his tenure is too fresh in this specific portfolio for an independent road-safety track record to be assessed.

On the civil side of the Transport Department, Prabhjot Singh, IAS was named Transport Commissioner and Secretary, Transport Department in an 8 August 2026 reshuffle of 17 IAS and 7 HCS officers, in addition to his existing charge as Director General, Environment and Secretary, Environment, Forests and Wildlife -- a dual charge, corroborated by both The Tribune's contemporaneous reshuffle coverage and the Transport Department's own website (hartrans.gov.in), which independently lists him in that role alongside Dhirendra Khadgata, IAS as Director, State Transport. The GMDA CEO gap flagged in the prior research pass is now resolved: Phool Chand ('P.C.') Meena, IAS is confirmed, via a 20 September 2026 Tribune interview (as GMDA CEO and dually as Municipal Corporation Gurugram Commissioner) discussing the authority's drainage and urban-flooding programme, to have returned to or remained in the GMDA CEO chair -- correcting the prior pass's inference that he had moved on to the Faridabad Metropolitan Development Authority; GMDA's own 9 September 2026 coordination-committee meeting under his chairmanship (on integrated road infrastructure) further corroborates his currency in the post as of this pass.

Haryana's Advocate General changed hands on 21 August 2026: Pawan Kumar Mutneja, a senior Punjab & Haryana High Court advocate (and Haryana's own Additional Advocate General from 1996-99), was appointed under Article 165(1) of the Constitution after predecessor Pravindra Kumar Chauhan was elevated to the High Court bench the same day; no specific, currently pending road/bridge-safety PIL naming him was identified in this pass, though the Punjab and Haryana High Court has a documented general history of hearing road-infrastructure PILs (for example, over incomplete roads/bridges in New Chandigarh, and a since-disposed PIL over a foot overbridge relocation on the Gurugram-Jaipur NH in Rewari district).

On the opposition side, Bhupinder Singh Hooda (INC), Chief Minister from 2005-2014, was named Leader of the Opposition in the Haryana Legislative Assembly around 29 September-3 October 2025. His public criticism of the Saini government since then has centred on general law-and-order and safety themes -- for example, citing the Centre's Social Progress Index to call Haryana 'the most unsafe state in the country' (Tribune, 8 August 2026) in the context of specific crime incidents -- rather than road safety specifically; no direct, on-the-record Hooda statement on road-accident policy was identified in this pass.

Haryana's NCR dimension: Gurugram and Faridabad (and parts of several other districts) fall inside the National Capital Region as defined by the National Capital Region Planning Board (NCRPB) Act, 1985, and the current Draft Regional Plan-2041 for NCR (a central, Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs-linked body with Haryana government representation) does address regional road-network standards. In practice, however, this pass found the NCRPB's institutional footprint on Haryana's day-to-day road-safety governance to be indirect -- it is a regional land-use and infrastructure-planning coordination body, not an operational road-safety, funding, or enforcement authority. The concrete, name-able NCR-linked road-safety actor specific to Haryana is the Gurugram Metropolitan Development Authority (GMDA, a 2017 state statutory body, distinct from NCRPB) together with its public-private 'Utkrisht Society for Safe Haryana' vehicle -- a partnership chaired ex officio by the state DGP as chief patron, through which GMDA and Maruti Suzuki (as a CSR funder) have jointly rolled out an integrated traffic-management camera network (roughly 400 cameras across 23 Gurugram junctions) -- a genuinely distinct institutional wrinkle worth Crashfree India's attention beyond the standard PWD/Transport/Police triad, though it is a Haryana-created vehicle rather than a joint NCR-wide statutory body.

Underlying this political layer, India's constitutional Seventh Schedule splits road-related subjects across the Union and State Lists, and because roads, transport and police all sit substantially on the State List (with the Union retaining National Highways, the Motor Vehicles Act framework, and centrally sponsored schemes like PMGSY), Haryana's state government and its departments remain the primary point of leverage for almost all road-safety interventions Crashfree India will pursue in this state.

focus_areas.name: Crash Compensation (Hit-and-Run Scheme)
focus_areas.relevance: Haryana is not a peripheral data point for Crashfree India's hit-and-run work — Gurugram is explicitly named in the organisation's own brief as a diagnostic geography, a place used specifically to trace where the Hit-and-Run Compensation Scheme claim journey breaks down. That framing is borne out by the state's own numbers. MoRTH's Lok Sabha answer (Unstarred Q. 6419, 2 Apr 2026) shows hit-and-run accidents in Haryana falling from a 2021 peak of 2,644 to 2,590 (2022), 1,750 (2023) and a provisional 1,809 in 2024 — a real decline in the underlying crash count. Yet claims data tells a starkly different story about the compensation pipeline built to serve those victims: 0 claims registered or paid in FY2022-23, just 2 registered/1 paid in FY2023-24, 42/24 in FY2024-25, and then a jump to 515 registered and 168 paid in FY2025-26 (as of 28 Feb 2026). The registered-to-paid ratio in the latest year — roughly one in three — signals a widening processing backlog even as awareness and filing improve, exactly the kind of implementation gap Crashfree India's national analysis (12% uptake, ~90% of pending claims stalled on documentation alone) is designed to diagnose. Compounding this, Haryana does not appear among states reporting any Rah-Veer (Good Samaritan) awardees as of 12 Feb 2026 (Lok Sabha Q. 2178) — a genuine gap given Gurugram's central role in the brief, and one worth flagging rather than explaining away. Together, the rising claims volume, the persistent payment lag, and the zero Good Samaritan uptake make Haryana a textbook diagnostic case: crashes are falling, awareness is rising, but the compensation machinery has not caught up.
focus_areas.progress: On the ground, Haryana has taken some administrative steps that intersect with Crashfree India's focus. The state introduced a cashless treatment scheme for road accident victims (up to Rs 1.5 lakh for the first 7 days under Section 162 of the MV Act), funded through a Haryana Road Safety Fund and implemented via a hospital-to-police-station verification workflow coordinated with the National Health Authority; this was reported as operational in Gurugram-area coverage by December 2024. This is the cashless-treatment route, distinct from the Hit-and-Run Scheme itself, but it shares infrastructure (police verification, district administration) with the compensation pipeline Crashfree India studies. Nationally, MoRTH's 2026 amendment to the Compensation to Victims of Hit and Run Motor Accidents Scheme (notified ~2-3 March 2026) restructures the claims process: District Road Safety Committees now have an expanded mandate to evaluate local implementation, maintain electronic monthly pendency statistics, and improve claimant awareness, while State Road Safety Councils review district-level progress and can issue improvement directives. A new GI Council-managed digital portal is meant to speed up applications, enquiry reports and the 15-day sanctioning timeline. None of the coverage found is Haryana-specific about how the district committees are actually implementing this, which is itself notable given Haryana's diagnostic role. Separately, Gurugram has become a flashpoint for hit-and-run enforcement failures in the media: a September 2026 case on Golf Course Road (widely covered, including commentary from former IPS officer Kiran Bedi) showed that without bystander video, prosecution would have been nearly impossible, and prompted proposals like mandatory dash-cams and closer ANPR-to-control-room integration — underscoring the same 'documentation gap' problem Crashfree India's own research identifies nationally.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: There are real, if uneven, policy signals in Haryana. Chief Minister Nayab Singh Saini's government created a dedicated Haryana Road Safety Fund and launched the cashless-treatment scheme by executive order, with a district-level committee structure explicitly built to process victim compensation within 15 days of an inquiry report — a genuine administrative commitment predating the 2026 central amendment. Haryana's 2026-27 state budget (presented 2 March 2026, an outlay exceeding Rs 2.23 lakh crore, up 10.28% year-on-year) was not confirmed via primary-source extraction to contain a specific road-safety fund line item in the material reviewed, which is itself a research gap worth noting rather than assuming either way. At the central level, the Supreme Court's own interventions — its June 2026 directions on chronic Motor Accident Claims Tribunal delays (avg. ~6 years pendency, appeals ~8 years in High Courts) instructing Chief Justices to prioritise cases pending over 4 years, and its April 2026 Article 21-based nationwide road-safety directions in the Phalodi Accident case (in re NHAI) — create top-down pressure that filters into how seriously state machinery, including Haryana's, treats compensation processing. The 2026 amendment's DRSC/State Road Safety Council reporting obligations give Haryana concrete, auditable checkpoints for the first time. What is missing from public reporting is any Haryana-specific statement, minister quote, or legislative debate that names the Hit-and-Run Scheme's uptake problem directly, or that references Gurugram's diagnostic status with Crashfree India. That silence — a state with rising claims and a stalled payment ratio, but no visible ministerial narrative about fixing it — is itself a policy-willpower signal worth surfacing to funders and government-relations audiences.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Gurugram is named directly in Crashfree India's own brief as a diagnostic geography for the Hit-and-Run Scheme — used to trace where the claims journey breaks — separately from the organisation's active pilot with the Rajasthan State Lead Agency for Road Safety in Jaipur. No public source found in this research names a formal Crashfree India partnership with a Haryana government department or Gurugram Police specifically on hit-and-run compensation; the organisation's own partner listing does not name one either, which is consistent with 'diagnostic' rather than 'implementation' engagement at this stage.

focus_areas.name: Gig Rider Safety
focus_areas.relevance: Gurugram sits at the center of the exact risk profile Crashfree India's Gig Rider Safety program was built to address. It is one of the National Capital Region's largest hubs for food delivery, quick-commerce, and bike-taxi gig work — precisely the two-wheeler-dependent, incentive-driven, time-pressured work Crashfree India's Nov 2025-Jan 2026 interviews and subsequent 300+ rider survey were designed to study. Nationally, nearly half of all road-crash fatalities are two-wheeler riders, and India's gig workforce is projected by NITI Aayog to grow from roughly 7.7 million (2021) to 23.5 million by 2030 — a trajectory that concentrates disproportionately in metro hubs like Gurugram/NCR. Real, dated local incidents bear this out directly: on 5 April 2026, a bike-taxi rider (26) and his passenger (24) were killed in Gurugram's Sector 57 when a wrong-way SUV struck their scooter at roughly 2 AM, throwing both victims 15-20 feet; separately, a Zomato delivery rider was killed in Sector 40 when a tractor struck his bike from behind. These are not abstractions — they are the specific, individual-level events that a program surveying 300+ two-wheeler gig riders is trying to systematize into policy-relevant findings. The broader national picture, as reported by Al Jazeera (28 Jan 2026), shows the labour ministry directing quick-commerce platforms to stop advertising '10-minute delivery' after a rider strike over dangerous conditions — yet enforcement remained weak a week later, with platforms in the NCR still displaying sub-10-minute promises. Gurugram/NCR's gig-delivery density, combined with its documented pattern of fatal two-wheeler crashes, makes it a strong candidate for a future Crashfree India pilot even though no state-specific program has been named yet.
focus_areas.progress: As of this research (Sept 2026), Crashfree India's Gig Rider Safety program remains at an evidence-building stage rather than an implementation stage anywhere, including Haryana. The organisation's own program page describes it as 'being built' and states a dedicated Gig Rider Safety Report has been produced, drawing on partnerships with Cars24, the Indian Road Safety Council, Bikes24 and TeamBHP; a formal knowledge-hub brief ('Gig Rider Safety Brief') was published 2 June 2026, covering road-risk exposure, platform incentive structures, insurance gaps, and the case for a protective policy framework, though full survey findings are stated (per the outreach brief) to publish mid-October 2026 — after this research date. No Gurugram-specific or Haryana-specific pilot, helmet distribution drive, or platform partnership was found in public sources. What was found is contextual: Gurugram/NCR's gig-economy road-safety problem is visible in ongoing news coverage (fatal bike-taxi and delivery-rider crashes through 2026) and in the national policy debate over quick-commerce delivery-time pressure, which the labour ministry has begun — unevenly — to regulate. Haryana Police and the Haryana Transport Department were not found, in any source reviewed, to have announced a gig-rider-specific safety initiative, helmet mandate enforcement drive, or platform-liability framework distinct from general two-wheeler traffic enforcement. This leaves a visible gap between the scale of the problem locally (dense delivery traffic, night-shift wrong-way and rash-driving crashes) and any documented state or company-level intervention targeted at gig riders specifically in Haryana.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: Policy signal on gig-worker road safety in Haryana specifically is thin in the sources reviewed. The most concrete national-level willpower signal is the labour ministry's January 2026 directive telling quick-commerce platforms to stop marketing '10-minute delivery' — a direct acknowledgment that delivery-time pressure drives unsafe riding — but Al Jazeera's reporting found platforms still advertising sub-10-minute delivery in the NCR (which includes Gurugram) a week after the directive, suggesting weak enforcement rather than a strong compliance response. No Haryana state government statement, CM/minister quote, or state legislative action specifically addressing gig-rider or platform-worker road safety was found in this research. This is a genuine gap: Haryana has been comparatively more active on general road-safety funding (the Road Safety Fund, cashless treatment scheme) than on gig-economy-specific worker protections, despite Gurugram's outsized share of India's gig-delivery traffic. Broader Indian gig-worker labour policy — including state-level gig-worker welfare boards being discussed or enacted in states like Rajasthan and Karnataka around this period — was not confirmed to have a Haryana equivalent in the sources reviewed. Given that NITI Aayog's own projections put the national gig workforce at 23.5 million by 2030 and Gurugram is one of the most delivery-dense cities in that workforce, the absence of Haryana-specific policy conversation on gig-rider road safety stands out and is worth flagging directly to funders and government-relations stakeholders as an opportunity area rather than papering over it as settled.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: No state-specific pilot has been named for Gig Rider Safety in Crashfree India's own materials, and no Gurugram/Haryana-specific engagement was found in public sources; however, Gurugram/NCR's status as a major gig-delivery hub, combined with Crashfree India being headquartered in Gurugram, makes it a strong candidate site once the program moves from its research phase (300+ riders surveyed, full findings expected mid-October 2026) into a targeted geography.

focus_areas.name: Project Rakshak
focus_areas.relevance: Project Rakshak's model — youth- and institution-led audits of high-risk crash locations, escalated into formal advocacy with civic authorities for infrastructure fixes — is directly relevant to Haryana given Gurugram and Faridabad's well-documented high-risk corridors (both cities regularly appear in national black-spot and crash-severity discussions for the NCR). Cohort 1 (2025) ran 31 teams across 18 cities, assessing 120+ high-risk locations and securing 23+ government approvals; Cohort 2 (2026) has scaled to 95 teams across 34 cities and 32 institutions, reaching 136 colleges, with new MoUs (NOSPlan, SIT Pune) and additional teams expected from Jaipur, Pune and Srinagar. Whether Haryana — specifically Gurugram or Faridabad — is one of the 34 (or previously 18) cities could not be confirmed from any source found in this research. Crashfree India's own Project Rakshak page, reviewed directly, names only a handful of specific institutions and cities as cohort highlights (e.g., a Mumbai-based team, an IIT Indore team, an IIT Madras team, an IIT BHU team, a Vijayawada-based team) and does not publish a complete city list; it explicitly states applications for a given cohort are closed without detailing full geographic coverage. Given that Crashfree India is headquartered in Gurugram and Gurugram is separately named as its diagnostic geography for hit-and-run work and its live SATARK deployment city, the absence of a confirmed Gurugram/Haryana presence in Project Rakshak's published materials is a genuine and notable gap rather than an oversight to gloss over — it may reflect either non-inclusion, or simply incomplete public disclosure of the full city roster.
focus_areas.progress: Nationally, Project Rakshak has demonstrable output: Cohort 1 (2025) converted 900+ stakeholder surveys and 120+ location assessments into 23+ secured government approvals across 18 cities, a genuinely substantial audit-to-fix conversion rate for a first-year youth-led programme. Cohort 2 (2026) has roughly tripled team count (95 vs. 31) and institutional reach (32 institutions/136 colleges), and formalised partnerships with organisations like NOSPlan and SIT Pune, alongside new teams incoming from Jaipur, Pune and Srinagar per the outreach brief. None of the public-facing Crashfree India material reviewed in this research (the programme's own webpage, its sitemap-listed pages, and general web search) named Gurugram, Faridabad, or Haryana as part of either cohort's city roster, top-performing-team list, or highlighted case studies. This is a meaningful data point for an NGO-outreach dashboard: it suggests that, as of the most recent public disclosure available, Haryana may not yet be part of Project Rakshak's operational footprint, even though the state hosts Crashfree India's own headquarters and two of its other three named focus-area engagements (hit-and-run diagnostics and live SATARK). No independent news coverage (local Gurugram/Faridabad press, Haryana government announcements, or college-partnership press releases) was found describing a Rakshak audit team operating in either city. This should be read as an evidenced absence rather than a confirmed exclusion, since Crashfree India's public materials do not publish an exhaustive list of all 18 (Cohort 1) or 34 (Cohort 2) cities.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: Because no Haryana-specific Rakshak activity was found, there is correspondingly no Haryana government response, DRSC engagement, or municipal approval process to report for this program specifically. What can be said is that the programme's core value proposition — youth audits escalating to civic-authority approvals — depends on responsive state and municipal infrastructure bodies (PWD, municipal corporations, RTOs) being willing to act on IRC/MoRTH-guideline-based audit findings; Cohort 1's 23+ approvals across 18 cities shows this model can generate real official uptake elsewhere in India. Whether Haryana's civic bodies — Gurugram Metropolitan Development Authority, Municipal Corporation of Faridabad, or the Haryana PWD — have engaged with, or would be receptive to, a Rakshak-style audit-to-fix advocacy process is untested in the public record reviewed here. Given Haryana's demonstrated administrative willingness on other road-safety fronts (the Road Safety Fund, cashless-treatment scheme, and the district-committee apparatus built around the 2026 hit-and-run amendment), there is no obvious structural reason Haryana's civic bodies would be less receptive than peer states to Rakshak-style engagement — but this is an inference, not a documented fact, and should be presented to stakeholders as an open opportunity rather than an established pipeline.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Haryana's presence in Project Rakshak's city roster (Cohort 1's 18 cities or Cohort 2's 34 cities) could not be confirmed from any source found in this research; Crashfree India's own programme page does not publish a complete city list, so this should be treated as an open question for direct confirmation with Crashfree India rather than a settled fact in either direction.

focus_areas.name: SATARK (ANPR Enforcement Technology)
focus_areas.relevance: SATARK is one of only three cities where Crashfree India's ANPR enforcement technology is confirmed live, and Gurugram — Haryana's own gig-and-commerce hub and Crashfree India's headquarters city — is one of them, alongside Bengaluru (the original Trinity Circle pilot, launched Sept 2025) and Jaipur. This makes SATARK the most concretely operational of Crashfree India's four programs in Haryana specifically, in contrast to the still-diagnostic hit-and-run work, the pre-launch gig-rider program, and the unconfirmed Project Rakshak footprint. The mechanism, as documented on Crashfree India's own blog for the Bengaluru pilot (the closest available public description of how SATARK operates), pairs ANPR cameras with a live lookup against a city traffic police database (challan, PUC, insurance status) and displays results on an LED billboard at a high-traffic junction within seconds — a model built jointly by Cars24 and Crashfree India with Bengaluru Traffic Police as the launch partner. Independently, Haryana-focused press reported in August 2026 that Gurugram had rolled out 'Haryana's first AI-powered smart traffic warning screen' at Sohna Chowk, displaying real-time pending-challan and PUC-expiry information as vehicles pass — a description that matches the SATARK billboard model very closely, though that coverage (sourced from a viral social-media video) did not itself name Cars24, Crashfree India, or 'SATARK' as the operator. Separately, Gurugram Police had already deployed a different, unrelated ANPR system (Staqu Technologies' 'JARVIS' software, reported Oct 2024, flagging fake/stolen/blacklisted plates) — meaning Gurugram has at least two distinct AI-vehicle-recognition deployments, which is worth distinguishing carefully rather than conflating.
focus_areas.progress: Per Crashfree India's own reporting (treated as ground truth per this task's brief), SATARK has scanned 5.5+ lakh vehicles and found compliance issues in 48%+ of them, enabling 600+ police interceptions, combined across its three live cities (Jaipur, Gurugram, Bengaluru) — figures that were recognised by the Supreme Court Committee on Road Safety at IIT Bombay's National Road Safety Technology Conclave. Independent, city-disaggregated confirmation of Gurugram's specific share of those numbers was not found in this research; the aggregate figures come from the organisation's own reporting rather than an independently-sourced, per-city breakdown in press coverage. The National Road Safety Technology Conclave itself was independently confirmed to have occurred 25-26 August 2026 at IIT Bombay, jointly organised with the ITS India Forum, convening Transport Commissioners, SSP Traffic officers, RTOs, PWD and highway engineers from 21+ states — a real, credible venue for the kind of technology recognition described in the brief, though the specific SATARK citation at that event was not separately verified via independent press in this research. On the ground in Gurugram, the closest independently-documented parallel is the August 2026 'AI smart traffic warning screen' at Sohna Chowk, which shows the same real-time challan-display behaviour as SATARK's billboard model, suggesting the deployment is visible and functioning in the city even where local press has not yet attributed it by brand name to Cars24/Crashfree India specifically.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: SATARK's Gurugram deployment sits within Haryana's broader, and comparatively active, embrace of AI-based traffic enforcement technology: the state's traffic police had already partnered with Staqu Technologies on JARVIS-based fake-plate detection by October 2024, with Police Commissioner Vikas Kumar Arora publicly crediting the system for identifying 1,500 suspect vehicles within weeks of rollout at just two checkpoints — evidence of institutional willingness in Gurugram to adopt and publicly endorse ANPR-based enforcement tools generally. CARS24's own 'Great Indian Challan Crisis' report (2025) found Gurugram collecting roughly Rs 10 lakh/day in traffic fines via 4,500+ daily challans, underscoring both the scale of the enforcement problem and the commercial/civic rationale for AI-assisted compliance tools in the city. The National Road Safety Technology Conclave's framing — 'from Reactive Response to Predictive Intelligence,' with a stated caution that technology must be 'certified, proven, and implemented correctly by the relevant authorities' rather than treated as a silver bullet — is a relevant policy-tone signal for how seriously state-level technology adoption is being scrutinised nationally, Haryana included. No explicit Haryana state government policy statement, budget allocation, or legislative reference to SATARK specifically (as opposed to AI traffic enforcement generally) was found in this research; the strongest available willpower signal is operational/administrative (police adopting and praising ANPR tools) rather than legislative or ministerial.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: SATARK is confirmed live in Gurugram per Crashfree India's own brief, one of only three cities (with Bengaluru and Jaipur) where the ANPR enforcement billboard system is currently operational, making it Crashfree India's most concretely active engagement with Haryana of the four focus programs; independent local press has documented a closely matching AI challan-display screen at Gurugram's Sohna Chowk (Aug 2026) without yet attributing it by name to Cars24/Crashfree India, which is a gap worth closing with direct confirmation from the organisation or Gurugram Traffic Police.

telangana.political_context: A. Revanth Reddy (Congress) has served as Chief Minister of Telangana since 7 December 2023, heading the state's first Congress government since Telangana's 2014 creation. Cabinet portfolios were allocated shortly after, with the CM personally retaining Municipal Administration & Urban Development (MAUD), General Administration, and Law & Order (i.e., Home/Police), plus all unallocated portfolios -- meaning the same office controls both statewide enforcement and Hyderabad's urban civic administration (GHMC oversight sits under MAUD), a pattern also seen in Bihar, Jharkhand, Tamil Nadu, Assam, and Haryana. Mallu Bhatti Vikramarka serves as Deputy Chief Minister and Finance Minister, giving him direct control over the treasury account into which the new Road Safety Cess revenue flows; he presented the state Budget in March 2025 and continues in the role (Deccan Chronicle, South First, ANI). The full December 2023 cabinet portfolio list rests primarily on a single South First article, with Komatireddy Venkat Reddy (Roads and Buildings), Ponnam Prabhakar (Transport), and N. Uttam Kumar Reddy (Irrigation and CAD, Food and Civil Supplies) independently cross-checked. On the bureaucratic side, Sanjay Jaju, IAS (1992 batch) became Chief Secretary on 26 June 2026, succeeding K. Ramakrishna Rao, and is set to remain in service until February 2029 (Deccan Chronicle, The News Minute). C. V. Anand, IPS, took charge as Telangana DGP on 1 May 2026 -- moving from the bureaucratic-facing post of Special Chief Secretary (Home) -- and immediately announced plans for a dedicated Traffic Management and Road Safety Bureau. That bureau, TG-TMARS (Telangana Traffic Management, Road and Rail Safety Bureau), was formally created by Government Order on 24 September 2026 (one day before this research pass), to be led by an officer of Additional DGP/IG rank across four wings (Traffic Management, Road & Rail Safety, Administrative, and Vigilance & Standards); DGP Anand said the bureau would help address roughly 8,000 road deaths recorded in Telangana in the preceding year, but no director has yet been named in any source found. Six senior IPS officers, including Mahesh Bhagwat (who held the ADG Railways & Road Safety post in 2024 before moving to ADG/DGP-rank Law & Order) and V. C. Sajjanar, were promoted to DGP rank in April 2026 while remaining in their existing postings (Newsmeter, The Hans India). On road infrastructure, K. Ilambarithi, IAS, was named State Transport Commissioner effective 31 October 2025 (moving from Secretary, MA&UD), and was still active in that post chairing a transport-tax rationalisation meeting reported by Deccan Chronicle on 31 July 2026. R. V. Karnan, IAS, has been GHMC Commissioner since mid-2025 (the fourth commissioner in roughly ten months at that point) and remained in post through Ganesh Festival preparations in September 2026; he is on record (Telangana Today, 1 September 2025) stating over 90% of Greater Hyderabad's potholes had been repaired under a 'Road Safety Drive'. Sarfaraz Ahmad, IAS, has served as HMDA Metropolitan Commissioner since June 2024 and held the post as of the most recent independently corroborated reporting found (2025); his 2026 status could not be independently reconfirmed in this pass and should be checked before outreach. HYDRAA Commissioner AV Ranganath, IPS, remains in post as of this audit but under continuing litigation: a Telangana High Court single judge ordered his removal (27 July 2026, citing 63 contempt cases), a division bench stayed that order (1 September 2026), and the matter is listed for a further hearing on 3 November 2026; Advocate General A. Sudarshan Reddy personally represented the state/Ranganath's position in that litigation (Telangana Today). In the Assembly, the Telangana Legislative Assembly passed the Motor Vehicles Taxation (Amendment) Bill, 2025 on 2 January 2026, creating a one-time Road Safety Cess on new vehicle registrations effective 1 March 2026, expected to raise roughly Rs 300 crore annually for black-spot rectification, speed cameras, Automated Driving Testing Stations, and District Road Safety Committee strengthening; Transport Minister Ponnam Prabhakar personally tabled it, citing incidents such as the Vikarabad bus accident. Roads and Buildings Minister Komatireddy Venkat Reddy has separately and repeatedly (2024 through 2026) named specific black-spot locations for remediation (e.g., 17 sites on the Hyderabad-Vijayawada highway; Choutuppal and Chityal) and has allocated Rs 500 crore toward flyovers/bridges at accident-prone black spots. On the opposition benches, K. Chandrashekar Rao (KCR), BRS, remains the formally recognised Leader of Opposition (since 16 December 2023) but has drawn sustained Congress criticism in 2026 for near-total Assembly non-attendance (Congress alleged just 3 days of attendance over roughly 1,000 days, per a September 2026 protest); his son K. T. Rama Rao (KTR) is BRS's more publicly active Working President and the more realistic opposition point of contact. At the city-police operational level, Joint CP (Traffic) Hyderabad D. Joel Davis, IPS, has built a genuinely data-driven, recurring road-safety profile across 2026 -- publishing accident and child-casualty statistics, school-zone infrastructure-gap surveys (school-zone signage, speed-limit signage, zebra crossings), and enforcement drives -- making him one of the most concretely engaged road-safety officials identified for Telangana in this pass.

Every citation in this document is a real, working URL from an allowed source tier: official Government of Telangana department pages (telangana.gov.in, transport.telangana.gov.in, pred.telangana.gov.in, hmda.gov.in, siddipet.telangana.gov.in), NHAI's own site (nhai.gov.in), a statutory-text reference site for Motor Vehicles Act Section 215 (devgan.in), and mainstream Indian press with clear bylines (Deccan Chronicle, Telangana Today, The Hans India, The South First, Siasat, Newsmeter, The News Minute, Sakshi Post, Punjab Kesari English, Social News XYZ). No Wikipedia, social-media or unsourced-blog citation was retained in this rebuild; where the prior-pass Telangana document had relied on Wikipedia for a cabinet portfolio-holder's name, that citation was either replaced with an official government source where one was directly fetched and confirmed the same fact (e.g. the Transport Commissioner, confirmed independently on two of the department's own official pages), or the underlying fact was left exactly as previously stated but flagged rather than re-asserted with a Wikipedia citation carried forward into new tables. The single most significant finding of this pass is the formal establishment, via a Government Order issued 24 September 2026 (one day before this audit) and reported identically across five independent allowed-tier outlets, of the Telangana Traffic Management, Road and Rail Safety Bureau (TG-TMARS) — a major, brand-new statewide traffic-enforcement institution with its own dedicated funding stream (40% of traffic fine collections), directly superseding the prior document's 'still not operational as of August 2026' status for the same initiative. A second significant finding is the direct, official confirmation (via two of the Transport Department's own pages) that K. Ilambarithi, IAS — not Surendra Mohan, as an earlier, now-superseded news report had suggested — is the current Transport Commissioner. A third finding is that HMDA's Metropolitan Commissioner, Sarfaraz Ahmad, IAS, now holds his HMDA post concurrently with the Managing Directorship of Hyderabad Metro Rail Limited, per a directly-dated news report. As in the companion Bihar document, the road_ownership_matrix, road_lifecycle and quick_reference_matrix tables are the document's own interpretation — applying mandates and structures already independently cited elsewhere in this document to a specific road category, lifecycle stage, or problem type — rather than being drawn from one single source that states each pairing verbatim; the 'Likely bottleneck'/'Implementer' columns reflect the document's own assessment/judgment in places, not always an empirically measured finding. focus_areas.name: Crash Compensation (Hit-and-Run Scheme)
focus_areas.relevance: Telangana's hit-and-run accident count has risen steadily and gradually every year for which MoRTH has data: 2,041 (2020), 2,065 (2021), 2,099 (2022), 2,126 (2023), and 2,408 (2024, provisional) — a roughly 18% increase over five years with no year-on-year decline. Against that rising caseload, the state's use of the dedicated Hit-and-Run Compensation Scheme (₹2 lakh death / ₹50,000 grievous injury, no fault needing proof) was essentially dormant for the scheme's first two full financial years on record: zero claims registered and zero paid in both FY2022-23 and FY2023-24, even though the scheme itself dates to 2022. Uptake only appears from FY2024-25 (45 registered / 10 paid) and grows in the current FY2025-26 (261 registered / 150 paid as on 28 Feb 2026). This mirrors, and in its early years exceeds, the national uptake problem CrashFree India's brief documents (~12% national claim rate against hit-and-run crash counts, ~90% of a sampled pending cohort stalled purely on documentation gaps). Telangana also sits alongside other compensation friction points relevant to this program: nationally ~10.46 lakh MACT (fault-based) claims remain pending, worth ~₹80,455 crore and averaging 3.6 years to resolve, and Telangana's own High Court has separately been directed by the Supreme Court to publish a live dashboard of unclaimed Motor Accident Claims Tribunal deposits, a related but distinct compensation-processing backlog signal for the state's judicial-administrative pipeline. Together, these facts frame Telangana as a state with rising hit-and-run incidence, a multi-year scheme-adoption lag, and broader compensation-claims friction — a plausible, evidence-backed case for outreach even though CrashFree India's current program brief does not name Telangana.
focus_areas.progress: The clearest concrete development is national, not Telangana-specific: MoRTH notified an amendment to the Hit-and-Run Victim Compensation Scheme around 2-3 March 2026 that digitises the whole claims pipeline. It mandates a GI Council-run electronic portal for applications, enquiry reports and sanction letters; redesigns Forms I-III to capture Aadhaar numbers, bank details and eDAR (electronic Detailed Accident Report) references; requires District Road Safety Committees (DRSCs) to maintain month-wise electronic statistics, evaluate local implementation, take corrective action, and improve claimant awareness; and adds a new paragraph 13A giving State Road Safety Councils (chaired, in Telangana, by the Chief Minister) a monthly review role over district-level statistics with power to issue directions. This is precisely the district-to-state review architecture CrashFree India's own brief flags for 2026. Whether Telangana's DRSCs and State Road Safety Council have yet acted on these new powers could not be confirmed: publicly posted DRSC minutes from several Telangana districts (Siddipet, Kamareddy, Nizamabad, Karimnagar) show routine accident-prevention and black-spot discussion but no located agenda item specifically addressing hit-and-run claim backlogs or the new portal. The claims data itself (45 paid FY24-25 rising to 150 paid by Feb FY25-26) suggests real, if recent and modest, on-the-ground improvement in either awareness or documentation support, but no Telangana Transport Department press release, circular or news report explaining the mechanism behind that improvement was found — this is a genuine gap rather than a confirmed causal story.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: The strongest and most current Telangana policy signal in this space is institutional rather than compensation-specific: on 24 September 2026 the state government created TG-TMARS (Telangana Traffic Management, Road and Rail Safety Bureau), a dedicated police bureau under the CM-chaired State Road Safety Council, headed by an Addl. DGP/IGP-rank officer, with about 300 personnel reassigned and dedicated "road accident response officers" posted at every police station to move crash victims within the golden hour. It is funded through a new Traffic Management Fund drawing 40% of fine collections for technology, vehicles and enforcement, with publicity spend capped at 5%. While TG-TMARS's stated mandate centres on traffic management, highway patrol, crash investigation and rail safety rather than compensation-scheme administration, its existence under the same State Road Safety Council that the 2026 amendment newly tasks with reviewing hit-and-run scheme statistics suggests institutional machinery now exists in Telangana that could plausibly absorb that oversight role. Separately, continued Supreme Court pressure nationally (an April 2025 rebuke of the Centre over delays in the related cashless-treatment scheme, summoning the Union Transport Secretary) and the Telangana High Court's own 2025 compliance filings on unclaimed MACT deposit dashboards indicate judicial-level pressure is actively touching Telangana's accident-compensation ecosystem, even where the hit-and-run scheme itself is not named. No Telangana-specific ministerial statement, assembly question, or budget line dedicated explicitly to the Hit-and-Run Scheme was located in this research; the willpower signal here is institutional and adjacent rather than scheme-specific.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Telangana is not named anywhere in CrashFree India's own Hit-and-Run Scheme brief; the program's pilot is Jaipur (Rajasthan), with feeder relationships in Gurugram, Bihar and Delhi's DRSC work. There is no evidence of CrashFree India engagement, presence, or planned expansion into Telangana for this program at this time.

focus_areas.name: Gig Rider Safety
focus_areas.relevance: Hyderabad is one of India's largest gig-delivery and tech hubs, with dense two-wheeler-based food, grocery and quick-commerce delivery operations (Swiggy, Zomato, Blinkit, Rapido, Uber and others), making it a natural candidate market for exactly the population CrashFree India's Gig Rider Safety initiative studies. Local reporting corroborates that this is a live, documented problem rather than a hypothetical one: The Hans India reported gig and platform-worker unions in Hyderabad publicly demanding "safety-first" regulation for private bike-taxi and delivery work, citing passenger-safety and driver-welfare gaps in fast-growing app-based mobility; separate local news covered a delivery worker's fatal road accident in Tolichowki, Hyderabad, and a helmet-distribution safety drive organised in April 2026 at IKEA Rotary by a civil-society coalition (Sarvejana Foundation, NTT DATA Business Solutions, the Telangana Facility Management Council and Telangana Police) explicitly targeting two-wheeler and delivery-worker fatalities. Academic and grey literature also frames the underlying occupational-safety mechanism relevant to Telangana's context: a peer-reviewed systematic review (ScienceDirect) on last-mile delivery worker occupational risk, and repeated commentary on algorithmic time pressure driving rule-breaking among delivery riders nationally. CrashFree India's own Gig Rider Safety program, however, is described on its website as "coming soon" / "being built," run in partnership with Cars24 and the Indian Road Safety Council, national/thematic in scope so far (interviews Nov 2025–Jan 2026, a 300+-rider two-wheeler survey, full findings due mid-October 2026), with no state-specific pilot city named anywhere in the material reviewed.
focus_areas.progress: On the CrashFree India side, progress remains pre-launch and research-stage: the program page frames itself as the output of "the research that started it all" (a completed Gig Rider Safety Report) but gives no state or city breakdown, and full findings are not due until mid-October 2026 — after this research date of 26 September 2026. No Telangana-specific fieldwork, survey site, or partnership was identified in any CrashFree India material. Independently, Telangana's own policy track has moved further and faster on the gig-worker front generally, though on welfare rather than road-safety specifically: the state Cabinet approved the draft Telangana Gig and Platform Workers (Registration, Social Security and Welfare) Bill, 2025, intended for tabling in a Budget session, covering an estimated 4+ lakh workers (delivery partners, ride-hailing drivers, logistics personnel). It creates a Gig and Platform Workers Welfare Board with unique worker IDs, a Welfare Fund Fee charged to aggregators (with escalating penalties for non-payment, from ₹50,000 up to five times the pending amount), due-process protections against arbitrary termination (seven-day written notice), and a right for workers to query the automated systems that set their fares, earnings and ratings. PRS Legislative Research's bill summary confirms these provisions. This is a substantive, further-along legislative track than CrashFree India's still-forming national research project, but its content is about labour/welfare rights rather than crash/road safety specifically, and no clause explicitly addressing helmet use, working-hour fatigue limits, or two-wheeler crash prevention was found in the reporting reviewed.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: Telangana shows genuine, above-average policy motion on gig-worker issues generally: cabinet approval of a dedicated Gig and Platform Workers Bill is further than most Indian states have gone (contemporaneous coverage frames it alongside Karnataka's ordinance as one of the two leading state-level frameworks in India). This signals real willpower to regulate the gig economy, which is adjacent to — though not the same as — road-safety willpower specifically. Concrete road-safety action for gig/delivery riders in Telangana currently looks civil-society- and police-led rather than legislated: the April 2026 IKEA Rotary helmet drive is a one-off multi-stakeholder event, not a recurring state program, and no state budget line, GO (Government Order), or ministerial statement earmarking funds specifically for gig-rider road safety (as distinct from general worker welfare) was located. The broader institutional build-out of TG-TMARS (see Crash Compensation section) could eventually intersect with delivery-rider enforcement and education given its traffic-management mandate, but no source reviewed draws that link explicitly. Overall, the willpower signal here is real but currently channelled into labour/welfare regulation rather than into crash-prevention-specific programming for two-wheeler gig workers, leaving room for an outreach angle bridging the two. Notably, none of the reporting reviewed on the Telangana Gig and Platform Workers Bill mentions road-safety metrics, crash data, or coordination with Telangana Police or the newly formed TG-TMARS bureau, suggesting the welfare and safety tracks are, at least publicly, running on separate policy rails within the same state government rather than being integrated into a single road-safety-for-gig-workers agenda. That separation is itself a useful outreach data point: it implies an opening for a program like CrashFree India's to connect the two, rather than duplicating work already underway.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Telangana/Hyderabad is not named as a location for CrashFree India's Gig Rider Safety work; the program remains national/thematic in scope, pre-launch, with full findings not due until mid-October 2026. No state-specific pilot has been announced.

focus_areas.name: Project Rakshak
focus_areas.relevance: Telangana is a plausible candidate for youth-led road-safety audit work of the kind Project Rakshak runs: it has a large registered vehicle population (over 1.8 crore per the TG-TMARS announcement), a 32,000 km road network, and a substantial student/engineering-college base in and around Hyderabad and other cities. Notably, Telangana Today reported Hyderabad was ranked India's safest metro for driving in an "India Road Safety Report 2026," a comparative-safety datapoint that could inform whether CrashFree India treats Telangana cities as lower-priority (already relatively safe) versus other black-spot-dense metros where Rakshak cohorts currently concentrate. Project Rakshak itself is CrashFree India's flagship youth-led initiative: Cohort 1 (2025) ran 31 student teams across 18 cities auditing 120+ high-risk locations, with 23+ civic-authority approvals for recommended interventions; Cohort 2 (2026-27) scaled sharply, with orientation completed 3 September 2026 for 95 teams across 3 tracks, 34 cities and 32 institutions, reaching 136 colleges, backed by new MoUs with NOSPlan and SIT Pune, and with roughly 15 more teams expected to join from Jaipur, Pune and Srinagar. Whether any Telangana city sits among either cohort's city list is the central open question for this section, and it could not be conclusively resolved from public material.
focus_areas.progress: CrashFree India's own Project Rakshak page names Cohort 1 examples including a blackspot audit at Chuttagunta Circle in Guntur — which is in Andhra Pradesh, not Telangana, and should not be mistaken for a Telangana engagement. The same page's blog section separately profiles "Gangadhara Tilak Katnam, the Pothole Man of Hyderabad," an independent Hyderabad citizen who self-funded fixing 1,100+ potholes; this appears to be editorial/inspirational content about civic action in Hyderabad rather than a confirmed official Rakshak team or city assignment, and should not be read as evidence Telangana is an active Rakshak site. Beyond CrashFree India's own materials, no independent news coverage, college press release, or local-government notice confirming a Hyderabad, Warangal, or other Telangana-based Rakshak team, audit, or MoU was found despite targeted searches combining "Rakshak" with Hyderabad, Warangal and Telangana. The full 34-city roster for Cohort 2 does not appear to be published in any single accessible source (CrashFree India's website gives cumulative counts — 34 cities, 32 institutions, 136 colleges — without naming all of them). This is a genuine, material gap for outreach purposes: it cannot currently be said with confidence whether Telangana participates in Rakshak Cohort 2 or not. The Safer Mobility Impact Fellowship (SMIF) 2026-27, CrashFree India's associated fellowship track that produced Project Rakshak, is based at Cars24's Gurugram headquarters per its own job listing, with no Telangana-based fellowship post or regional office referenced, which is a mild further indicator (though not proof) that current organisational infrastructure for Rakshak is concentrated in the north/west rather than in south India.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: Telangana's state and district administrative apparatus already performs some of the underlying civic functions Project Rakshak's model depends on — black-spot identification, inter-departmental coordination on accident-prone locations, and now (via TG-TMARS, established 24 September 2026) a dedicated bureau with crash-investigation and highway-patrol functions plus a State Road Safety Council chaired by the Chief Minister. District Road Safety Committee activity is visible and routine: for example, the Karimnagar Additional Collector was reported directing officials toward regular inspections of accident-prone locations, a task structurally similar to what Rakshak's student teams do independently. This suggests a receptive institutional environment for a program like Rakshak, in principle, even though no direct state government partnership, MoU, or invitation involving CrashFree India was found. No Telangana state education department or AICTE/JNTU-affiliated engineering college system announcement referencing Project Rakshak specifically was located either, meaning any potential linkage between the state's existing road-safety administrative culture and CrashFree India's youth program remains unconfirmed and would need to be established rather than assumed. Telangana also has a dense concentration of engineering and planning institutions (IIIT-Hyderabad, JNTU-Hyderabad, NIT Warangal, and numerous private engineering colleges) comparable in scale to states already hosting Rakshak cohorts, meaning the absence of a confirmed Telangana team is unlikely to reflect a shortage of eligible institutional partners; it more plausibly reflects either non-selection in this cohort's outreach or a genuine gap in this research rather than a structural barrier.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Telangana's presence in Project Rakshak's city roster is unconfirmed in either direction. Cohort 1's only located Telangana-adjacent reference (Guntur) is actually in Andhra Pradesh, and a Hyderabad blog profile appears editorial rather than programmatic; the full 34-city Cohort 2 list is not published anywhere located in this research, so Telangana's inclusion or exclusion cannot be verified.

focus_areas.name: SATARK (ANPR Enforcement Technology)
focus_areas.relevance: Telangana, and Hyderabad specifically, is structurally different from SATARK's current target cities in that it already operates large-scale, independent ANPR/AI traffic-enforcement infrastructure rather than lacking one. Reporting describes Hyderabad as having "the densest camera network in South India," and in 2025 the city (via IIIT-Hyderabad's Applied AI Research Centre and Centre for Visual Information Technology, with iHub-Data support) piloted and then unveiled (announced publicly in July 2026) "VIOLA," an AI system that installs low-cost dashcams (₹8,000–₹10,000 each) in existing police patrol vehicles, uses ANPR to identify vehicles, and detects helmet violations, triple-riding, wrong-side and other offences, auto-forwarding verified cases to Telangana Police's e-Challan system — functionally very similar to what CrashFree India's SATARK program (built with Cars24) does in its current LIVE cities (Bengaluru, Gurugram, Jaipur). This makes Telangana simultaneously highly relevant as a proof point that state-police/academic partnerships can build ANPR-AI capability without CrashFree India, and a lower-priority near-term SATARK expansion target because the core capability gap SATARK addresses elsewhere may already be substantially filled in Hyderabad. TG-TMARS, the new state traffic bureau (established 24 September 2026), further entrenches this by explicitly equipping its highway patrol units with ANPR, dashboard cameras and speed detectors as part of its founding mandate.
focus_areas.progress: VIOLA's reported performance: Telangana Police verification found approximately 96% of AI-flagged violations were confirmed accurate by human officers reviewing the footage (a human-in-the-loop model, per INAI Operations Manager Prithvi Jonnada, described as placing "the human as the primary actor rather than replacing humans"), and IIIT-Hyderabad describes the system as having become "one of the largest contributors to challan generation" for Telangana Police. Developers are reportedly in discussions to expand VIOLA to police departments outside Telangana and are adding speed-detection and road-infrastructure-defect (pothole, missing lane markings) identification using the same dashcam footage — meaning Telangana is currently a technology exporter in this space rather than an importer. At the same time, reporting from November 2025 on Hyderabad's existing (pre-VIOLA) city-wide ANPR camera network across its three police commissionerates (Hyderabad, Cyberabad, Rachakonda) found over 26,000 wrong challans were issued in the first ten months of 2025 — officials characterised this as under 1% of total challan volume, attributing errors to detection/plate-reading sync failures, smudged or ambiguous plates, and "double challaning" from overlapping cameras, with manpower for manual verification (350-500 challans/day per constable) badly outstripped by daily challan volume (10,000+/day). This indicates Hyderabad's ANPR infrastructure operates at a scale and error-management maturity stage well beyond SATARK's current pilot cities, which are earlier in adoption.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: Telangana's policy willpower on ANPR/AI enforcement technology is demonstrably strong but channelled through in-state academic-police partnership rather than external NGO/corporate collaboration: VIOLA is a Telangana Police plus IIIT-Hyderabad (a Telangana-based, state-linked technical institute) initiative, and TG-TMARS institutionalises continued investment via its Traffic Management Fund (40% of fine collections ring-fenced for technology, vehicles, and enforcement). This suggests the state sees ANPR/AI enforcement as core, ongoing infrastructure rather than a pilot needing outside help. The November 2025 wrong-challan controversy also shows this is a live public-accountability issue in the state — officials are on record acknowledging the error rate and describing remedial steps (camera recalibration, e-challan dispute portal, stronger manual verification) — meaning any future CrashFree India engagement in Telangana on ANPR would need to differentiate itself from an already-scaled, already-scrutinised local system, most plausibly around quality-control/error-reduction methodology or cross-validation rather than introducing the base technology. There is no public record of Telangana state government funding directed at CrashFree India or Cars24 specifically, nor any indication the state has sought outside ANPR vendors given VIOLA's low per-unit cost (₹8,000–₹10,000 per dashcam) and in-house academic pipeline; the state's apparent preference is to build and own this capability locally rather than adopt an externally provided model, which is a relevant strategic signal for how CrashFree India might frame any Telangana-directed SATARK outreach — likely as a peer/knowledge-exchange proposition rather than a vendor-style rollout.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Telangana does not appear among SATARK's current LIVE cities (Bengaluru, Gurugram, Jaipur) or UNDERWAY cities (Pune, Rajkot, Gandhinagar, Thiruvananthapuram). Given Telangana's own mature, large-scale ANPR/e-challan infrastructure and its home-grown VIOLA AI system, the state looks like a low near-term priority for a SATARK-style capability-introduction pilot, though it could be a relevant partner for a different kind of engagement (e.g., benchmarking, error-reduction, or cross-state technology exchange).

maharashtra.political_context: Maharashtra is governed by the Mahayuti coalition (BJP + Shiv Sena-Shinde + NCP-Ajit Pawar faction) formed after the November 2024 state assembly election. Devendra Fadnavis (BJP) became Chief Minister for a third time on 5 December 2024. On 28 January 2026, Deputy CM Ajit Pawar (NCP), who held Finance, Planning, State Excise and other portfolios, died along with four others when the Learjet 45 charter aircraft carrying him to Baramati crashed on approach in low visibility (confirmed via India's official news service and independently by Reuters wire coverage). Finance and Planning passed to CM Fadnavis the same week, and NCP's Legislature Party unanimously chose Pawar's widow, Sunetra Pawar (sitting Rajya Sabha MP), as his successor; she was sworn in as Deputy CM on 31 January 2026, becoming Maharashtra's first woman Deputy CM, and was allotted State Excise, Sports & Youth Welfare, and Minority Development & Aukaf -- not Finance or Planning. Multiple Jan-Feb 2026 reports indicated NCP intended to press for Finance/Planning to be handed to the party after the 2026-27 budget session (which began 23 February 2026); this research pass could not independently confirm whether that handover has actually occurred by September 2026, so Fadnavis should be treated as the last-confirmed holder of Finance & Planning pending fresh verification (flagged). Deputy CM Eknath Shinde (Shiv Sena) continues to hold Urban Development, Housing, and Public Works (including Public Undertakings), and is ex officio Chairman of both the MMRDA Authority and MSRDC by virtue of the Urban Development portfolio. PWD itself remains split between a 'Public Works (excluding Public Undertakings)' wing held by a dedicated PWD minister (Shivendrasinhraje Bhosale) and a 'Public Works (including Public Undertakings)' wing nominally under Shinde -- a jurisdictional split distinctive to Maharashtra among the states researched so far. CM Fadnavis is widely reported to personally direct the Home Department and state police (a July 2026 government press item shows him directly instructing the Home Department and police on enforcement matters), consistent with the established pattern of the CM retaining Home. The Chief Secretary is Rajesh Aggarwal (in post since 1 December 2025, reconfirmed current via an 18 March 2026 Raj Bhavan record of him meeting the Governor). On the road-safety governance front, the single most significant development this pass is that Maharashtra's statutory State Road Safety Council -- dormant since 3 April 2023 -- finally reconvened on 23 September 2026 (its 13th meeting, 1,267 days after the 12th), with Transport Minister Pratap Sarnaik directing coordinated action across police, PWD and health departments amid 1,17,070 accidents and 50,488 deaths recorded statewide since the Council's last sitting. Sarnaik's ministry also announced a slate of initiatives the same week: a digital 108/private ambulance integration platform, mandatory road-safety audits with 10% of the PWD budget earmarked for safety, trauma-centre expansion, a PM-RAHAT cashless-treatment rollout, and an 11-district 'Zero Fatality District' programme, alongside a reported 6% year-on-year decline in fatalities for Jan-Jul 2026 vs the same 2025 period. Separately, Transport Commissioner Vivek Bhimanwar's office issued a 11 February 2026 circular declaring 2026 the 'Save Two-Wheeler Riders & Pedestrians Year' following a state-level review (two-wheeler riders were 57% of 2025's 15,549 road deaths, pedestrians 21%). On the opposition side, the formal post of Leader of the Opposition in the Legislative Assembly has been vacant since 23 November 2024 because no single opposition party crossed the 10%-of-seats threshold after the 2024 rout of the Maha Vikas Aghadi bloc; Congress's Vijay Wadettiwar functions as the de facto senior opposition voice as Congress Legislature Party leader (a status distinct from the vacant formal LoP title) and has repeatedly criticised the government on infrastructure and fund-allocation issues, including the Mumbai-Pune Expressway 'Missing Link' closure. The opposition's position weakened further in June 2026 when six of Shiv Sena (UBT)'s seven Lok Sabha MPs defected to merge with CM ally Eknath Shinde's Shiv Sena, cementing the Mahayuti's dominance and reducing Uddhav Thackeray's parliamentary strength to three MPs -- a realignment that also reduces the number of distinct opposition channels Crashfree India can engage for cross-party road-safety advocacy. Given India's Seventh Schedule division of subjects, roads, transport and police sit substantially on the State List, making Maharashtra's state government and its departments (rather than the Union) the primary point of leverage for most road-safety interventions, with the Union mattering mainly for National Highway stretches, the Motor Vehicles Act framework, and centrally sponsored schemes.

governance_bodies.name: Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC / MCGM)
governance_bodies.mandate: Municipal governance for Greater Mumbai, including construction, maintenance and safety of the city's municipal road network, drains, and civic infrastructure -- one of India's richest civic bodies by budget.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Approximately 1,950 km of the roughly 2,000 km of roads within Greater Mumbai are BMC-maintained municipal roads (the remaining c. 50 km being State Highway stretches under PWD), per BMC's own City Development Plan documentation. governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: City Engineer's department (Roads & Traffic); ward-level Assistant Engineers for local road maintenance and complaint resolution.

governance_bodies.name: Public Health Department -- Maharashtra Emergency Medical Services (MEMS) & Trauma Care
governance_bodies.mandate: Institutional home for pre-hospital emergency response and trauma care, operating the Maharashtra Emergency Medical Services (MEMS) '108' free ambulance programme statewide.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None (health/trauma-care role, not road ownership).
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Minister, Public Health -> Public Health Department secretariat -> MEMS programme management (a state-run/PPP-supported ambulance dispatch and operations structure) -> district Civil Surgeons for hospital-side trauma-centre coordination.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: MEMS ambulance fleet -- 937 ambulances deployed phase-wise statewide (233 Advanced Life Support/ALS and 704 Basic Life Support/BLS units), per the Public Health Department's own scheme page.
governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Runs the 108 toll-free, 24x7, free-of-cost ambulance dispatch system on a 'Golden Hour' response strategy (patient to nearest hospital within the first hour); trauma/injury cases account for 13.32% of all 108 call reasons statewide, per the department's own published utilisation data. At the 23 September 2026 State Road Safety Council meeting, the Health Department was directed to help bring 108 and private ambulances onto a single digital dispatch platform, to support an air-ambulance policy for expressways/coastal routes/remote areas, to support trauma-care centres within every 50 km, and to implement the PM-RAHAT scheme for cashless treatment up to Rs 1.5 lakh for road-accident victims.
governance_bodies.data_role: One of the core stakeholder departments feeding hospital-side/trauma data into any future integrated crash database; specific iRAD/e-DAR integration for Maharashtra not independently confirmed in the sources reviewed for this pass.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: MEMS's stated ambulance fleet (937 units) relative to Maharashtra's population and geography, and the state's actual average ambulance response time, were not independently benchmarked against a 'Golden Hour'/10-minute national standard in the sources reviewed for this pass -- flagged as a research gap analogous to the documented response-time gaps found in other states' MEMS-equivalent services.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not established from the sources reviewed for this pass; participates in the State Road Safety Council's coordination cadence.

governance_bodies.name: Maharashtra State Disaster Management Authority (MSDMA) / Disaster Management Department
governance_bodies.mandate: Statutory authority under the Disaster Management Act 2005 for hazard management (landslides, floods, cyclones, earthquakes, droughts, lightning), early-warning coordination, preparedness/capacity-building, mitigation, and relief coordination statewide; institutionally linked to mass-casualty response (e.g. major bus/truck crashes, bridge collapses) rather than routine single-vehicle crash response, which sits with Police/Health.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: The Authority is chaired ex officio by the Chief Minister (per the Disaster Management Act 2005's standard state-authority structure, with the Chief Secretary as CEO); day-to-day departmental administration runs through a dedicated Minister for Disaster Management/Relief & Rehabilitation.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: State Emergency Operations Centre; coordination links to the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), IMD, INCOIS and CWC for early warning.

Inference (not directly documented): as the politically dominant figure in a coalition that has just absorbed a competitor party's MPs and lost a coalition partner's leader, his near-term bandwidth for a discretionary reform like road-safety-council revival is likely secondary to coalition management, which is consistent with that revival having been driven publicly by the Transport Minister rather than the CM's office.

maharashtra.source_audit: This pass rebuilt Maharashtra's governance_bodies, road_ownership_matrix, road_lifecycle, district_level_actors, quick_reference_matrix and funding_architecture sections from scratch, applying Crashfree India's source-tier policy strictly: allowed sources used were (a) official government sources -- pwd.maharashtra.gov.in, transport.maharashtra.gov.in, mahapolice.gov.in, mumbaipolice.gov.in, highwaypolice.maharashtra.gov.in, mmrda.maharashtra.gov.in, sdma.maharashtra.gov.in, rajbhavan-maharashtra.gov.in, msrdc.in (a wholly state-government-owned corporation's own official site), and zpthane.maharashtra.gov.in/zpnagpur.maharashtra.gov.in for Zilla Parishad structure; (b)/(c) mainstream Indian press with clear bylines -- Free Press Journal, The Quint, Tribune India, Nagpur Today, and newsdrum.in -- used where no equivalent government source was locatable (e.g. the State Road Safety Council's meeting history and the 23 September 2026 meeting's specific directives, which are reported but not yet published as a government notification/minutes document as of this pass). No Wikipedia, social-media or unsourced-blog citations were used anywhere in these six sections; every citation carries a real, working URL. The single most significant finding of this pass is that Maharashtra's State Road Safety Council -- documented in the prior pass as inactive since 3 April 2023, with an unconfirmed promise of a 'first week of July 2026' revival meeting -- in fact met on 23 September 2026 (its 13th meeting, 1,267 days after the 12th), per Free Press Journal's same-week coverage; this closes what had been flagged as the state's single largest documented road-safety-governance failure, while opening a new, immediate-term question (whether the meeting's specific commitments are implemented) that could not be assessed given the two-day gap between that meeting and this pass's reference date. A number of named office-holders carried over from the prior pass's Wikipedia-sourced key_positions entries (Chief Secretary Rajesh Aggarwal's personal RSF chairmanship; the DGP and Mumbai CP's identities) were independently re-verified in this pass against each office's own official government website rather than Wikipedia, and are now sourced accordingly. One office-holder claim from the prior pass (State Transport Commissioner Vivek Bhimanwar) was found, via an official Raj Bhavan Maharashtra notice, to be stale -- he was sworn in as MPSC Chairman on 18 February 2026 -- and his successor's name could not be confirmed in this pass; per the sourcing policy's 'omit anything that cannot be referenced' rule, no successor's name is asserted, and this is carried instead as an explicit research gap. This pass's WebSearch quota was exhausted before every open question (e.g. the current PWD Engineer-in-Chief, the current NHAI Regional Officer for Maharashtra, and Maharashtra's district-specific Road Safety Committee notification) could be independently resolved; these are disclosed as genuine, budget-limited gaps in the research_gaps array rather than silently omitted or guessed at. Several official Maharashtra government domains (msrdc.in, mmrda.maharashtra.gov.in, sdma.maharashtra.gov.in, pwd.maharashtra.gov.in, transport.maharashtra.gov.in) intermittently returned HTTP 503 errors on direct re-fetch during this pass; where a fact from one of these domains could not be re-fetched directly but had already surfaced in a dated, 2026-specific search-engine snippet drawn from that same official domain (e.g. MMRDA's Metropolitan Commissioner), it was retained with a note of the transient fetch failure rather than discarded, since the underlying evidence (the domain, the URL, and the dated official content) remained intact.
research_gaps: The current State Transport Commissioner's name is unresolved: Vivek L. Bhimanwar (the previously documented holder) was sworn in as Chairman of the Maharashtra Public Service Commission on 18 February 2026 per an official Raj Bhavan Maharashtra notice, but no successor's name as Transport Commissioner could be independently confirmed before this pass's search budget was exhausted. This should be directly confirmed with the Transport Department before any outreach material names the office-holder.
The Engineer-in-Chief, PWD (a position distinct from the Additional Chief Secretary and the two parallel Secretary posts identified in this pass) was not named in the sources reviewed for this pass.

NHAI's specific Regional Officer(s) for Maharashtra (the state is served by at least a Mumbai/Navi Mumbai regional office) were not named in the sources reviewed for this pass; only the office's physical address was confirmed.

Maharashtra's District Road Safety Committee-specific Gazette notification (composition, and whether it follows the Supreme Court Committee on Road Safety's post-2022 uniform national template) could not be independently located in this pass -- a genuine gap given that the analogous notification was locatable for Bihar in a separate research pass.

Whether Maharashtra's District Road Safety Committees continued to function as a reporting channel during the State Road Safety Council's 1,267-day (April 2023-September 2026) inter-meeting gap, or whether district-level coordination lapsed alongside the state-level Council, is unresolved and is a strong candidate for direct field verification by Crashfree India.

Whether the specific commitments made at the 23 September 2026 State Road Safety Council meeting (single-platform ambulance dispatch, air-ambulance policy, trauma centres every 50 km, electronic weigh-in-motion systems, PWD's 10%-safety-fund earmark) are actually implemented, and on what timeline, could not be assessed in this pass since the meeting occurred only two days before this research pass's reference date (25 September 2026) -- a natural follow-up checkpoint for Crashfree India in early-to-mid 2027.

The precise division of rural-road responsibility between MRRDA (PMGSY-funded works) and each district's own Zilla Parishad Works Department for non-PMGSY rural roads was not fully resolved -- specifically, whether Maharashtra has a state-funded rural-road scheme directly analogous to other states' Mukhya Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana-type programmes, and if so, which agency executes it, is unconfirmed.

MSDMA's own road-safety-specific programming (as opposed to its general natural-hazard mandate) was not documented on the Authority's own website in this pass; its road-safety relevance to Crashfree India's work is inferred rather than directly evidenced, and is a candidate for direct follow-up with the Authority.

Maharashtra Emergency Medical Services (MEMS)'s actual average ambulance response time was not independently confirmed against the 'Golden Hour' standard the programme cites -- unlike some other states' MEMS-equivalent services, where a documented response-time gap (e.g. national 10-minute standard vs. an actual multi-times-longer average) was found in this multi-state research programme.

No Section A (recurring, personally-engaged road-safety champion) individual was independently identified for Maharashtra in this pass, echoing the prior pass's finding; worth checking directly with civil-society groups (e.g. SaveLIFE Foundation's Maharashtra-specific engagement) or IIT Bombay road-safety research groups, neither of which surfaced concretely in the sources reviewed.
