focus_areas.name: Crash Compensation (Hit-and-Run Scheme)
focus_areas.relevance: Maharashtra sits at the centre of the hit-and-run compensation gap Crashfree India's brief describes nationally. MoRTH data given to the Lok Sabha (Unstarred Question No. 6419, answered 2 April 2026) shows Maharashtra recorded 6,049 hit-and-run accidents in 2020, rising to 8,987 in 2023 before a provisional drop to 6,485 in 2024 -- consistently the second-highest count of any state after Madhya Pradesh across most of these years. Yet claims filed against the Hit-and-Run Compensation Scheme are strikingly disproportionate to this volume: 2 claims registered (1 paid) in FY2022-23, 21 (10 paid) in FY2023-24, 47 (49 paid, reflecting carryover) in FY2024-25, and 135 (58 paid) in FY2025-26 as of 28 February 2026. Against 6,485-plus accidents in a single year, 135 claims is an uptake rate under 2% -- one of the widest accident-to-claims gaps among major states, consistent with the ~12% national uptake and ~90% documentation-stalled rate CFI's brief cites. Compounding this, Maharashtra reports zero cumulative Rah-Veer (Good Samaritan) awardees as of MoRTH's 12 February 2026 answer -- a state with among India's highest accident volumes and no recorded Good Samaritan recognition. On the separate MACT compensation track, the ~Rs 459 crore Crashfree India cites as unclaimed in Bombay's Motor Accident Claims Tribunal deposits is corroborated by the Supreme Court's May 2025 suo motu proceeding on unclaimed MACT/labour-court compensation nationwide, in which Bombay's high court jurisdiction reported the single largest unclaimed sum (Rs 459.10 crore) of the participating jurisdictions (Gujarat Rs 282 crore, Allahabad Rs 239 crore, Goa and Calcutta far smaller). Together these figures describe a Maharashtra paradox: very high crash and death volumes, but weak administrative throughput on every compensation and recognition channel MoRTH and the courts track.
focus_areas.progress: Maharashtra's road-safety machinery has moved more on prevention and enforcement than on the hit-and-run compensation process itself. The Supreme Court's May 2025 order (In Re: Compensation Amounts Deposited with Motor Accident Claims Tribunals and Labour Courts) required all high courts, including Bombay's, to collect claimants' Aadhaar, PAN and bank details, enable direct bank transfers, and build a digital dashboard for pending payouts -- directions that apply to the Rs 459 crore in Bombay's MACT deposits, though no Maharashtra-specific disbursement drive or compliance report under this order was found in public reporting. On the hit-and-run track specifically, MoRTH notified the Compensation to Victims of Hit and Run Motor Accidents (Amendment) Scheme, 2026 in March 2026, introducing a digital 'Portal' (run by the General Insurance Council) through which Claims Settlement Commissioners and Claims Enquiry Officers must now process applications -- a structural change aimed at the documentation bottleneck CFI's brief blames for ~90% of stalled claims nationally. Locally, Mumbai Traffic Police's own 2023 crash data (published with Bloomberg Philanthropies' Initiative for Global Road Safety in early 2025) found hit-and-run collisions made up 38% of all fatal crashes on Mumbai's roads that year, pedestrians the majority of victims -- underscoring the scale of the underlying problem even as claims filings stay minimal. No public evidence was found of a Bombay High Court PIL specifically targeting the Rs 459 crore unclaimed deposit or Maharashtra's near-zero hit-and-run claims uptake; this remains a gap between the scale of the problem and dedicated litigation or audit activity in the state.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: Maharashtra's transport establishment has shown visible political energy on road safety in 2026, concentrated on prevention (helmets, two-wheeler and pedestrian safety) rather than the hit-and-run compensation pipeline. In February 2026 the state Transport Commissioner declared 2026 'Save Two-Wheeler Riders and Pedestrians Year' following 15,549 road deaths in 2025 (two-wheeler riders 57% of the total), with helmet enforcement at toll plazas, radar-based interceptor vehicles and pedestrian infrastructure upgrades. At the state's 13th Road Safety Council meeting on 23 September 2026, Transport Minister Pratap Sarnaik reported a 6% year-on-year fatality decline for January-July 2026, announced an 11-district 'Zero Fatality District' initiative, and directed 10% of Public Works Department funds toward road safety, alongside a digital ambulance-linkage platform and a proposed air-ambulance policy. Neither 2026 initiative references the hit-and-run scheme, the Rah-Veer scheme's zero-awardee record, or the unclaimed MACT deposits -- the visible willpower is aimed at crash prevention and emergency response, not post-crash compensation administration. Earlier, CM Eknath Shinde's 2024 pledge (after the high-profile Worli BMW hit-and-run case) to pursue harsher penalties regardless of an accused's influence reflects episodic, case-driven attention rather than sustained administrative reform of claims processing. The 2026 national amendment to the Hit-and-Run Scheme, which pushes district-level review through District Road Safety Committees rolled up to the state, gives Maharashtra a fresh, MoRTH-mandated structure through which its low claims uptake could now be surfaced -- but no public evidence yet shows Maharashtra's DRSCs acting on this mandate.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Maharashtra is not named among Crashfree India's Hit-and-Run Scheme pilot or feeder geographies (Jaipur is the pilot; Gurugram, Bihar and Delhi's DRSC work are the feeders), but it is explicitly named in CFI's brief for the ~Rs 459 crore of unclaimed MACT compensation sitting in Bombay's tribunal deposits -- a separate, MACT-track issue distinct from the Hit-and-Run Scheme itself.

focus_areas.name: Gig Rider Safety
focus_areas.relevance: Maharashtra is arguably the most consequential state for Crashfree India's Gig Rider Safety program, even though the program (launched February 2026) has so far operated at a national/thematic level with no confirmed state-specific pilot. Mumbai and Pune are among India's largest quick-commerce and food-delivery hubs, employing large numbers of two-wheeler gig riders for platforms including Swiggy, Zomato, Zepto and Blinkit; Maharashtra's Labour Department has begun mapping gig and platform workers across hundreds of e-commerce platforms operating in the state as part of a new regulatory framework. This scale overlaps directly with the risk profile CFI's brief describes: gig riders are a living case study in India's two-wheeler safety crisis, facing delivery-time pressure and greater on-road risk than other motorists. Maharashtra's own 2025 data reinforces this -- two-wheeler riders were 57-60% of the state's 15,549 road deaths that year -- and the state has separately made two-wheeler safety its top 2026 policy priority via the 'Save Two-Wheeler Riders and Pedestrians Year' campaign. Nationally, gig-rider risk drew direct government intervention in January 2026, when the Union Labour Ministry pressed major delivery aggregators -- platforms with major Maharashtra operations -- to abandon rigid 10-minute delivery targets after safety concerns; several platforms complied. That intervention was national, but its practical effect concentrates in dense urban gig markets like Mumbai and Pune. Maharashtra is not yet named in CFI materials as a Gig Rider Safety pilot state, but its combination of gig-worker scale, new state labour legislation, and acute two-wheeler fatality data make it a natural, currently untapped expansion geography for the program.
focus_areas.progress: Progress specific to gig rider safety in Maharashtra is best understood as adjacent regulatory and market activity rather than direct CFI program delivery, since Crashfree India's Gig Rider Safety initiative has stayed at a national, research-and-advocacy stage since its February 2026 launch with no confirmed Maharashtra deployment identified. The clearest state-level development is the Maharashtra Gig and Platform Workers Rights and Protection Bill, 2026, issued by the state government on 3 July 2026, which creates a legal framework for registering gig and platform workers, mandates social-security contributions from aggregator platforms, and establishes grievance-redressal and implementation mechanisms -- a welfare-focused bill with no explicit road-safety provisions, but one that creates a formal state registry of the gig workforce a future road-safety intervention could build on. Separately, and nationally rather than Maharashtra-specifically, major delivery platforms operating heavily in Mumbai and Pune dropped explicit '10-minute delivery' branding and deadline pressure in January 2026 following Union Labour Ministry intervention, citing rider safety concerns after weeks of gig-worker protests demanding better pay and the scrapping of arbitrary delivery-time targets. No Maharashtra-specific crash data on gig/delivery riders, no state-level gig-rider road-safety audit, and no CFI program activity targeting Mumbai or Pune gig riders was identified in public reporting as of September 2026. Maharashtra has the regulatory building blocks (a worker registry, aggregator obligations) and the market scale, but no publicly documented road-safety-specific intervention yet connects the two.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: Maharashtra has shown real, if indirect, policy willpower on gig-worker welfare in 2026, though this legislative energy has not yet been explicitly channelled into gig-rider road safety. The Gig and Platform Workers Rights and Protection Bill, 2026, places Maharashtra among a small group of Indian states (alongside Telangana and Jharkhand, which have pursued similar draft legislation) moving to formally regulate platform work, and the Labour Department's mapping exercise reportedly covers hundreds of thousands of workers across more than 300 platforms. This willingness to legislate on gig-worker conditions runs parallel to, but does not yet intersect with, the state's separate and vigorous 2026 push on two-wheeler road safety -- the 'Save Two-Wheeler Riders and Pedestrians Year' campaign and the State Road Safety Council's September 2026 directives on helmet enforcement, interceptor vehicles and PWD-funded infrastructure. No public statement from the Maharashtra Transport Department, Labour Department or Chief Minister's office was found explicitly linking the new gig-worker welfare law to two-wheeler crash risk, or proposing gig-rider-specific road-safety measures (mandatory protective gear for delivery riders, delivery-time-pressure limits tied to safety, or employer liability for rider crashes). At the national level, the Union Labour Ministry's January 2026 intervention on 10-minute delivery targets shows Delhi-level willingness to treat rider safety as a labour-policy matter aggregators must answer to -- a precedent Maharashtra's own new regulatory apparatus could invoke, though no public evidence shows it has done so yet.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Crashfree India's Gig Rider Safety program remains national/thematic in scope with no confirmed Maharashtra-specific pilot; Mumbai and Pune's status as major Indian gig-delivery hubs, combined with Maharashtra's new 2026 gig-worker welfare law, make the state a strong candidate for future program expansion, though no such expansion has been announced.

focus_areas.name: Project Rakshak
focus_areas.relevance: Maharashtra has a direct and explicit role in Project Rakshak's second cohort (Rakshak 2026), primarily through Pune. Crashfree India's own materials name Pune as one of three cities -- alongside Jaipur and Srinagar -- expected to contribute 15 additional teams to Cohort 2 in the coming weeks, and the program's institutional partnerships include an in-progress MoU with SIT Pune (Symbiosis Institute of Technology), a Pune-based engineering institution. Pune is also independently established as a road-safety-research hub in Maharashtra: Symbiosis Skills and Professional University (SSPU) set up a dedicated road-safety and accident-research centre of excellence with J.P. Research India as far back as 2019, giving Pune's academic ecosystem pre-existing infrastructure a Rakshak partnership could draw on. Cohort 2, whose orientation began on 3 September 2026, scaled sharply from Cohort 1's 31 locations and 18 cities to 95 teams across 34 cities and 19 states and union territories, spread over three tracks, 32 institutions and 136 colleges reached -- a five-fold-plus increase in team count that places Maharashtra's participation (via Pune) inside a much larger, more institutionally diverse national footprint than the program's first year. Maharashtra's relevance to Rakshak is reinforced by the state's own hit-and-run and two-wheeler crash burden: the youth-led infrastructure audits Rakshak conducts (identifying crash hotspots, engineering fixes, and advocacy with civic authorities) map directly onto the road-engineering gaps implicated in Maharashtra's high two-wheeler and pedestrian fatality shares.
focus_areas.progress: Project Rakshak's concrete, dated progress in 2026 is substantial at the national level, and Maharashtra's Pune-anchored participation sits inside that broader trajectory. Cohort 1 (2025) produced a 115-page report documenting youth-led road-safety audits across 18 cities, with 23-plus civic approvals secured for the on-ground fixes teams proposed -- a track record that gave the program credibility heading into its second year. Cohort 2's orientation, held 3 September 2026, formally launched with 95 teams across 34 cities and 19 states and union territories, organised into three tracks and drawing from 32 institutions and 136 colleges reached in total outreach; per Crashfree India's brief, this cohort already includes Pune-based participation and an in-progress MoU with SIT Pune, with 15 further teams expected imminently from Jaipur, Pune and Srinagar. Crashfree India has also built out Rakshak's public profile through events such as a National Road Safety Forum at IIT Delhi, mentor-led expert sessions, and content distributed via its own channels, positioning the program as the flagship of its 'Engineering' workstream (crash-hotspot audits) alongside its Emergency, Enforcement and Behavioural-Change pillars. No independently-bylined news coverage (distinct from Crashfree India's own website and social channels) was found specifically documenting a completed SIT Pune MoU signing, a named Pune team roster, or a Pune-specific crash-hotspot audit result; the Pune dimension of Rakshak's progress is confirmed primarily through Crashfree India's own materials rather than third-party reporting.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: Project Rakshak's model depends less on state government policy willpower than on civic-agency and institutional buy-in at the city level, and here Maharashtra's Pune shows favourable, if still-developing, conditions. Pune's civic and educational institutions have a documented history of engaging with road-safety research -- SSPU's 2019 centre of excellence with J.P. Research India, and SIT Pune's in-progress MoU with Rakshak itself -- both signalling an institutional environment receptive to youth-led road-safety collaboration, the currency Rakshak trades in (civic-agency cooperation, engineering-expert mentorship, public advocacy for fixes). At the state level, Maharashtra's 2026 'Save Two-Wheeler Riders and Pedestrians Year' campaign and the State Road Safety Council's September 2026 push for regular road-safety audits, a 'Safe System Approach', and district-level accident-data mapping create a policy environment broadly aligned with what Rakshak teams do on the ground; Transport Minister Pratap Sarnaik's explicit September 2026 call for 'regular road safety audits' is a rare instance of state-level rhetoric matching a CFI program's actual activity almost exactly, even though no direct coordination between the state government and Project Rakshak has been publicly confirmed. Whether Pune's municipal or district authorities have committed to acting on any specific Rakshak team's audit findings -- the kind of civic approvals that made Cohort 1 credible in other cities -- remains undocumented in public sources as of this research window, marking the clearest gap between Maharashtra's stated road-safety ambitions and confirmed, program-specific follow-through.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Pune's role in Project Rakshak is explicitly confirmed in Crashfree India's own program materials: an in-progress MoU with SIT Pune (Symbiosis Institute of Technology) and Pune named as one of three cities (with Jaipur and Srinagar) expected to contribute 15 additional Cohort 2 teams, giving Maharashtra a direct, named stake in the program's second-year expansion, though independent press confirmation of these specifics was not found.

focus_areas.name: SATARK (ANPR Enforcement Technology)
focus_areas.relevance: Pune's explicit 'underway' status as one of SATARK's next four ANPR enforcement installations gives Maharashtra a direct, though still-pending, stake in Crashfree India's newest and most technology-intensive program. SATARK, built with Cars24 and live in Bengaluru, Gurugram and Jaipur since its September 2025 launch, uses automatic number-plate recognition to shift traffic enforcement from manual, reactive penalty issuance toward automated, preventive detection -- exactly the kind of infrastructure Pune's own severe two-wheeler and pedestrian safety numbers argue for. Pune, alongside Mumbai, is one of Maharashtra's and India's largest urban centres by traffic volume and two-wheeler density, and the state's 2025 data showing two-wheeler riders at 57-60% of all road deaths gives Pune's traffic-enforcement gaps outsized relevance to any technology aimed at catching the violations -- speeding, red-light running, and (via plate capture) hit-and-run identification -- that lead to fatal crashes and bear directly on the compensation-claims gap described elsewhere in this brief. Cars24's own separate road-safety partnership with the Indian Road Safety Campaign (IRSC), reported in February 2025, already runs pothole-reporting and first-responder training initiatives with a described presence in Pune, suggesting Cars24-linked road-safety activity in the city predates the SATARK rollout and could provide an operational bridge for it. As with Project Rakshak's Pune connection, the SATARK Pune installation is confirmed by Crashfree India's own brief rather than by independent news reporting identified in this research, making it the single most CFI-specific, least externally-verified claim in this Maharashtra dossier.
focus_areas.progress: SATARK's national rollout has moved from a single-city pilot to a multi-state expansion within roughly a year, and Pune sits inside the newest wave of that expansion rather than the proven, already-live cohort. The program went live in Bengaluru in September 2025, then expanded to Gurugram and Jaipur, establishing a three-city operational base before four additional installations -- Pune, Rajkot, Gandhinagar and Thiruvananthapuram -- were placed into an 'underway' (not yet live) status, per Crashfree India's own account. This places Pune roughly a year behind Bengaluru in program maturity, with no public reporting found confirming an installation date, a partnering enforcement agency (Pune City Traffic Police or Pune Municipal Corporation), or first-phase results specific to Pune. Independently, Cars24's broader road-safety collaboration with the Indian Road Safety Campaign -- including pothole-reporting via its consumer app and first-responder (CPR/first-aid) training for its own staff -- was reported in February 2025 with a described presence in Pune, giving Cars24 an existing operational footprint in the city that may explain why Pune was selected for SATARK's second wave ahead of many other large Indian cities. Separately, Pune already has its own long-standing citizen-reporting traffic app, 'Satark Punekar', run by Pune Traffic Police for citizens to photograph and report violations -- a same-named but institutionally distinct tool from Crashfree India's SATARK ANPR platform. This is a notable naming collision: a casual web search for 'SATARK Pune' surfaces the Pune Traffic Police citizen app rather than CFI's program, and outreach material should take care not to conflate the two.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: SATARK's expansion depends on the willingness of local police and municipal traffic authorities to adopt automated, ANPR-based enforcement -- a different form of 'policy willpower' from the legislative and budgetary announcements dominant elsewhere in this brief, and one where Maharashtra's public record is thinner. The state's 2026 'Save Two-Wheeler Riders and Pedestrians Year' campaign explicitly calls for 'radar-equipped interceptor vehicles' and technology-based speed and helmet enforcement, and the September 2026 State Road Safety Council meeting directed the Transport, Police, Public Works and Health departments to make 'greater use of modern technology' to cut fatalities -- rhetoric broadly compatible with an ANPR system like SATARK, though neither announcement names SATARK, Cars24, or Crashfree India specifically, and neither confirms Pune Traffic Police's participation in the CFI-Cars24 rollout. Cars24's pre-existing IRSC partnership activity in Pune (pothole reporting, staff first-responder training, reported February 2025) suggests at least an operational relationship between Cars24 and the city already exists, which could ease the path for the ANPR installation once it moves from 'underway' to live. No Maharashtra Transport Department or Pune Police statement referencing SATARK, ANPR enforcement partnerships with Cars24/Crashfree India, or a target date for the Pune installation was identified in public reporting as of this research window -- the strongest evidence of policy alignment is the state's independent, parallel push for 'modern technology' in enforcement, not a confirmed institutional commitment to this specific program.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Pune is explicitly named in Crashfree India's brief as one of four cities (with Rajkot, Gandhinagar and Thiruvananthapuram) where a SATARK ANPR installation is 'underway' following the live Bengaluru-Gurugram-Jaipur rollout -- an accurate, CFI-confirmed but not-yet-live status that independent press reporting was not found to corroborate.

gujarat.political_context: Gujarat is governed by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which has held power continuously since 1998. Bhupendra Patel has been Chief Minister since 13 September 2021 and was re-sworn in for a second consecutive term on 12 December 2022 after the BJP's landslide win in the December 2022 assembly election, giving the party an outsized majority in the 182-seat Vidhan Sabha. The most consequential recent development is a major cabinet reorganisation: on 16 October 2025 all 16 sitting ministers resigned, and on 17 October 2025 Governor Acharya Devvrat swore in an expanded 26-member Council of Ministers (CM plus 25) at Mahatma Mandir, Gandhinagar, with BJP national president J.P. Nadda in attendance (News on AIR, 17 Oct 2025, https://www.newsonair.gov.in/gujarat-cabinet-reshuffle-all-16-ministers-resign-ahead-of-strategic-reset). This reshuffle came nearly three years into the government's term and just months before municipal corporation and panchayat (local body) elections, which were still unfolding as recently as late September 2026 (BJP was declaring Gandhinagar Municipal Corporation candidates on 25 September 2026, per DeshGujarat), and is widely read as a refresh ahead of the 2027 assembly election. The headline change for road-safety-relevant governance is that Harsh Sanghavi, previously Minister of State for Home, was elevated to Deputy Chief Minister (Gujarat's sixth) and now holds a very large portfolio combining Home (police, jails, border security, prohibition and excise) AND Transport, alongside Law and Justice, Industries, MSME, Tourism and Civil Aviation (News on AIR, 17 Oct 2025; English Gujarat Samachar, 17 Oct 2025, https://english.gujaratsamachar.com/news/gujarat/gujarat-govt-concludes-first-cabinet-meeting-announces-portfolio-allocation-72143635655.html). This concentration of Home and Transport in one Deputy CM is structurally significant for CFI: a single political principal now controls both the traffic-enforcement (police) and vehicle/licensing/road-transport regulatory levers. Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel retained a broad portfolio for himself that includes Roads and Buildings and Capital Projects (effectively the PWD-equivalent department that builds and maintains state roads), plus General Administration, Revenue and Disaster Management, Narmada and Ports. Kanubhai (Kanu) Desai holds Finance and Urban Development & Urban Housing; Kunvarjibhai Bavaliya holds Rural Development; Rushikesh Patel holds Energy/Petrochemicals plus Panchayat and Rural Housing; and Praful Pansheriya (Minister of State, Independent Charge) holds Health, Family Welfare and Medical Education — all confirmed still in these roles as recently as August–September 2026 via multiple dated news items (ANI, Economic Times, FM Bharat, NDTV Profit). On the bureaucratic side, Manoj Kumar Das (1990-batch IAS) became Chief Secretary on 31 October 2025; Dr. Rajender Kumar (2004-batch IAS) was appointed Commissioner of Transport in a 26-officer reshuffle on 23–24 December 2025; Hareet Shukla (1999-batch IAS) has held additional charge as Principal Secretary, Ports & Transport Department since December 2025 and was still active in that capacity in an August 2026 maritime investment event; M. Thennarasan (2000-batch IAS) has been Principal Secretary, Urban Development & Urban Housing since mid-2025 and remained active in that role through August 2026; and P.R. Patelia was promoted to Secretary, Roads & Buildings Department in January 2025 (no subsequent replacement found, though this is the least freshly re-confirmed of the bureaucratic appointments). On policing, Gyanendra Singh Malik (1993-batch IPS, former Ahmedabad Police Commissioner) was appointed Gujarat's Director General of Police on 6 June 2026, a notably fresh appointment, succeeding an in-charge arrangement under Dr. K.L.N. Rao. Despite extensive searching, no named officer could be confirmed as the current ADG/IG (Traffic) — a post that exists on paper under both the Gujarat Road Safety Authority Act, 2018 and the police hierarchy — nor could NHAI's regional officer for Gujarat be named from available press. Overall, the government is politically stable (BJP supermajority, no coalition risk), but is in a period of significant personnel churn at both ministerial and secretary level, meaning CFI should treat every named contact here as provisionally current and re-verify before high-stakes outreach.

governance_bodies.name: Roads and Buildings (R&B) Department, Government of Gujarat
governance_bodies.mandate: Planning, construction and maintenance of state highways, major district roads, government buildings, and (through its Panchayat wing) rural roads; administers the state's own works code and PWD-style engineering manual. Operates under the general Gujarat PWD/R&B administrative framework rather than a single standalone Act.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: State highways, major district roads (MDRs), and government building infrastructure; the R&B (Panchayat) wing also historically executes rural road works including PMGSY works in coordination with GSRRDA.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Chief Minister holds the Roads and Buildings & Capital Projects portfolio (as of the October 2025 cabinet reallocation) with a Secretary (IAS, technical cadre often assisted by a Secretary-rank engineer) heading the administrative side, a Chief Engineer (State Roads) and Chief Engineer (Panchayat/Rural) heading the engineering side, below whom sit Superintending Engineers (zone/circle level), Executive Engineers (division level, one per district roughly), Deputy Executive Engineers and Assistant Engineers (sub-division/section level).
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Works Monitoring System (WMS) cell for R&B; historically linked to GSRDC (for BOT/PPP state highway projects) and GSRRDA (for PMGSY rural roads), though these are separately incorporated entities rather than direct subordinates.

governance_bodies.name: Gujarat Road Safety Authority (GUJROSA), constituted under the Gujarat Road Safety Authority Act, 2018
governance_bodies.mandate: Statutory lead agency for road safety in the state, established by the Gujarat Road Safety Authority Act 2018 to implement the National Road Safety Policy and Gujarat's own road safety policy, coordinate across departments, collect and analyse accident data, set annual accident/fatality-reduction targets, oversee helmet/seatbelt/insurance compliance, sanction road-safety expenditure and victim assistance, and act as secretariat for the State Road Safety Council.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None — a coordinating/policy and funding body, not a road-owning agency.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: The Authority is a 14-member statutory body chaired by the Minister for Transport (Vice-Chairman: Secretary, Transport Department), with members including the Secretaries of Home, Health, Education and Roads & Buildings departments, the Director General of Police, the Managing Director of GSRTC, the Municipal Commissioner of Ahmedabad, the Chief Engineer of NHAI, the Chairman of the Western India Automobile Association, the Transport Commissioner, two nominated road safety experts, and a Chief Enforcement Officer as Member-Secretary. Day-to-day executive functions are headed by a Road Safety Commissioner, who is also the Authority's Chief Executive Officer. Below the state level sits a State Road Safety Council and Executive Committee (chaired by the Additional Chief Secretary, Transport, meeting bimonthly), and at the district level, District Road Safety Committees (DRSC) chaired by the District Magistrate & Collector (meeting fortnightly virtually and monthly in person, per a training-material summary reviewed).
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: State Road Safety Council and Executive Committee; District Road Safety Committees (DRSCs) in every district, chaired by the District Magistrate/Collector.

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Can sanction expenditure from the Gujarat Road Safety Fund for safety schemes, research, training and victim assistance; can set annual accident-reduction targets and coordinate enforcement priorities across departments; cannot itself amend the Motor Vehicles Act or override departmental budgets — its authority is coordinative/advisory-cum-financial rather than a substitute for line departments' own powers.
governance_bodies.data_role: Central state-level repository for road accident data analysis (a dedicated 'Accident data' section exists on its website, gujrosa.gujarat.gov.in/accident-data); intended to be the fusion point for police FIR data, hospital/health data and R&B/NHAI engineering data.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: A Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) audit found that between 2012-13 and 2023-24 only about 87% (₹974.49 crore of ₹1,123.29 crore collected) of traffic-fine compounding fees were actually transferred into the Gujarat State Marg Suraksha Nidhi (GSMSN) Personal Ledger Account that funds the Authority's work, despite a 2006 state directive mandating 100% transfer; the shortfall (~₹148.80 crore) was attributed by the audit to inadequate reconciliation between the police/treasury collection chain and the GSMSN fund, with compliance improving over the period from about 60% (2012-13) to about 88% (2023-24). The CAG recommended tighter monitoring and regular reconciliation.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: State Road Safety Council/Executive Committee: bimonthly (per available secondary summary). District Road Safety Committees: fortnightly virtual meetings and monthly in-person meetings (per the same summary).

governance_bodies.name: Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority (GSDMA) and 108 Emergency Ambulance Service (operated by EMRI Green Health Services, formerly GVK EMRI)
governance_bodies.mandate: GSDMA, constituted under the Gujarat State Disaster Management Act 2003 (in force from 1 September 2003), is responsible for disaster mitigation, preparedness and coordinating emergency relief/response across the state (headquartered in Gandhinagar); road accidents are handled operationally through the 108 Emergency Ambulance Service, run in Public-Private Partnership mode by EMRI Green Health Services, which provides the 'golden hour' pre-hospital emergency response relevant to road-crash trauma survival.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None — an emergency-response/coordination body, not a road-owning agency.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: GSDMA sits under the Chief Minister's Revenue and Disaster Management portfolio; it is governed by a Chief Executive Officer under a Governing Council chaired by the Chief Minister. The 108 service is run by EMRI Green Health Services as the PPP operator under a state contract with the Health & Family Welfare Department, with a state-level Programme/Operations head and district/zonal ambulance dispatch and crew structures across Gujarat.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Gujarat Institute of Disaster Management (GIDM) as GSDMA's training arm; the 108 service maintains its own call-centre and ambulance-fleet operational structure across the state (EMRI operates over 9,600 ambulances across the 17 states it serves, including Gujarat).

focus_areas.name: Crash Compensation (Hit-and-Run Scheme)
focus_areas.relevance: Gujarat is doubly relevant to this program even though it is not a named pilot or feeder geography. First, its hit-and-run claims trajectory is one of the strongest in the country: from a near-standstill of 1 claim registered / 0 paid in FY2022-23, uptake rose to 18/11 in FY2023-24, 678/350 in FY2024-25, and 819 registered / 720 paid by 28 February 2026 in FY2025-26 -- a ~88% paid-to-registered ratio that suggests claims, once filed, move efficiently through the state's district machinery. This sits against a hit-and-run accident count that rose from 1,552 (2020) to a peak of 2,214 (2023) before easing to 1,902 in 2024 (provisional), per MoRTH's Lok Sabha answer. Second, and more unusually, Gujarat carries a specific unresolved liability inside the broader compensation ecosystem: the Supreme Court's 22 April 2025 suo motu judgment (In Re: Compensation Amounts Deposited with MACTs and Labour Courts, 2025 INSC 530) independently corroborates the Crashfree India brief's figure that roughly Rs 282 crore sits unclaimed in Gujarat's MACT deposits (plus Rs 6.6 crore in labour courts) -- a case that originated from a Gujarat retired District Judge's own email to the Chief Justice of India in May 2024. That the figure is verified by an actual Supreme Court order (not just an internal estimate) strengthens its evidentiary weight for outreach purposes. Taken together, Gujarat presents a paradox worth surfacing to donors/partners: strong forward-flow claims processing for hit-and-run victims, alongside a large backlog of stranded historical MACT compensation that the state's own judiciary flagged as a national governance failure.
focus_areas.progress: On the hit-and-run scheme itself, MoRTH notified the Compensation to Victims of Hit and Run Motor Accidents (Amendment) Scheme, 2026 (dated on/around 2-6 March 2026), which restructures the 2022 scheme, introduces a digital portal run by the General Insurance Council for e-filing and tracking, and tightens processing timelines (Claims Settlement Commissioners must now sanction within 15 days of the enquiry report). This is consistent with the brief's note that a 2026 amendment pushes district-level review through District Road Safety Committees (DRSCs), rolled up to the state -- Gujarat's DRSCs are structured under the standard national template (chaired by a Claims Settlement Commissioner, with police, RTO, health and insurance-council representation), which appears to be functioning well enough to produce the state's high FY2025-26 paid/registered ratio. On the unclaimed MACT deposits, the Supreme Court's April 2025 judgment issued pan-India directions -- mandatory Aadhaar/PAN/bank-detail collection, direct bank transfer instead of tribunal deposit, digital dashboards, and coordinated tracing via Legal Services Authorities -- with an initial compliance deadline of 30 July 2025 and a further review fixed for 18 August 2025. We could not find, within available search capacity, a later 2026 status update confirming how much of Gujarat's Rs 282 crore has actually been traced and disbursed since that hearing; this is flagged as a research gap rather than assumed resolved.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: Gujarat is one of a small number of states with a dedicated statutory road-safety body -- the Gujarat Road Safety Authority (GUJROSA), created under the Gujarat Road Safety Authority Act, 2018 -- which functions as a lead coordinating agency across Transport, Home, Roads & Buildings, NHAI, Health, Urban Development and Education departments. That kind of standing, multi-department statutory architecture is unusual among Indian states and, on paper, gives Gujarat more institutional capacity than most to execute a scheme like hit-and-run compensation or DRSC-level review. The state's actual claims-processing numbers (88% paid-to-registered in FY2025-26) are consistent with that capacity translating into real execution rather than remaining paper structure. However, the MACT deposits case complicates a purely positive read: it took a retired judge's personal intervention and a Supreme Court suo motu order -- not proactive GUJROSA or Transport Department action -- to surface and start addressing a decades-deep backlog of Rs 282 crore in stranded compensation. That gap between statutory capacity and follow-through on legacy liabilities is worth naming plainly in outreach materials: GUJROSA/DRSC machinery appears to work well for new claims moving through defined timelines, but institutional willpower to proactively audit and clear historical unclaimed funds seems to have required external judicial pressure rather than internal initiative. We found no Gujarat CM or Transport Minister statement specifically addressing the MACT backlog within the available search window -- another explicit gap.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Gujarat is not named among Crashfree India's hit-and-run scheme pilot (Jaipur, Rajasthan) or feeder geographies (Gurugram, Bihar, Delhi's DRSC work), so there is no confirmed direct CFI program presence in the state for this focus area. It is, however, explicitly named in the brief for its Rs 282 crore unclaimed MACT deposit figure -- a fact now independently corroborated by the Supreme Court's 2025 INSC 530 judgment -- making it a strong illustrative data point rather than an active engagement site.

focus_areas.name: Gig Rider Safety
focus_areas.relevance: Gig Rider Safety is CrashFree India's newest program (started February 2026) and remains national/thematic in scope, but Gujarat's two largest cities are structurally significant to it. Ahmedabad is Gujarat's quick-commerce centre of gravity with roughly 122 mapped dark stores -- about three times any other city in the state -- while Surat, a ~7-million-population diamond-and-textile hub, has around 35 stores and has seen Blinkit (late 2022) and Zepto (early 2023) roll out multi-store launches across Vesu, Athwa, Adajan and City Light. Both cities therefore carry meaningful and growing populations of two-wheeler delivery riders, the exact vulnerable-road-user group this program targets. Gujarat's broader two-wheeler safety context reinforces the relevance: helmet-violation data shows roughly 8 out of 10 fatal two-wheeler riders in Gujarat were not wearing helmets, with 3,015 unhelmeted-rider deaths recorded in 2024, and Ahmedabad alone logged 1,634 fatalities and 3,100+ severe injuries across 6,000+ collisions between 2021 and July 2026, with two-wheeler riders suffering disproportionately higher mortality (665 deaths / 2,236 crashes) than car occupants. Nationally, the program's salience was sharpened in January 2026 when the government directed platforms to withdraw 10-minute delivery guarantees following worker protests over unsafe, time-pressured riding conditions -- a policy shift directly upstream of the crash-risk drivers Crashfree India is studying. No Gujarat-specific rider-safety intervention, data partnership, or platform engagement tied to this program was found in available sources as of the research date.
focus_areas.progress: Nationally, Crashfree India has run NextMile, a road-safety ideathon offering cash prizes, which reportedly generated 250+ policy submissions on themes including gig rider safety and crash-claim compensation, with shortlisted proposals formally submitted to the Government of India. The organization has also opened applications for a Safer Mobility Impact Fellowship (SMIF) Cohort 2026-27, which includes research into gig-worker safety and post-crash legal challenges, and has published LinkedIn-based research framing gig riders as 'a living case study in India's two-wheeler safety crisis,' arguing that official crash datasets do not capture profession-specific risk for delivery workers -- a data gap the program appears to be trying to fill. These are program-building and evidence-generation activities rather than city- or state-level rollouts, consistent with the brief's description of the program as still national/thematic since its February 2026 start (roughly seven months old as of this research). We found no evidence of Ahmedabad- or Surat-specific fieldwork, platform partnerships (e.g., with Zomato, Swiggy, Blinkit, Zepto, or Porter operating in those cities), or Gujarat state-government engagement under this program banner. Separately and nationally, the January 2026 rollback of 10-minute delivery commitments (covered by international wire/feature press) represents an external policy development in the same problem space that Crashfree India could plausibly reference or build on for Gujarat-specific outreach, but no such linkage was found to date. Given the program's youth, an absence of Gujarat-specific activity at seven months is not itself surprising, but it does mean Gujarat currently has no demonstrated foothold in this focus area.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: At the national level, the government's January 2026 intervention to curb 10-minute delivery guarantees demonstrates some regulatory willingness to act on gig-rider safety pressure, but this was a Union government/platform-level move, not a Gujarat state action. We did not find evidence of a Gujarat-specific gig-worker welfare or road-safety policy analogous to platform-worker welfare boards or fee-based welfare cess schemes enacted in some other states (e.g., Rajasthan, Karnataka, both of which have moved on gig-worker social-security legislation). Gujarat's Motor Vehicles Department and GUJROSA machinery discussed under Crash Compensation could, in principle, extend to gig riders -- who fall within the same two-wheeler fatality statistics the state already tracks and reports on (helmet-violation data, corridor-level accident counts in Ahmedabad) -- but no announcement, budget line, or task force specific to gig/delivery riders in Gujarat was located. Gujarat's demonstrated policy energy so far runs toward general road infrastructure and enforcement (see the Crash Compensation and SATARK sections' budget and camera-network findings) rather than toward gig-economy labor conditions specifically. This is a genuine research gap rather than an assessed absence of willpower: it reflects the limits of what surfaced in available search results, and a targeted Gujarat legislative-assembly or Labour Department search (not completed here due to search-budget constraints) could plausibly surface more.

focus_areas.name: Project Rakshak
focus_areas.relevance: Project Rakshak is Crashfree India's youth-led, campus-based road-safety audit program, now in its 2nd edition after Cohort 1 (2025: 31 locations, 18 cities, 23+ authority approvals). Gujarat is relevant as a potential expansion geography given its large higher-education base (IITs, NIDs, and state universities in Ahmedabad, Gandhinagar, Surat and Vadodara) and its acute two-wheeler/pedestrian safety problem documented under the Gig Rider Safety section above -- exactly the kind of high-risk-corridor, youth-audit target the program is designed for. However, based on Crashfree India's own published materials (its Project Rakshak page and 18-city Cohort 1 report), the confirmed Cohort 1 cities we could identify by name are Vijayawada, Indore, Chennai, Mumbai, Varanasi, and Guntur, spanning institutions such as IIT Madras, IIT Indore, IIT BHU, IIT Kharagpur, IIT Delhi, St. Xavier's College Mumbai, School of Planning and Architecture Vijayawada, and Vignan's Foundation. None of Ahmedabad, Surat, Gandhinagar, Vadodara, or Rajkot appear by name in the material we were able to access. The brief states Cohort 2 spans 3 tracks, 95 teams, 34 cities/32 institutions and 136 colleges reached, with MoUs signed with NOSPlan and SIT Pune, and 15 more teams expected from Jaipur, Pune and Srinagar -- but a full city-by-city list for the 34-city cohort was not publicly available, so Gujarat's presence or absence in Cohort 2 cannot be confirmed either way from public sources.
focus_areas.progress: Cohort 1's public materials describe a four-phase methodology (research on a problem area, stakeholder surveys, case-study/solution development, and final report plus authority presentations) applied across the 18 confirmed cities, culminating in a 115-page cross-city audit report documenting recurring infrastructure risks, city-wise findings with photographs, and proposed interventions, framed explicitly as 'the case for scaling Project Rakshak nationwide.' Cohort 2 has scaled substantially per the brief (3 tracks, 95 teams, 34 cities, 32 institutions, 136 colleges reached, institutional MoUs with NOSPlan and SIT Pune, and 15 more teams expected from Jaipur, Pune and Srinagar), suggesting an active recruitment and expansion phase likely still underway as of September 2026. We found no independent press coverage (as distinct from Crashfree India's own official website and channels) confirming city-level rollout details for Cohort 2, and no announcement of a Gujarat college, university, or civic authority joining either cohort. Given that the Cohort 2 expansion explicitly names Jaipur, Pune and Srinagar as sources of additional teams but not any Gujarat city, the current signal -- while not definitive given incomplete public listings -- leans toward Gujarat not yet being part of the active pipeline.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: Gujarat's dense higher-education and civic-tech ecosystem (GUJROSA's own multi-department coordination model, the state's Smart City programs in Ahmedabad, Surat and Gandhinagar, and existing student-body engagement around road safety awards run by GUJROSA itself, e.g. its 'e-Citizen Road Safety Awards') suggests institutional readiness for a program like Rakshak, which pairs students with civic agencies and engineering experts to work high-risk corridors end-to-end. GUJROSA's statutory convening power across Transport, Home, R&B, Health and Education departments could in principle make it easier for Crashfree India to secure the kind of city/institutional approvals Rakshak needs (the brief notes 23+ approvals were required for Cohort 1 alone, implying significant administrative coordination is a prerequisite for scale). Gujarat's own recent road-and-buildings hiring push (3,100 new posts announced March 2026) and elevated share of state budget spent on roads/bridges (7.1% in 2026-27, above the ~4.3% average across states) further suggest a state government with above-average fiscal and administrative bandwidth to support a partnership if approached. However, we found no evidence that GUJROSA, the Gujarat Education Department, or any Gujarat college has engaged with Project Rakshak specifically, so this institutional readiness remains theoretical rather than demonstrated. This is a clear instance where the state's on-paper capacity and fiscal commitment to road safety broadly has not yet been shown to translate into an actual CFI partnership on this particular program.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Gujarat is not confirmed in Project Rakshak's published Cohort 1 city list, and its presence in Cohort 2's 34-city expansion cannot be confirmed or ruled out from available public sources; this should be reported as an open question rather than an inclusion or exclusion.

focus_areas.name: SATARK (ANPR Enforcement Technology)
focus_areas.relevance: SATARK is CrashFree India's ANPR (Automatic Number Plate Recognition) enforcement-technology partnership with Cars24, launched September 2025 in Bengaluru. Per the brief, it is now LIVE in Bengaluru, Gurugram and Jaipur, with four more installations UNDERWAY in Pune, Rajkot, Gandhinagar and Thiruvananthapuram -- meaning Gujarat has two cities (Rajkot and Gandhinagar) in the 'underway' pipeline, more than any other single state in that list. This is a meaningful concentration signal: both Rajkot and Gandhinagar already have a documented base of camera and ANPR infrastructure to build on. Rajkot's Smart City program has installed roughly 1,000 CCTV cameras feeding an Integrated Command and Control Centre, with ANPR already used to auto-generate e-challans from detected violations. Gandhinagar Municipal Corporation has installed 207 cameras including ANPR units as part of its Smart City rollout (Gandhinagar was ranked 9th among India's 2017 Smart City Mission cohort), and Gujarat Police more broadly has deployed a CCTV-based Intelligent Traffic Management System with a dedicated fibre (TTBS) backbone linking city surveillance networks. This pre-existing hard infrastructure plausibly explains why Gujarat surfaced with two 'underway' SATARK sites: the marginal technical lift to integrate a new ANPR enforcement layer is lower where camera networks and e-challan pipelines already exist.
focus_areas.progress: We found no independent news coverage (police statements, launch events, or local press) explicitly naming a 'SATARK' installation in Rajkot or Gandhinagar; this program name does not yet appear to have public-facing coverage distinct from Crashfree India's own materials, which is consistent with it being a young (September 2025-launched), still-scaling partnership roughly a year old as of this research. What we can independently confirm is the underlying municipal ANPR/CCTV infrastructure in both cities described above, which is the kind of base layer a SATARK rollout would plug into rather than build from scratch: Rajkot's roughly 1,000-camera Integrated Command and Control Centre and Gandhinagar's 207-camera network (both already generating automated e-challans) suggest that an 'underway' installation in these two cities is plausibly more about integrating a new enforcement/analytics layer on top of existing hardware than standing up a greenfield camera network, which would typically be a faster and cheaper path to going live than in a city starting from zero. We also found no independent confirmation of the three cities described as already LIVE (Bengaluru, Gurugram, Jaipur) under the SATARK name specifically, though Gurugram separately has its own large-scale, city-led ANPR camera-network initiative (reported at up to 380 cameras) that is a distinct program, not confirmed to be the same as SATARK. Overall, the program's progress in Gujarat cannot be independently verified beyond the brief at this time, and this should be flagged plainly to anyone using this research for external-facing claims.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: Gujarat Police's system-wide investment in CCTV-based Intelligent Traffic Management (with a dedicated fibre network across cities including Gandhinagar) and Rajkot Municipal Corporation's Integrated Command and Control Centre both indicate real, funded institutional commitment to camera-based enforcement infrastructure -- not just a pilot project. Rajkot's own municipal messaging positions it as 'a model Smart City with innovative initiatives,' and its roughly 1,000-camera network already feeds automated e-challan generation, which is functionally similar to what an ANPR enforcement layer like SATARK would need. Gandhinagar's 207-camera network, installed as part of a Smart City Mission ranking of 9th nationally in 2017, likewise reflects nearly a decade of accumulated investment and operational experience in camera-based traffic governance, not a fresh or untested capability. This is a stronger and more concrete willpower signal than a policy statement alone, since it reflects capital already spent on hardware, integration, and staff training rather than an announced intention. Whether that existing capacity translates into willingness to adopt a third-party (Cars24/Crashfree India) ANPR enforcement layer specifically, versus continuing to build enforcement capability in-house or through existing vendors (e.g., the Tata Tele Business fibre/VPN partnership already serving Gujarat Police statewide), is not something we could confirm from public sources. No Gujarat Police or Rajkot/Gandhinagar municipal statement referencing 'SATARK' or a Cars24 partnership was found in any government, police, or press source searched. On balance, the evidence supports a reading of high institutional readiness (infrastructure, budget, prior camera-enforcement experience) but does not yet support a claim of confirmed willingness to specifically adopt the SATARK program -- that remains attributable only to the Crashfree India brief.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Per the Crashfree India brief, both Rajkot and Gandhinagar are named as 'underway' SATARK installations -- the only state with two cities in that category. We were not able to independently verify either installation through public news, government, or police-department sources as of the research date; this should be reported as brief-sourced and not yet independently corroborated.

uttar_pradesh.political_context: Yogi Adityanath (BJP) has been Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh since 19 March 2017, now in his second term following the 2022 election, and remained CM through the state's constitutional Seventh Schedule-driven governance structure at least as recently as 25 September 2026, confirmed via a same-day report of his attendance at the Uttar Pradesh International Trade Show (UPITS-2026) inauguration. His personal portfolio concentration remains the single most extensive found across states researched to date: he directly holds Home, Public Works Department (PWD, Cabinet-rank charge vacant since June 2024), Law, General Administration, Cabinet Affairs, Information & Public Relations, Housing, Revenue, Mining & Geology, Institutional Finance, Planning, Civil Aviation, Food Safety & Drug Administration and other unallotted departments -- 25+ departments overall (Verified, The Print). PWD's Cabinet-rank charge history: Keshav Prasad Maurya (now Deputy CM) held it 19 March 2017 - 25 March 2022, succeeded by Cabinet Minister Jitin Prasada (25 March 2022 - 11 June 2024), who resigned on becoming a Union Minister of State; no Cabinet-rank successor has been appointed since. Minister of State Brijesh Singh (BJP MLA, Deoband) has held the PWD MoS portfolio continuously since 25 March 2022 and is the closest thing to a day-to-day ministerial face for PWD, though independent 2026-dated confirmation of his continuation was limited to lower-tier regional outlets (see flags). The two Deputy CMs -- Keshav Prasad Maurya (Rural Development since 25 March 2022; Food Processing Industries since 19 March 2017) and Brajesh Pathak (Health & Family Welfare, Medical Education since 25 March 2022) -- were reconfirmed in place through the UP cabinet's second expansion on 10 May 2026 (six new ministers inducted, taking the ministry to the constitutional ceiling of 60), a reshuffle that added Bhupendra Chaudhary and Manoj Pandey as Cabinet Ministers and four MLAs as Ministers of State without altering the Transport, PWD or Deputy CM portfolios. The Transport Minister is Daya Shankar Singh, Minister of State (Independent Charge) since 25 March 2022, reconfirmed still in post as recently as 23 September 2026 (Free Press Journal) and notable among all UP political figures for the most consistent, dated, road-safety-specific track record found in this pass -- spanning a December 2025 CM-chaired road-safety review, the January 2026 statewide 'Road Safety Month', and an April 2026 PPP-based bus-station-safety modernisation programme. Chief Secretary Shashi Prakash Goyal (1989-batch IAS, UP cadre) took charge on 1 August 2025, succeeding Manoj Kumar Singh, and is slated to serve until his own retirement in January 2027; no successor or 2026 transfer was found in this pass (absence-of-contradiction only). Rajeev Krishna (1991-batch IPS) was confirmed as UP's first permanent DGP since 2022 on 31 May 2026, ending an extended acting period, and remained active in the role as of 21 September 2026 (Indian Masterminds, addressing new recruits). Below the political layer, a September 2025 IPS reshuffle installed A. Satish Ganesh (1996-batch IPS) as ADG, Traffic & Road Safety Directorate, and he remained in that post and publicly engaged on road-safety technology as of August 2026 (Safe City & Intelligent Mobility India Summit). A parallel September 2025 IAS reshuffle resolved a standing research gap from the prior file: Deepak Kumar, IAS, was named Infrastructure & Industrial Development Commissioner (IIDC) and concurrently CEO of the Uttar Pradesh Expressways Industrial Development Authority (UPEIDA) -- the body that builds and operates UP's high-speed expressway network (Purvanchal, Bundelkhand, Ganga, Agra-Lucknow) where a large share of the state's highest-severity crashes occur -- resolving the prior file's 'UPEIDA CEO unconfirmed' flag. In a further structural shift reported in mid-2026, UPEIDA itself was moved out of the Industrial Development Minister's (Nand Gopal Gupta's) nominal oversight and placed directly under the Chief Minister's Infrastructure Development Department (The Print), meaning expressway safety and construction-quality accountability now runs more directly through the CM's office and IIDC Deepak Kumar than through the Industries portfolio. On the bureaucratic side, Sanjay Prasad (1995-batch IAS) was promoted to Additional Chief Secretary, Home & Confidential in January 2026, making him the senior-most bureaucrat under the CM's own Home portfolio and therefore a central node for traffic-enforcement policy and budget. On the opposition side, Mata Prasad Pandey (Samajwadi Party) has been Leader of the Opposition in the UP Legislative Assembly since 28 July 2024 (PRS Legislative Research), though no road-safety-specific statement by him was found in this pass; Samajwadi Party national president and former CM Akhilesh Yadav has instead been the most visible and recurring critical voice on road/expressway safety, most recently in a 17 September 2026 statement (The Print) alleging systemic construction-quality failures across the Purvanchal, Bundelkhand and Ganga Expressways. Separately, Congress Legislature Party leader Aradhana Mishra 'Mona' delivered a detailed, data-heavy road-safety intervention in the UP Assembly on 13 February 2026 (IANS), citing ~45,000 annual accidents and over 24,000 deaths and demanding engineering audits of black spots, statewide ITMS rollout and a traffic-police staffing fix (state has roughly 9,000 traffic personnel against an estimated requirement of 30,000, per her own figures as reported). As in the other pilot states, India's constitutional Seventh Schedule splits road-related subjects across the Union and State Lists, and because roads, transport and police sit substantially on the State List, Uttar Pradesh's state government and its departments -- not the Union -- are the primary point of leverage for almost all road-safety interventions Crashfree India will pursue in the state, with the Union mattering mainly for National Highway stretches, PMGSY funding rules and the Motor Vehicles Act framework.

governance_bodies.mandate: The state's premier works department: construction, improvement, strengthening and maintenance of State Highways (SH) and Major District Roads (MDR), plus bridges, flyovers and rail-over-bridges (ROBs); also runs a dedicated Road Safety and IDS (road information/data system) programme area under its own portal.

governance_bodies.mandate: A regulatory department implementing the Motor Vehicles Act 1988, Central Motor Vehicle Rules 1989, and State Taxation Acts, regulating road transport, passenger/freight movement, and public bus transport (via UPSRTC); also administers the UP Road Safety Fund Rules 2014 jointly with Police and Finance.

governance_bodies.performance_issues: A CAG Performance Audit of the UP Transport Department (Report No. 5 of 2016, Revenue Sector) examined 44 of the department's 76 audit units (DTOs/RTOs/ARTOs plus the Transport Commissioner's office in Lucknow) for 2015-16 and found deficiencies in monitoring vehicle registration, licence issue/renewal, permits, and collection of taxes/fees/fines, spanning 33 audit paragraphs and about Rs 14.41 crore in identified irregularities; as of mid-2010, 100 inspection reports with 267 unresolved audit observations (about Rs 9.44 crore) were still outstanding. This is an older-vintage report (2016, covering 2015-16); a more recent department-specific CAG performance audit analogous to Bihar's 2025 DTO audit was not located with confirmable content in this pass (a Transport Department chapter dated 2025 was found on cag.gov.in but its content could not be reliably extracted).
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not specified beyond Road Safety Council/Fund Management Committee cadence covered elsewhere in this document.

governance_bodies.name: Home Department / Uttar Pradesh Police (incl. Traffic Directorate)
governance_bodies.mandate: Overall command of law and order and traffic enforcement statewide, under the Home Department (portfolio held directly by CM Yogi Adityanath).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None -- an enforcement body, not a road-owning one. Enforcement decisions (checkpoints, helmet drives, ITMS camera siting) are made at ADG (Traffic & Road Safety) and district SSP/SP level; infrastructure decisions that police influence but don't own require joint sign-off with the road-owning department.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Director General of Police (DGP) heads UP Police. An Additional Director General of Police heads the Traffic & Road Safety Directorate statewide. Below the state level, UP Police is organised into 8 police zones (each headed by an ADG), 18 police ranges (each headed by an IG or DIG), and district units headed by a Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) or Superintendent of Police (SP); each district is further divided into police circles headed by a Circle Officer (CO, DSP rank; a circle typically comprises 3-5 police stations), and circles into Thanas (police stations) headed by Inspectors/Sub-Inspectors. Several large cities (Lucknow, Kanpur, Varanasi, Agra, Ghaziabad, Prayagraj, Noida, and others) have been converted to the Police Commissionerate system, under which a Commissioner of Police holds magisterial as well as policing powers, distinct from the district-SSP model used elsewhere in the state.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Traffic & Road Safety Directorate; State Disaster Response Force (SDRF), organisationally a Police unit rather than reporting to UPSDMA directly (see UPSDMA entry); UP Police Academy and training establishments.

governance_bodies.name: Rural Development Department, Uttar Pradesh Rural Road Development Agency (UPRRDA) and Rural Engineering Department (UPRED)
governance_bodies.mandate: Rural infrastructure and PMGSY (Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana) implementation. UPRRDA is the state's formally designated nodal/implementing agency for PMGSY in Uttar Pradesh, operating under the Rural Development Department. The Rural Engineering Department (UPRED), established 1972, is a separate technical/engineering agency historically tasked with rural (and some urban) engineering works.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Rural roads equivalent to Other District Roads (ODR) and Village Roads (VR) elsewhere -- built and maintained via PMGSY (Union+State Centrally Sponsored Scheme) and any state-funded equivalent schemes; the specific state-funded scheme name/budget line for UP (an MMGSY-equivalent) was not established from the sources reviewed in this pass.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Deputy CM Keshav Prasad Maurya (Minister, Rural Development) and MoS Vijay Laxmi Gautam -> Rural Development Department Secretary/Principal Secretary (not independently named in this pass) -> UPRRDA (as the PMGSY nodal/coordinating agency, with District Programme Implementation Units, DPIUs, headed by an Executive Engineer in each district) -> executing agencies, which per national PMGSY guidelines may include UPRRDA's own technical staff, the Rural Engineering Department (UPRED), or other empanelled technical agencies.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Uttar Pradesh Rural Road Development Agency (UPRRDA) -- the PMGSY nodal agency, responsible for programme coordination across departments, state-level quality control, maintenance-policy development for the PMGSY Core Network, and uniform reporting across executing agencies; Rural Engineering Department (UPRED, est. 1972).

governance_bodies.name: Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs), Uttar Pradesh
governance_bodies.mandate: Rural local self-government under the United Provinces Panchayat Raj Act, 1947 (Gram Panchayats) and the Uttar Pradesh Kshettra Panchayats and Zila Panchayats Adhiniyam, 1961 (the two higher tiers), both amended to conform to the 73rd Constitutional Amendment.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Very limited -- Gram Panchayats can maintain purely internal village streets/drains where GP funds (15th Finance Commission grants, MGNREGA convergence, own tax revenue) allow; cannot independently execute PMGSY-scale road construction, which the state government (via UPRRDA) retains responsibility for even on roads serving Panchayat areas.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Three tiers: Gram Panchayat (village level), Kshettra Panchayat (block level; historically called Kshetra Samiti), and Zila Panchayat (district level; historically called Zila Parishad). The state's own Panchayati Raj Department page lists 75 Zila Panchayats as the district-level count, consistent with UP's 75 administrative districts.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Elected political heads: Pradhan (Gram Panchayat), Block Pramukh (Kshettra Panchayat), Adhyaksha (Zila Panchayat). Administrative/executive counterparts report up the state administrative line (Panchayati Raj Department -> Director -> district cadre), not to the elected head, mirroring the pattern documented in other states.

governance_bodies.name: Urban Development Department and Urban Local Bodies (Nagar Nigams, Nagar Palika Parishads, Nagar Panchayats) and Development Authorities
governance_bodies.mandate: The Urban Development Department sets urban policy and oversees Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), constituted under the Uttar Pradesh Municipal Corporations Act, 1959 (for Nagar Nigams/Municipal Corporations) and the UP Municipalities Act, 1916 (for Nagar Palika Parishads/Nagar Panchayats); separately, Development Authorities (constituted under the UP Urban Planning and Development Act, 1973) handle land-use planning and new-area development for major cities -- e.g. Lucknow Development Authority (LDA), Kanpur Development Authority (KDA, formed 1973), Agra Development Authority (ADA), Varanasi Development Authority (VDA), Ghaziabad Development Authority (GDA), and the separately statute-constituted New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA) and Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority (GNIDA), both under the UP Industrial Area Development Act 1976 (the same Act underpinning UPEIDA).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Municipal roads within ULB limits: 17 Municipal Corporations (Nagar Nigams) including Lucknow, Kanpur, Varanasi, Agra, Ghaziabad and Prayagraj, plus Municipal Councils and Nagar Panchayats statewide, own and maintain roads within their limits; Development Authorities own/plan roads within their development-scheme areas until handover to the relevant ULB, a handover that (per the pattern documented in other states' development-authority relationships) is frequently delayed.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Cabinet Minister A.K. Sharma (Urban Development & Energy) -> Principal Secretary, Urban Development -> Directorate of Local Bodies (for Nagar Nigams/Councils/Panchayats) and separately the individual Development Authorities (each with its own Vice-Chairman/CEO, typically an IAS officer, and a Chairman who in some cases is the Divisional Commissioner or another senior state appointee). Each Nagar Nigam has an elected wing (Mayor plus ward councillors) and a separate administrative wing headed by a Municipal Commissioner (an IAS or senior PCS officer appointed by the state government, not answerable to the elected Mayor for personnel matters) -- e.g. Lucknow Municipal Corporation (LMC) is headed administratively by an IAS-rank Municipal Commissioner with full executive powers, operating alongside but organisationally separate from LDA.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Directorate of Local Bodies; State Urban Development Agency (SUDA); Uttar Pradesh Jal Nigam (water/sewerage); the individual Development Authorities (LDA, KDA, ADA, VDA, GDA, NOIDA, GNIDA, and others for each major city) function as parastatal bodies distinct from -- and sometimes overlapping in jurisdiction with -- the Nagar Nigams.

governance_bodies.data_role: Municipal Engineer/Commissioner is presumptively the "Road" stakeholder in iRAD for municipal-road crashes, by the pattern documented in other states; not independently confirmed for UP in this pass.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: Overlap risk: for a single street in a city like Lucknow or Noida, the Nagar Nigam may own the carriageway/footpath, a Development Authority (LDA, NOIDA, GNIDA) may control an arterial stretch or land-use/setback rules along the frontage, and city Traffic Police controls signalling/enforcement -- a single 'fix this junction' request can require sign-off from three or more institutions, mirroring the pattern documented in Bihar's Patna case. UP's Development Authority landscape is unusually large and fragmented (a distinct authority per major city, plus NOIDA/GNIDA as separate industrial-development authorities), which this pass judges likely increases -- though does not have direct quantified evidence for -- this coordination burden relative to states with fewer or more consolidated development authorities.

governance_bodies.name: Health & Family Welfare Department, Emergency Response & Trauma Care
governance_bodies.mandate: Institutional home for pre-hospital emergency medical response and trauma care, operating through the National Health Mission, Uttar Pradesh (UPNRHM) for scheme implementation, including the 108 (Emergency Medical Transport Service, EMTS) and 102 (patient-referral/maternal-child) ambulance services, and the Uttar Pradesh Trauma and Emergency Network (UPTEN).

governance_bodies.name: Uttar Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority (UPSDMA)
governance_bodies.mandate: Constituted under the Disaster Management Act, 2005 (applied to UP via the state's own disaster-management framework) as the apex state body for disaster policy, planning and coordination; institutionally linked to mass-casualty response (major bus/truck crashes, pile-ups, bridge collapses) rather than routine single-vehicle crash response, which sits with Police/Health.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Chairman: Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath (by statute, the standard pattern for State Disaster Management Authorities under the Disaster Management Act 2005). Vice-Chairman: Lt. Gen. Yogendra Dimri, AVSM (since on or about 15 January 2024, succeeding Lt. Gen. Ravindra Pratap Sahi, AVSM, who served 2018-2024). A CEO/Member-Secretary post exists per the Authority's standard organisational documents, but a specific current named officeholder was not confirmed via a working primary source in this pass (the Authority's own website returned repeated server errors).
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) -- notably, UP's SDRF is organised as a unit of UP Police (headquartered in Lucknow, with Regional Response Centres across Western, Central and Eastern zones covering Bareilly/Moradabad, Lucknow/Etawah, and Ayodhya/Prayagraj/Mirzapur/Varanasi/Gorakhpur respectively) rather than reporting directly to UPSDMA -- a structural point worth flagging since it differs from a model where SDRF reports through the disaster-management authority itself. UP Police's own SDRF page explicitly lists "Road Accident" and "Train Accident" among the disaster categories SDRF responds to, alongside flood, earthquake, fire, and chemical/biological/radiological/nuclear incidents; Aapda Mitra (community-volunteer first-responder training) also operates in the state as part of the national programme.

Permitted uses: road signage and traffic signals; accident-data management systems; ambulance services; corrective measures at accident-prone locations (black spots); traffic-enforcement equipment; driving-test tracks; vehicle-inspection facilities; and traffic-safety-education programmes. Explicit restriction: Fund monies may never be placed in fixed-deposit schemes or used to extend loans.

Road Safety Fund Rules 2014), a CAG audit report, or -- only where tiers 1-3 were unavailable -- a named-byline mainstream Indian press report, marked as tier-4 in the relevant citation's confidence note. Wikipedia was not used as a source anywhere in this pass; where the prior UP document had relied on Wikipedia for cabinet/ministerial facts, this pass either replaced the claim with a fresh government/press source (e.g. the Panchayati Raj Minister and Urban Development Minister claims, now sourced to Zee News and cross-checked cabinet-formation reporting) or explicitly flagged the claim as 'retained from prior pass pending a government-source replacement' where no fresh source was found and the underlying fact was judged very unlikely to have changed (e.g. long-standing ministerial incumbencies since March 2022) -- this labelling is deliberate and should be read as lower-confidence than a freshly-sourced claim. A significant proportion of UP's official .gov.in and .nic.in domains (uppwd.gov.in, sdma.up.gov.in, upsdma.up.nic.in, upred.gov.in) returned persistent HTTP 503 errors across repeated fetch attempts in this session, despite being successfully indexed and quoted by web search; where a specific fact could only be sourced to such a domain via a search-engine snippet rather than a direct, rendered fetch, this is disclosed in the relevant confidence note rather than silently presented as a directly-verified read. The Road Ownership Matrix, Road Lifecycle, Quick-Reference Matrix and Funding Architecture tables are, as with Bihar, INTERPRETATIONS: they apply departmental mandates and legal bases that are separately cited elsewhere in this document to a specific road category, lifecycle stage, problem type, or funding source, rather than being drawn from one single source that states each cell verbatim; the 'Likely bottleneck' column is this document's own assessment, not an empirically measured finding, exactly as flagged in Bihar's document. Major resolutions achieved in this pass, closing gaps explicitly flagged as unresolved in the prior UP document: (1) the U.P. Road Safety Fund's funding mechanism, governance structure and permitted uses, sourced directly to the Rules' own text; (2) UPEIDA's actual CEO succession chain (Manoj Kumar Singh -> Deepak Kumar, Sept 2025 -> Shailendra Bhatia, Sept 2026), resolving the prior pass's 'likely stale CEO' flag, while surfacing a new observation (rapid turnover) rather than a stable answer; (3) a comparable-in-spirit, though older-vintage, CAG performance-audit finding for the Transport Department (2016, not 2025 as hoped -- a 2025-dated Transport Department CAG chapter was located but its content could not be extracted due to a PDF-rendering failure, and a separate, directly-relevant 2025 CAG report on PWD's Central Road Fund utilisation was substituted as the closest available recent audit). district_level_actors.Role: Presumptive chair of the District Road Safety Committee per the MV Act 215(3) national template; controls land acquisition for road projects; top-most official of revenue and civil administration in the district (IAS cadre), assisted by ADMs, with the district divided into subdivisions headed by Sub-Divisional Magistrates (SDMs).

district_level_actors.Role: Heads district (or city) law-and-order and traffic enforcement. In Commissionerate cities (Lucknow, Kanpur, Varanasi, Agra, Ghaziabad, Prayagraj, Noida, and others converted to this system), the Commissioner of Police holds magisterial as well as policing powers, replacing the DM/SSP dual structure for policing matters within city limits.

District-level licensing, registration, permits and enforcement (Administration and Enforcement postings); reports up to the divisional Regional Transport Officer (RTO). UP's two-tier RTO(divisional)/ARTO(district) structure differs from a single-tier DTO model used in some other states.
The engineering decision-maker for SH/MDR design changes, signage, and maintenance within the district.

district_level_actors.Actor: Executive Engineer, UPRRDA (District Programme Implementation Unit)
district_level_actors.Role: The engineering decision-maker for PMGSY-funded rural-road (ODR/VR) works within the district; heads the District Programme Implementation Unit (DPIU) per national PMGSY guidelines.

District's senior health official and in-charge of the District Hospital; relevant to trauma-centre readiness and post-mortem/medico-legal processes after fatal crashes. UP's official district portals (e.g. mau.nic.in, kanpurnagar.nic.in) list a named CMO for each district.

Where the district headquarters or another town is a Nagar Nigam/Nagar Palika Parishad/Nagar Panchayat, controls municipal roads within town limits; the Municipal Commissioner (Nagar Nigam) is a state-appointed IAS/PCS officer with executive powers independent of the elected Mayor.

District-level rural body (75 statewide, one per district); the elected Adhyaksha chairs the body, while an administrative executive (reporting up the state Panchayati Raj cadre line, per the pattern documented in other states) carries out day-to-day functions.

Replicate the DM/SP relationship at subdivision/circle level -- the CO (DSP rank) typically heads a police circle of 3-5 police stations; useful when a problem is very localised and doesn't need full-district escalation.
