focus_areas.name: Crash Compensation (Hit-and-Run Scheme)
focus_areas.relevance: Uttar Pradesh is the single most striking case for this program nationally, even though Crashfree India's own brief does not currently name UP as a pilot or feeder state. MoRTH data placed before the Lok Sabha show hit-and-run accidents in UP rising from 5,823 (2020) to 6,770 (2021), 7,585 (2022), and 6,867 (2023), before jumping to 11,209 in 2024 (provisional) - a nearly 63% single-year increase and the largest jump of any major state in the dataset. This lines up with UP's broader 2024 accident profile: MoRTH's Road Accidents in India report and secondary coverage put UP among the states with the highest raw fatality counts (reported around 24,000+ deaths) and a severity rate near one death for every two crashes, among the worst in the country. Set against this, UP's uptake of the Hit-and-Run Compensation Scheme itself is strikingly thin: only 1 claim registered in FY2022-23, 54 in FY2023-24 (5 paid), 164 in FY2024-25 (104 paid), and 219 registered / 106 paid in FY2025-26 as of 28 Feb 2026. Against 11,209+ hit-and-run accidents in a single year, 219 claims represents one of the largest accident-to-claims gaps of any major state, and is consistent with Crashfree India's national finding that documentation gaps, not fault disputes, stall roughly 90% of pending claims. UP's own state-level Rah-Veer (Good Samaritan) cumulative awardee count of just 14 (as of 12 Feb 2026) further suggests weak on-the-ground uptake of victim/bystander-facing schemes generally, not just the hit-and-run compensation route specifically. Together, the 2024 spike and the compensation gap make UP a high-priority, currently-unaddressed geography for this program.
focus_areas.progress: There is no evidence Crashfree India currently runs Hit-and-Run Scheme work in UP; the program's pilot remains Jaipur, Rajasthan, with feeders in Gurugram, Bihar, and Delhi's DRSC work, and UP is absent from the organisation's own published program pages. On the government side, UP's Public Works Department (UPPWD) maintains a standing Road Safety / IDS (Integrated Data System) portal, and the state ran a month-long 'Road Safety Month' campaign (1-31 January 2026) built around a 4E model (Education, Enforcement, Engineering, Emergency Care) targeting 20 accident-prone districts, followed by a 'Zero Fatality District' (ZFD) scheme that MoRTH/UP DGP data describe as covering 242 critical police stations across those 20 districts, later expanded to 487 critical police stations across all 75 districts, with state and wire-service reporting citing roughly 566 lives saved in the scheme's first four months of 2026. However, none of this reporting specifically addresses the hit-and-run compensation claims process, District Road Safety Committee (DRSC) reviews of the Hit-and-Run Scheme, or documentation-gap remediation - the enforcement and infrastructure focus of ZFD/Road Safety Month is distinct from the victim-compensation pipeline this program targets. UP separately announced its own state-level Rah-Veer (Good Samaritan) reward scheme (₹25,000, reported around October 2025) modeled on the Centre's scheme, but this addresses bystander incentives, not hit-and-run victim compensation directly, and its cumulative awardee count (14, per the Lok Sabha answer) suggests limited reach so far. No UP-specific DRSC activity on the 2026 hit-and-run scheme amendment was found in available reporting.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: There is clear, visible policy energy in UP on road safety broadly - CM Yogi Adityanath has personally chaired review meetings, announced Road Safety Month, and pushed the Zero Fatality District scheme with explicit targets (aiming to bring accident-prone-district deaths to zero) and follow-through reporting of results (566 lives saved cited in state/wire coverage). The Chief Minister has also directed that repeat traffic offenders face licence or permit cancellation and instructed the PWD to identify remaining black spots for engineering fixes (signage, table-top speed breakers). This signals real executive attention to road safety as a political priority in UP. However, none of the located statements, campaign materials, or reviewed coverage specifically name the hit-and-run compensation scheme, the 2024 spike in hit-and-run accidents, or the accident-to-claims gap as a distinct problem being addressed - the visible willpower is directed at enforcement, infrastructure and overall fatality reduction, not at the compensation-claims pipeline. UP's own parallel launch of a state Rah-Veer good-samaritan reward (~₹25,000) shows some willingness to legislate/announce victim-adjacent incentive schemes, but its low cumulative awardee count (14) suggests announcement has not yet translated into uptake, a pattern that likely also holds for the hit-and-run compensation scheme given the tiny claims-to-accidents ratio. No evidence was found of UP legislative debate, state budget line-item, or gazette notification specifically on hit-and-run compensation administration.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Uttar Pradesh is not named in Crashfree India's brief for the Crash Compensation program; the pilot is Jaipur with Gurugram, Bihar and Delhi's DRSC work as feeders, and no UP-specific engagement by Crashfree India on this program was found in research.

focus_areas.name: Gig Rider Safety
focus_areas.relevance: Uttar Pradesh, and specifically Noida and Lucknow, are significant gig-delivery hubs (quick-commerce and food-delivery riders serving the NCR extension into Noida/Ghaziabad and the state capital Lucknow), making the state directly relevant to this program's two-wheeler safety focus even though Crashfree India's brief names no state-specific pilot yet (the program is described as national/thematic, launched February 2026). Noida in particular has a documented history of fatal incidents involving delivery riders under time-pressure delivery models: reported cases include a Blinkit delivery partner from Hathras (UP) killed in Noida within two days of joining, after riding the wrong side of the road to meet delivery-time targets, and a Swiggy rider (Kaushal Yadav, from Etawah, UP) killed when a speeding car struck and dragged his two-wheeler about one kilometre near Sector 14-A, Noida. These cases, while not all from 2026, illustrate a persistent structural risk pattern - out-of-state migrant riders, on two-wheelers, under delivery-time pressure, on NCR-adjacent UP roads - that is exactly the population Crashfree India's Gig Rider Safety Report and coming programme are meant to address. Broader national coverage (e.g. reporting on the rollback of ultra-fast '10-minute delivery' commitments after government scrutiny) also implicates UP-based riders as part of the same national quick-commerce workforce under safety pressure.
focus_areas.progress: Crashfree India's own site describes Gig Rider Safety as 'coming soon' - a dedicated programme still being built (combining policy, platforms and partnerships, in collaboration with Cars24 and the Indian Road Safety Council), with a foundational 'Gig Rider Safety Report' published but no announced city rollout, and no Uttar Pradesh-specific presence. Separately, quick-commerce and food-delivery platforms operating heavily in UP (Zomato, Swiggy, Blinkit/Zepto) have made some national-level safety concessions - notably dropping explicit '10-minute delivery' framing after government/regulatory pressure, as reported by Al Jazeera in late January 2026 - and provide baseline accident insurance and mandatory safety-training modules to riders, per Storyboard18's reporting on Zomato's rider safety training rollout after a gig-worker strike. These are company-level, national policies, not UP-specific interventions, and none of the reviewed coverage describes a Noida-, Lucknow-, or UP-specific safety pilot by any platform. No UP state government programme specifically targeting gig/delivery-rider road safety (e.g., a dedicated helmet, protective-gear, or insurance mandate for platform riders) was found in available reporting, and neither the UP Labour Department nor the UP Transport Department's public materials reviewed mention gig/platform workers as a distinct road-safety category.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: There is no UP-specific legislative or executive signal located on gig/delivery-rider safety specifically; the state's road-safety political energy (Road Safety Month, Zero Fatality District) is general-population-focused and does not appear to single out gig workers as a distinct target group in available coverage, despite CM Yogi Adityanath's otherwise hands-on public statements on enforcement (repeat-offender licence cancellation, PWD black-spot identification). At the national level, government scrutiny of ultra-fast delivery commitments (reported around January 2026, e.g. in international coverage of India's quick-commerce sector by Al Jazeera) shows some regulatory willingness to address rider-safety pressures created by delivery-time targets, which indirectly affects UP-based riders given the state's large NCR-adjacent (Noida, Ghaziabad) and state-capital (Lucknow) gig workforce, but this has not been localized to UP policy specifically - it is a Union-government/industry-level shift, not a UP state initiative. No UP Labour Department or Transport Department scheme addressing gig-worker road safety specifically was identified in this research pass, and no UP legislative assembly discussion of gig/platform-worker safety was located either.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Uttar Pradesh is not named in Crashfree India's brief for Gig Rider Safety; the program remains national/thematic in scope (started February 2026) with no state-specific pilot announced, and the organisation's own site currently describes it as 'coming soon' with no city list.

focus_areas.name: Project Rakshak
focus_areas.relevance: Project Rakshak's model - pairing college students with road-safety mentors and civic agencies to audit high-risk corridors and win 23+ concrete authority approvals in Cohort 1 - is highly applicable to Uttar Pradesh given the state's large student population, numerous engineering/technical colleges (including in Lucknow, Noida, Kanpur, and Prayagraj), and its status as the state with among the highest raw accident and fatality counts nationally (UP recorded roughly 44,534 accidents and 23,652-24,776 fatalities in 2023, per MoRTH-sourced reporting reviewed in this research, and 46,223 accidents with 24,776 deaths reported to November 2025 per CM Yogi Adityanath's own January 2026 statement). This is precisely the kind of high-volume, high-severity state where youth-led corridor audits could plausibly find fertile ground and receptive civic authorities. However, Crashfree India's own published Project Rakshak page (as reviewed) lists aggregate figures for Cohort 1 - 31 teams, 900+ stakeholder surveys, 23+ authority approvals, 120+ high-risk locations assessed, 18 cities - without naming the specific 18 (or, per the broader brief, 34) cities/institutions involved, and no Uttar Pradesh city was found explicitly named in currently available Crashfree India materials or in secondary coverage (LinkedIn, YouTube) reviewed for this research.
focus_areas.progress: Cohort 1 (2025) is complete per Crashfree India's site: 31 teams, 900+ stakeholder surveys, 23+ authority approvals, an estimated 20-30% crash-reduction potential at assessed locations, and applications for 'Cohort 2' are stated as closed on the page reviewed - though the broader program brief describes a larger, still-expanding 2nd edition (3 tracks, 95 teams, 34 cities, 32 institutions, 136 colleges reached, MoUs with NOSPlan/SIT Pune, 15 more teams expected from Jaipur/Pune/Srinagar). Neither the Crashfree India site content retrieved nor available secondary reporting (LinkedIn posts, YouTube session listings) provided a complete, named list of the 34 (or 18) cities, so it could not be confirmed or ruled out that Lucknow, Noida, Kanpur, or Prayagraj are included. No UP-specific Project Rakshak news coverage, college MoU announcement, or local press mention was found in this research pass, and no UP engineering or technical college (e.g. IIT-BHU Varanasi, MNNIT Allahabad/Prayagraj, AKTU-affiliated colleges in Lucknow or Noida) was named as a Project Rakshak partner in any source reviewed. This is presented as an honest gap, not as confirmation of UP's exclusion.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: No UP-government-side policy willpower signal specific to Project Rakshak was found, which is expected since this is a Crashfree India-run youth program rather than a government scheme; the relevant 'willpower' signal would be whether UP civic authorities (municipal corporations, traffic police, PWD) have approved or acted on any Project Rakshak team's corridor-audit recommendations, and no such UP-specific approval was located in available sources. UP's own general road-safety policy activity - Road Safety Month, the Zero Fatality District scheme's expansion to 487 critical police stations, and PWD black-spot identification for engineering fixes (signage, table-top speed breakers) - shows an active civic-engineering appetite and a state government already comfortable acting on location-specific accident data, which would plausibly be receptive to the kind of youth-led corridor audits Project Rakshak produces elsewhere. But no direct linkage between UP's existing black-spot program and a Crashfree India youth audit was found, and no UP official statement referencing Project Rakshak, Crashfree India, or Cars24 by name was located in this research pass.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Available Crashfree India materials on Project Rakshak do not name any Uttar Pradesh city among Cohort 1's 18 cities, and no city list confirming or ruling out Lucknow, Noida, Kanpur, or Prayagraj for the expanded 2nd edition (34 cities) could be located in this research pass; UP's inclusion remains unconfirmed either way.

focus_areas.name: SATARK (ANPR Enforcement Technology)
focus_areas.relevance: Uttar Pradesh is not named as a current or planned SATARK location (LIVE: Bengaluru, Gurugram, Jaipur; UNDERWAY: Pune, Rajkot, Gandhinagar, Thiruvananthapuram), and Crashfree India's own SATARK program page was not found live/published (a direct fetch attempt returned a 404), suggesting the program's public-facing city-specific detail may still be limited to the aggregate brief facts. That said, UP is independently and separately one of the more technologically active states on ANPR/e-challan enforcement outside of Crashfree India's ecosystem: Noida has run the Integrated Security and Traffic Management System (ISTMS) since May 2022, an ANPR/CCTV network (82 camera locations, adaptive signal control at 40 locations) that generated nearly 296,000 e-challans in its first year of operation and assisted police in resolving 182 criminal cases, and similar automated CCTV/ANPR-based challan systems are reported as operating in Lucknow and Kanpur as well. This makes UP relevant less as a SATARK expansion target and more as a state with pre-existing, non-Crashfree-India ANPR infrastructure that a future SATARK-style effort could potentially interface with, audit, or learn from.
focus_areas.progress: No Crashfree India SATARK activity in UP was found; the program remains concentrated in its three LIVE cities plus four UNDERWAY cities as per the brief, none of which are in UP. Independently, UP's existing ANPR/e-challan infrastructure (Noida's ISTMS, and broadly similar systems reported in Lucknow/Kanpur/Ghaziabad) continues to operate under state/municipal management (Noida Authority and UP Traffic Police, with private operator Efkon India Pvt Ltd for ISTMS), with reported operational issues including tampered/damaged number plates reducing detection accuracy and occasional duplicate challans - exactly the kind of implementation friction that a dedicated enforcement-technology effort like SATARK is designed to address elsewhere. ISTMS's coverage (82 camera locations, adaptive signal control at 40 junctions, SOS/public-address at 82 locations) is itself a meaningfully large deployment by Indian city standards, which suggests UP would not be starting from zero infrastructure if a SATARK-style layer were ever proposed there - it might instead be a question of upgrading detection/analytics on top of an existing camera network rather than building one from scratch. National reporting from 2026 also describes new nationwide e-challan rules (a 5-strike licence-suspension rule effective 1 January 2026, and stricter challan-delivery timelines), which apply to UP's existing camera networks by default even without any Crashfree India involvement. No comparably detailed, sourced description of Lucknow's or Kanpur's systems was found to confirm whether they match Noida's scale.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: UP's state and city administrations have shown sustained institutional commitment to camera-based enforcement generally: continuous ISTMS operation in Noida since May 2022 (run jointly by Noida Authority and UP Police, operated by private contractor Efkon India Pvt Ltd), the Zero Fatality District scheme's use of enforcement and monitoring data across 487 critical police stations by 2026, and CM Yogi Adityanath's direct public statements favouring licence/permit cancellation for repeat offenders identified via challans (a policy that presupposes and depends on reliable automated detection). This indicates a policy environment broadly receptive to, and already partially built around, ANPR-style enforcement technology - UP is not a state that needs to be persuaded of the enforcement-technology concept in the abstract. However, no evidence was found of UP specifically requesting, negotiating, or being offered a Crashfree India/Cars24 SATARK deployment, nor of any UP state budget allocation, cabinet decision, or gazette notification tied to SATARK by name. The nationwide 5-strike e-challan/licence-suspension rule effective 1 January 2026 applies to UP's existing ANPR infrastructure by default, showing continued Union-level regulatory tightening around automated enforcement, but this is a national rule rather than a UP-specific policy signal or a SATARK-linked one.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Uttar Pradesh is not named as a current (LIVE) or planned (UNDERWAY) SATARK location in Crashfree India's brief for this program, and no additional detail confirming or changing that was found on the organisation's own site (its SATARK page returned a 404 on direct fetch) or in broader search.

bihar.political_context: Bihar held Legislative Assembly elections in November 2025, and the state's government changed hands in April–May 2026: Nitish Kumar's uninterrupted run as Chief Minister ended on 15 April 2026, and Samrat Choudhary (BJP) was sworn in as the 24th Chief Minister the same day, with the full cabinet reshuffled and portfolios allocated on 7–8 May 2026. As of the most recent verification (9 September 2026), Samrat Choudhary was confirmed still actively functioning as CM through contemporaneous press coverage of his public appearances (felicitating students, attending public events). Under the 8 May 2026 portfolio allocation, the CM retains Home, General Administration, Vigilance, Election, Civil Aviation and unallocated departments; Deputy CM Vijay Kumar Chaudhary holds Water Resources & Parliamentary Affairs; Deputy CM Bijendra Prasad Yadav holds Finance & Commercial Taxes; Road Construction went to Kumar Shailendra; and Energy went to Shailesh Kumar ("Bulo Mandal"). This is a structural change with direct road-safety consequences: the Transport Minister (now Damodar Rawat), the Road Construction Minister (now Kumar Shailendra), and both Deputy Chief Ministers are all different people than a year ago, meaning most of Bihar's road-safety-relevant political leadership is newly in role and has, by definition, no track record yet in its current position. Underlying this political layer, India's constitutional Seventh Schedule splits road-related subjects across the Union and State Lists, and because roads, transport and police all sit substantially on the State List (with the Union retaining National Highways, the overarching Motor Vehicles Act framework, and centrally sponsored schemes like PMGSY), Bihar's state government and its departments are the primary point of leverage for almost all road-safety interventions Crashfree India will pursue — the Union government matters mainly for NH stretches, PMGSY funding rules, and the national legal framework. Additionally, this pass resolved a previously unnamed gap: the 7–8 May 2026 cabinet expansion allocated the Health portfolio to Nishant Kumar, son of former CM and JD(U) national president Nitish Kumar, his first ministerial appointment (LatestLY, Republic World, Daily Pioneer) — relevant background given JD(U)’s continuing weight in the coalition despite Nitish Kumar himself now sitting in the Rajya Sabha.

governance_bodies.name: Transport Department, Government of Bihar
governance_bodies.mandate: A Regulatory Department responsible for implementation and enforcement of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988, Central Motor Vehicle Rules 1989, other rules made thereunder, and State Taxation Acts, to regulate road transport, passenger and freight movement.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None directly (regulatory, not road-owning); road-related functions: vehicle registration, driving licences, permits, vehicle fitness, road tax, enforcement policy, public transport (via Bihar State Road Transport Corporation), and the road-safety lead-agency function.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Secretary/Chairman-STA (State Transport Authority) → State Transport Commissioner (cum Addl. Secretary, cum Secretary-STA) → Deputy Transport Commissioners → District Transport Officers (DTOs) and Regional Transport Authorities (RTAs) in the field. The department's field forces comprise 38 DTOs and 9 RTAs (some sources put the RTO count at 39).
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Bihar State Road Transport Corporation (BSTC, public bus operator); Automated Driving Testing Centres (ADTCs); the Bihar Road Safety Council Secretariat/Lead Agency sits inside this department.

governance_bodies.data_role: Holds the vehicle registration database (VAHAN) and driving licence database (SARATHI), permit records; one of the four core data-contributing departments to iRAD/e-DAR.

governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not specified beyond Road Safety Council/DRSC cadence covered elsewhere in this document.

governance_bodies.name: Road Construction Department (RCD)
governance_bodies.mandate: A premier works department conducting planning, designing, construction, improvement, strengthening and maintenance of roads and bridges — including flyovers, ROBs (rail-over-bridges) and elevated corridors.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: State Highways (SH), Major District Roads (MDR), and National Highways segments not entrusted to NHAI (the "NH Wing, RCD" roads — historically the majority of Bihar's NH length; NHAI directly holds a smaller, growing share as projects are handed over).
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Secretary (IAS) → Engineer-in-Chief (E-in-C) for technical matters (with a separate Additional Secretary/Joint Secretary line for personnel/admin) → eight Wings, each headed by a Chief Engineer (CE) → Circles → Divisions → Sub-Divisions, following the standard PWD-style "Wing–Circle–Division–Sub-Division" hierarchy.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Bihar State Road Development Corporation (BSRDC) — a public limited company fully owned by the Government of Bihar, established in 2009 to promote surface infrastructure by taking up road works, bridges, widening, strengthening and maintenance of roads — and Bihar Rajya Pul Nirman Nigam Ltd (BRPNNL), both reporting to the RCD Secretary; not shown in the department's main organogram but report to the Secretary, RCD.

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Technical sanction of state road/bridge projects, contractor debarment, day-to-day maintenance decisions on SH/MDR. Land acquisition needs district revenue machinery; large projects need Finance Department budget sanction and often Cabinet approval; NH works funded/sanctioned by MoRTH still need MoRTH clearance even when executed by the NH Wing.
governance_bodies.data_role: Acts as the road-owning-agency stakeholder in iRAD's engineer-alert workflow for design review after crashes on SH/MDR/NH-not-with-NHAI roads.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: A section of the Vikramshila Bridge in Bhagalpur collapsed in 2026, after which the executive engineer responsible for the bridge's maintenance was suspended pending investigation; a string of earlier collapses led the Supreme Court to issue notices to the Bihar government, NHAI, the RCD Additional Chief Secretary, the BRPNNL chairperson, and the Rural Works Department Additional Chief Secretary, on a PIL seeking a structural audit of the state's bridges.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not specified.

governance_bodies.name: Rural Works Department (RWD)
governance_bodies.mandate: Responsible for construction of rural roads with necessary culverts and cross-drainage structures.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Other District Roads (ODR) and Village Roads (VR), with the objective of improving "Farm to Market Connectivity"; implements PMGSY (Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana, a Centrally Sponsored Scheme) and state-funded equivalents — Mukhya Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (MMGSY, launched 2013–14), MMGSY (Remaining) (launched 2023), and the Gramin Tola Sampark Nischay Yojana.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Structure parallel to RCD: Engineer-in-Chief (RWD), Chief Engineers, Superintending Engineers, Executive Engineers at Circle/Division level. RWD's internal Wing/Circle organisational structure was not found in as much organogram detail as RCD's (a carried-over gap).
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Not always executed by RWD's own engineering staff — in the initial 2000s ramp-up, the Government of Bihar asked the Ministry of Rural Development to engage central agencies, and tripartite agreements were signed with IRCON International, National Buildings Construction Corporation, National Hydroelectric Power Corporation and National Projects Construction Corporation, along with CPWD, covering 33 of Bihar's 37 districts at the time.

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Holds the engineering and budgetary machinery for construction/maintenance even on roads that serve individual villages; under PMGSY-III, "responsibility of construction and maintenance of PMGSY works lies with the state government" (i.e., RWD), not the local body, even though the roads serve local body areas.
governance_bodies.data_role: Acts as the road-owning-agency stakeholder in iRAD for ODR/VR crash-site design review.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: PMGSY has a three-tier quality monitoring system — internal QC by contractors at the project level, a second tier of independent State Quality Monitors inspecting in three stages, and a third tier of National Quality Monitors carrying out random field inspections and grading execution quality.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Progress of PMGSY is reviewed through Regional Review Meetings, Performance Review Committee meetings, and Empowered Committee meetings with states, plus Bihar's own internal reviews. RWD's 2025–26 budget of ₹11,101.64 crore was presented to the Assembly, reporting 764 km of MMGSY roads built in 2024–25 and a target of a further 8,600 km in 2025–26, alongside 700 new rural bridges planned for the year.

governance_bodies.name: Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs)
governance_bodies.mandate: Rural local self-government under the Bihar Panchayat Raj Act, 2006, implementing the 73rd Constitutional Amendment.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Very limited — Gram Panchayats can maintain purely internal village streets/drains where GP funds (15th Finance Commission grants, MGNREGA convergence, own tax revenue) allow; cannot independently execute PMGSY/MMGSY-scale road construction.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Three tiers: Gram Panchayat (GP) at village level, Panchayat Samiti at Block level, and Zila Parishad at District level — at present 8,053 Gram Panchayats, 533 Panchayat Samitis and 38 Zila Parishads are functional, with Gram Panchayats divided into roughly 1.15 lakh wards. A Gram Kachahry (village-level dispute-resolution body) exists at each GP; a Ward Sabha exists at each ward under the Ward Member, alongside the Gram Sabha at GP level.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Elected political heads: Mukhiya (GP), Pramukh (Panchayat Samiti), Adhyaksha (Zila Parishad). Administrative/executive counterparts: Panchayat Secretary (GP), BDO-cum-Executive Officer (Panchayat Samiti), and Deputy Development Commissioner-cum-CEO (Zila Parishad) — reporting up the state administrative line (Panchayati Raj Department → Director → district BDO/DDC cadre), not to the elected head.
governance_bodies.decision_making_power: A Gram Panchayat may impose a yearly tax on occupants of holdings, and on professions, trades, callings and employment carried on within its jurisdiction, subject to State Government approval of the maximum tax rate (Section 27, BPRA 2006); the State Government retains rule-making power (Section 146) and the power to issue model regulations and inquire into Panchayat affairs (Sections 150 and 152). Every Gram Panchayat must prepare a development plan annually and submit it to the Panchayat Samiti (Sections 166–167).
governance_bodies.data_role: PRIs have a formally recognised awareness/participation role in road safety — the 2020 amendment to Bihar's Road Safety Council Rules explicitly tasks the Transport Department's coordination committee with ensuring "active participation of Panchayati Raj Institutions, Urban Local Bodies and NGOs in road safety awareness programmes" — distinct from an engineering role.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: The state government intimated in Feb. 2005, based on department resolutions from September 2001, that functions of 20 departments had been devolved to PRIs — but a CAG review found that while activity mapping had been done, actual transfer of functions, functionaries and funds to PRIs by these departments had not fully materialised — a documented, audited gap between paper devolution and real administrative control.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Annual development-plan submission cycle (Sections 166–167, BPRA 2006); Gram Sabha/Ward Sabha meetings for local matters.

governance_bodies.name: Home Department / Bihar Police (incl. Traffic Police)
governance_bodies.mandate: Overall command of law and order and traffic enforcement statewide, under the Home Department (headed politically by the Chief Minister, who traditionally also holds the Home portfolio in Bihar).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None — an enforcement body, not a road-owning one. Enforcement decisions (checkpoint locations, helmet/seatbelt drives, drunk-driving campaigns) are made at ADG (Traffic) and district SP level; infrastructure decisions that police influence but don't own (camera placement, signal timing, physical traffic-calming) require joint sign-off with the Transport Department and/or the road-owning engineering department.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Director General of Police (DGP) heads Bihar Police. An Additional Director General of Police (ADG), Traffic heads traffic policing statewide; district-level traffic enforcement is typically headed by an SP (Traffic) in major cities (e.g., Patna) or handled by the general district SP/SSP elsewhere, with Traffic DSPs and Traffic Inspectors/Sub-Inspectors at the operational level. Bihar has 43 Police Districts (headed by SP/SSP) and 853 Police Stations; a Police District is divided into Police Subdivisions headed by a DSP. Patna and other large cities have designated City SPs (e.g., SP City East/West) separate from rural SPs, plus a dedicated SP (Traffic), Patna.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Crime Investigation Department (CID) for serious/fatal hit-and-run or negligence cases; Economic Offences Unit; Bihar Police Academy and Constable Training School/Military Police training centres.

governance_bodies.data_role: Police are the first-entry stakeholder for both FIR/crime records and the iRAD/e-DAR crash database; once police enter accident details with photos/videos and a unique ID is created, an alert automatically goes to a PWD/local-body engineer under iRAD's design.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: The Transport Department has directed all DTOs to identify roughly 700 sites for an Integrated Traffic Management System (ITMS), with the State Transport Commissioner instructing that site selection be carried out in coordination with Traffic Police for technical accuracy.

governance_bodies.name: Urban Development & Housing Department (UDHD) and Urban Local Bodies
governance_bodies.mandate: UDHD sets urban policy; its principal implementing arm for infrastructure is BUIDCO (Bihar Urban Infrastructure Development Corporation), established 2009 under the Companies Act 1956, functioning as the apex body for planning, coordination and implementation of urban development projects (water supply, sewerage, urban transport, housing, solid waste management).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Municipal roads within Urban Local Body limits (Nagar Nigams/Municipal Corporations, Nagar Parishads/Municipal Councils, Nagar Panchayats) under the Bihar Municipal Act, 2007 — as of April 2026 there were 264 Urban Local Bodies in the state. Patna Municipal Corporation (PMC, established 1952) handles municipal roads, drains, streetlights within Patna.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Each ULB has an elected wing (Mayor for Corporations, Chairperson for Councils, President for Nagar Panchayats, plus ward councillors) and a separate administrative wing; day-to-day execution runs through a Municipal Commissioner (Corporations) or Executive Officer (Councils/Nagar Panchayats), state cadre officers not directly under the elected Mayor's control for personnel matters.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: BUIDCO; the Patna Metropolitan Area Authority (PMAA) — the current metropolitan planning body, constituted under the Bihar Urban Planning & Development Act, 2012, as successor to the defunct Patna Regional Development Authority (PRDA, established 1979, dissolved 2007 when the Bihar Municipal Act, 2007 repealed its enabling legislation).

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: The Bihar Municipal Act 2007 gives the State Government powers to monitor ULB functioning, with decision-making on all key issues ultimately resting with the state and ULBs having only some powers over service delivery; government may inspect any ULB office or call for its records — i.e., ULB autonomy is legally constrained.
governance_bodies.data_role: ULB engineer is the "Road" stakeholder in iRAD for municipal-road crashes.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: Overlap risk: for a single Patna street, PMC may own the carriageway/footpath, RCD/BSRDC may own a flyover/arterial stretch, Traffic Police controls signalling/enforcement, and a development authority (e.g. PMAA) may control land-use/setback rules along the frontage — a single "fix this junction" request can require sign-off from three or four institutions.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: PMC's Empowered Standing Committee (its key internal decision body) has directed executive officers and ward councillors to make daily ward visits to resolve complaints on roads, drainage and streetlights on the spot.

governance_bodies.name: Health Department, Emergency Response & Trauma Care
governance_bodies.mandate: Institutional home for trauma care and emergency medical response, operating through the State Health Society, Bihar (SHSB) for scheme implementation.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None (health/trauma-care role, not road ownership).
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Minister, Health; Principal Secretary/Additional Chief Secretary, Health; Executive Director, SHSB; Civil Surgeon (district-level health officer, relevant to trauma-centre coordination and medico-legal/post-mortem processes after fatal crashes).
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: State Health Society, Bihar (SHSB) — provides pre-hospital care via Advanced Life Saving Ambulances (108 service) piloted under Public-Private Partnership.

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Directed, alongside the Transport Department, to operationalise integration of private ambulances into the unified Dial 112 emergency helpline; directed for 11 upgraded trauma centres to have ICU operations running by mid-2026 (a target that appears to have slipped — as of 1 July 2026, a month past deadline, still described as forward-looking plans, with no later confirmation found that rollout has since been completed).
governance_bodies.data_role: One of the four core stakeholder departments (alongside Police, Transport, and the road-owning agency) feeding hospital-side data into iRAD/e-DAR.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: Bihar currently has around 3,700 ambulances (government and private combined), of which only about 2,000 operate under the government system; national standards recommend a 10-minute ambulance response, but Bihar's average is around 25 minutes — a documented, quantified capacity gap directly relevant to post-crash survivability. 55 hospitals are designated trauma centres (10 Level Two, 35 Level Three, 10 integrated trauma-and-emergency facilities).
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not specified.

governance_bodies.name: Disaster Management Department / Bihar State Disaster Management Authority (BSDMA)
governance_bodies.mandate: Institutionally linked to mass-casualty response (e.g., major bus/truck crashes, bridge collapses) rather than routine single-vehicle crash response, which sits with Police/Health; copied on Bihar's Road Safety Council notifications as a stakeholder.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Not detailed beyond BSDMA/Disaster Management Department structure.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: State Disaster Response Force (SDRF); Aapda Mitra ("disaster friend") volunteer scheme.
governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Runs "Safety Weeks" (Road Safety, Earthquake Safety, Fire Safety, Flood Safety), safe-school programmes, and public IEC (information-education-communication) material distribution as part of structural and non-structural disaster-risk-reduction work; runs the Aapda Mitra volunteer scheme, under which trained community volunteers contribute to prevention, rescue work and public awareness specifically around road accidents, alongside flood and fire response.

His current portfolio, Rural Development and Information/Public Relations, points his day-to-day priorities toward rural infrastructure/welfare delivery and government messaging rather than transport. His 2025–26 record as Transport Minister (documented in this file's track_record) shows he was willing to frame road safety in enforcement and administrative terms (black-spot data, review meetings, vehicle-seizure orders) when it was his portfolio, suggesting road safety is a plausible re-entry topic for him as a sympathetic former minister, but it is not his current institutional mandate. Inference (not directly documented): given his proximity to Nitish Kumar and his new role managing the JD(U) legislature bench, his main near-term interest is likely intra-coalition positioning ahead of any future reshuffle, with road safety a secondary, reputational asset rather than an active priority.

focus_areas.name: Crash Compensation (Hit-and-Run Scheme)
focus_areas.relevance: Bihar occupies a unique position in Crashfree India's own hit-and-run compensation brief: it is named explicitly, not as a pilot site, but as the positive benchmark against which the organisation's Rajasthan (Jaipur) pilot is being designed — "Bihar, with higher uptake, shows what works better." The MoRTH figures given to Lok Sabha (Unstarred Question No. 6419, Annexure B) bear this out dramatically: Bihar's hit-and-run compensation claims registered/paid ran 1/0 in FY2022-23, then jumped to 2,774/2,047 in FY2023-24 and 3,959/2,912 in FY2024-25, with 2,811 registered against 2,872 paid in the part-year to 28 Feb 2026 — a volume roughly 3 to 10 times any other state's, against a national backdrop where only ~205 claims were filed nationally in FY2022-23 against ~25,000 hit-and-run crashes. At the same time, the same Lok Sabha question package that supplied Bihar's aggregate numbers was itself triggered by a specific complaint about non-payment in "hundred hit and run cases in the Banka district of Bihar," meaning Bihar's compensation delivery has drawn direct parliamentary scrutiny even as its state-level totals look comparatively strong. And Bihar's underlying accident base is also worsening sharply: hit-and-run accidents rose from 774 (2020) to 5,759 (2024, provisional), a more than 7x increase in four years, per the same Annexure A. For Crashfree India's Bihar-outreach thesis, this combination — held up as "what works," yet carrying an unresolved district-level payment complaint and a fast-rising accident base — makes Bihar simultaneously the strongest comparator case study and a state whose model needs closer, verified scrutiny before being generalised to Rajasthan or elsewhere.
focus_areas.progress: Bihar's comparatively strong claims uptake traces to a specific 2021 administrative reform, not to the hit-and-run scheme in isolation. An amendment to the Bihar Motor Vehicle Rules, notified in the Bihar Gazette on 11 August 2021 and effective 15 September 2021, took victims and dependents largely out of civil litigation: it created a revolving ₹50 crore corpus (the Bihar Motor Vehicle Accident Assistance Fund) from which Sub-Divisional Officers, acting as accident-claim inquiry officers, and District Magistrates, as claims evaluation officers, could sanction an interim ex-gratia payment of ₹5 lakh for death within 15 days, with the State Transport Appellate Tribunal required to settle the full claim within 60 days; grievous-injury interim payments were later raised from ₹50,000 to ₹2.5 lakh. Bihar's transport secretary called it "the first of its kind initiative in India." Claims are now filed and tracked through a dedicated NIC-supported portal (accidentclaim.bihar.gov.in) run by the Transport Department, which separately tags hit-and-run and non-hit-and-run cases — a likely contributor to Bihar's unusually high registered-claims count relative to other states. However, this model is not uncontested: in June 2025, Union Minister and LJP(RV) president Chirag Paswan publicly urged Chief Minister Nitish Kumar to revert to the older DM/SDO-disbursed model, arguing the revised process — which routes victims through the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal and insurer interactions — was "complex and troublesome" and delayed relief to grieving families. This suggests Bihar's headline volume advantage coexists with real friction in individual case handling, consistent with the Banka district complaint reaching Parliament. A 2026 national amendment now pushes district-level review of the scheme through District Road Safety Committees (DRSCs), rolling up to the state — Bihar's existing DRSC/DM review infrastructure (see policy_willpower) plausibly positions it to absorb this change relatively smoothly, though no Bihar-specific DRSC hit-and-run review data was found.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: Bihar's transport administration has shown sustained, visible engagement with road-safety governance in the past year, even if hit-and-run compensation specifically remains only partly transparent. State Transport Minister Shravan Kumar told a January 2026 meeting of state transport ministers in New Delhi that the government was targeting "zero fatality" status for six of its highest-accident districts (Patna, Muzaffarpur, Saran, Motihari, Gaya and Nalanda), and disclosed that the department held 484 district-level review meetings through 2025 involving District Magistrates, police superintendents and infrastructure officials — evidence of an active DRSC-adjacent review cadence rather than a dormant compliance structure. The department also reports reducing identified black spots from 160 (2022) to 114 (2024), rolled out a January 2026 month-long road-safety awareness campaign on helmet/seatbelt compliance, and is running the Rah-Veer Good Samaritan scheme (₹25,000 reward for bystanders who help crash victims within the Golden Hour) with dedicated driver-training sessions in Patna in January 2026 (224 vehicle drivers trained in one reported session, per the Transport Secretary). Bihar's 95 cumulative Rah-Veer awardees (as of 12 Feb 2026) are second nationally only to Uttarakhand's 251, reinforcing a genuine, if uneven, state commitment to victim-assistance policy rather than pure paperwork compliance. Set against this, the Chirag Paswan intervention and the Banka parliamentary question both indicate that political and public pressure on the compensation mechanism specifically (as distinct from broader road-safety messaging) is real and ongoing in 2025-26, meaning the state's own narrative of a well-functioning scheme is contested internally — useful nuance for Crashfree India to carry into how it presents Bihar as a benchmark to Rajasthan stakeholders, rather than treating it as an unqualified success story.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Bihar is named explicitly and only as a comparator geography in Crashfree India's own hit-and-run brief — held up as the state with "higher uptake" whose claims-processing approach is being studied to inform the design of Crashfree India's first pilot in Jaipur, Rajasthan. Crashfree India has no operational program presence of its own in Bihar under this focus area; its engagement is analytical/benchmarking rather than on-the-ground.

focus_areas.name: Gig Rider Safety
focus_areas.relevance: Crashfree India's Gig Rider Safety program, launched February 2026, remains national/thematic in scope with no state-specific pilot named in the organisation's own brief — but Bihar's gig economy is large and growing fast enough to be a plausible future target. As of 1 September 2026, 1,16,376 gig and platform workers were registered on Bihar's Labour Resources and Migrant Workers Welfare Department portal, with Patna alone accounting for 8,473 registrations, followed by West Champaran (6,074) and East Champaran (5,879); food and grocery delivery, cab/bike rides, logistics and package delivery were named as the state's principal gig-work categories. Most consequential for a safety-focused NGO, the Bihar Legislative Assembly passed the Bihar Platform Based Gig Workers (Registration, Social Security and Welfare) Act, 2025 in late July 2025, making Bihar the third (by some counts, alongside Jharkhand, the fourth) Indian state to legislate specifically for platform workers, after Rajasthan and Karnataka. Secondary legal-commentary coverage (The Leaflet) states the Bihar Act goes further than its Rajasthan/Karnataka counterparts by directly granting workers statutory entitlements to accident compensation and maternity benefits, rather than leaving these to a discretionary welfare-board framework — a potentially significant hook for road-safety-linked advocacy, though this could not be independently verified against the Act's primary text (the PRS-hosted PDF could not be parsed for this research). This combination of large registered gig-worker numbers, heavy urban two-wheeler delivery activity concentrated in Patna, and a fresh statutory welfare architecture makes Bihar a state where CFI's Gig Rider Safety thesis has real underlying relevance, even without a confirmed program presence yet.
focus_areas.progress: Bihar's gig-worker safety net is at an early implementation stage. The 2025 Act establishes a Welfare Board and a Social Security and Welfare Fund, to be financed through a welfare fee levied on aggregator platforms, and covers registration of both workers and platforms, payment-timeline rules, insurance coverage, occupational safety, data protection, algorithmic transparency and grievance redressal — a comprehensive framework on paper. Worker registration itself appears to be progressing at meaningful scale (over 116,000 registrants by September 2026), suggesting the administrative registration pipeline is functioning, which is a precondition for any safety or accident-compensation benefit to actually reach riders. However, no evidence was found in this research of the Welfare Board being operationalised with actual disbursements, of any helmet-mandate or rider-training program specific to Bihar, or of any Crashfree India activity (training, audits, advocacy) targeting Bihar's gig-delivery workforce specifically. Broader national commentary on India's gig economy (East Asia Forum, April 2026) notes that protections are generally growing more slowly than the workforce itself, and while some reports describe platforms elsewhere in India being pushed to drop aggressive delivery-time guarantees after safety-related worker protests, no Bihar-specific instance of such a directive was confirmed in this research, so that claim is deliberately not asserted here as a Bihar fact. On current evidence, Bihar's gig-rider safety progress is legislative/registrative rather than operational.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: The passage of a dedicated, comparatively strong gig-worker Act after more than a year of union mobilisation and protests (per UNI Global Union's own account of the campaign) is itself a meaningful policy-willpower signal: Bihar's government chose to legislate specific, justiciable entitlements (including accident compensation, per secondary sources) rather than issue non-binding guidelines, placing it ahead of several larger states that have not yet passed comparable legislation. The state's Labour Resources and Migrant Workers Welfare Department is visibly running the registration portal and publishing district-level registration data, indicating some institutional follow-through beyond the bill's passage. That said, no budget figures, welfare-fee collection data, or Board disbursement records were located for this research, so it is not yet possible to say how much of the Act's stated ambition has translated into funded, delivered services — a common gap between legislative willpower and implementation capacity in early-stage Indian welfare-board schemes. There is also no visible link yet between this labour-welfare policy track and Bihar's road-safety/transport-department track (the DRSC and hit-and-run infrastructure discussed under Crash Compensation); the two currently appear to be separate government workstreams, which may itself be an opening for Crashfree India to propose bridging gig-rider road safety into the existing Transport Department review architecture.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Per Crashfree India's own brief, Gig Rider Safety is a national/thematic program with no state-specific pilot named as of its February 2026 launch, and this research found no evidence of any Bihar-specific Crashfree India gig-rider activity, partnership, or announcement as of September 2026.

focus_areas.name: Project Rakshak
focus_areas.relevance: Project Rakshak's second edition (Cohort II, 2025-26) is a substantial scale-up from its first: orientation for the new cohort was completed on 3 September 2026 with 95 student teams across 34 cities and 32 institutions spanning 19 states and Union Territories, versus Cohort I's reported 31 crash-prone-corridor locations across roughly 13 states and 18 cities with 23+ civic approvals secured. Given Bihar's road-safety salience — Patna is one of the six districts the state government itself has flagged as a top-accident-prone "zero fatality" target — whether Patna or another Bihar city sits inside that 34-city roster matters directly for whether Project Rakshak already gives Crashfree India an on-the-ground footprint in Bihar, or whether the state remains untouched by this flagship youth program. This is the single clearest open question in Project Rakshak's relevance to a Bihar outreach strategy.
focus_areas.progress: This research reviewed Crashfree India's own Project Rakshak page and its Cohort II public LinkedIn announcement, both of which name specific example cities and institutions (among them Vijayawada, Indore, Chennai, Mumbai, Varanasi, Guntur, Hyderabad, Delhi, Kharagpur and Chandigarh, with partner institutions including IIT Madras, IIT Delhi, IIT Kharagpur, IIT BHU, St. Xavier's College Mumbai, and the School of Planning and Architecture, Vijayawada) plus MoUs referenced with NOSPlan and SIT Pune, and an expectation of roughly 15 additional teams from Jaipur, Pune and Srinagar. Patna and Bihar do not appear among any of the cities or institutions named in either the program page or the Cohort II announcement reviewed. However, neither source publishes the complete 34-city (or the earlier 18-city) roster — the named cities are illustrative examples in program copy and social posts, not an exhaustive list — so Bihar's absence from this research's source material is suggestive but not conclusive. No independent news coverage of Project Rakshak activity in Patna or any other Bihar city was found in this research.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: Project Rakshak is a Crashfree India-run youth program rather than a government scheme, so "policy willpower" here is best read as institutional momentum and partner buy-in rather than state legislative action. karnataka.political_context: Siddaramaiah resigned as Chief Minister on 28 May 2026 and D. K. Shivakumar was sworn in as the 18th Chief Minister of Karnataka on 3 June 2026, with G. Parameshwara as Deputy CM (Revenue, Youth Empowerment and Sports), under an internal Congress power-sharing arrangement whose exact terms were never formally announced. Portfolios were allocated on 4 June 2026 and reshuffled again on 27 August 2026 when the cabinet was expanded. As of Shivakumar's 100th day in office (10 September 2026, an event his predecessor Siddaramaiah himself inaugurated and publicly endorsed) he remains Chief Minister with no rotation back to Siddaramaiah having occurred, though persistent speculation about a power-sharing 'rotation' understanding means this should be re-checked before any future use of this document. Priyank Kharge became Home Minister (excluding Intelligence, which the CM retains) from the June 2026 reshuffle, with a strongly technology/digital-policing-focused agenda; Byrathi Suresh became Transport Minister, succeeding Ramalinga Reddy (who moved to Major and Medium Irrigation/Water Resources, then to Forest, Ecology and Environment on 13 August 2026 after briefly resigning over being denied the Bengaluru Development portfolio); and Satish Jarkiholi retained Public Works through the August 2026 reshuffle. The single most significant new development remains that, on 9 September 2026, the Enforcement Directorate conducted money-laundering raids at roughly 18-21 locations linked to PWD Minister Satish Jarkiholi, including his Bengaluru residence and properties tied to his MP daughter Priyanka Jarkiholi and other relatives/associates, seizing roughly Rs 3.3 crore in unaccounted cash; Chief Minister Shivakumar publicly called the raids 'politically motivated', and as of the most recent reporting located (13 September 2026) Jarkiholi remains PWD Minister with no resignation or removal reported — this is an active, fast-moving situation that could affect the stability of the PWD ministerial relationship on short notice, and no news dated after 13 September 2026 could be located despite a direct search. A second significant thread, newly surfaced in this pass, is genuine contradictory sourcing over who currently holds the state's ADGP Traffic and Road Safety post: prior reporting names both R. Hithendra (additional charge, reported June 2025) and Alok Kumar (continuously from June 2023 until his own transfer to ADGP Training around May 2026), and no confirmed successor to Alok Kumar in that specific post was located — Crashfree India should confirm this post's current holder directly before any outreach premised on it. Separately, Bengaluru's Joint Commissioner of Police (Traffic) changed hands in July 2025, from M. N. Anucheth (transferred to DIG, Recruitment) to Karthik Reddy, who has publicly framed his own mandate explicitly around improving road safety and traffic management — Crashfree India's working-level Bengaluru traffic-enforcement contact should be updated accordingly. Any reference to 'Transport Minister Ramalinga Reddy,' 'CM Siddaramaiah,' or 'Joint CP Traffic M. N. Anucheth' is now historically relevant only, not a current contact.

governance_bodies.name: Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) and the five City Corporations
governance_bodies.mandate: Greater Bengaluru Governance Act, 2024 (Karnataka Act No. 36 of 2025) abolished the Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike (BBMP) and the BBMP Act, 2020, effective 15 May 2025, and replaced them with a three-tier structure: GBA at the apex (chaired by the Chief Minister); five City Corporations (Bengaluru Central, North, South, East and West); and Ward Committees below that. Fully operationalised from 2 September 2025.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Each of the five City Corporations is the formal owner/custodian of municipal roads, footpaths, drains and streetlights within its zone, exactly as BBMP was before it.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: GBA (chaired by CM Shivakumar, bringing together all state ministers, Bengaluru-area MPs/MLAs/MLCs, and once elected, the five corporations' Mayors) -> Five City Corporations, each headed (in the absence of an elected Mayor) by an appointed IAS Municipal Commissioner -> Ward Committees. Bengaluru's roughly 198 former BBMP wards were redrawn and expanded into 369 wards across the five corporations (63 Central, 72 North, 72 South, 50 East, 112 West).
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Parastatal bodies coordinated under the GBA umbrella: BESCOM (electricity), BWSSB (water/sewerage), BMTC (city bus transport), BMRCL (metro rail); also Bengaluru Solid Waste Management Ltd.

key_individuals.name: Dr. G. (Gopalkrishna) Gururaj
key_individuals.role: Dean, Centre for Public Health, Department of Epidemiology; Head, WHO Collaborating Centre for Injury Prevention and Safety Promotion, NIMHANS, Bengaluru
key_individuals.priority: Technical/research partnership route
key_individuals.influence: Leads the single most institutionally credible road-safety research and technical-assistance body headquartered in Karnataka, with a working relationship with Bengaluru Traffic Police and international funders.
key_individuals.road_safety_relevance: Has led the Bangalore Road Safety and Injury Prevention Programme since 2007; worked with Indian ministries and state governments on road safety, alongside international work advising Oman, Egypt, Iran and Indonesia on national road-safety frameworks; two-decade documented publication record on Indian road-traffic-injury epidemiology.

track_record.text: His institute co-authored and released, with Bengaluru Traffic Police, Johns Hopkins International Injury Research Unit and Bloomberg Philanthropies, a joint drunk-driving assessment report, discussed at a NIMHANS symposium on human behavioural risk factors in road traffic injuries.

citation.label: Deccan Herald, 22 Dec 2023, 'Bengaluru symposium addresses human behavioral factors in road traffic injuries'

track_record.text: A peer-reviewed paper on 'passive drink driving' interventions in Bengaluru lists Gururaj as a co-author alongside Bengaluru Traffic Police and Karnataka CID co-authors and Johns Hopkins/Bloomberg partners — evidence the collaboration is still active into 2026.

citation.label: PMC (PubMed Central), 2026

track_record.text: NIMHANS' WHO Collaborating Centre launched a 'lay responder care' module — scene safety, hands-only CPR, bleeding control, basic fracture management — that had trained over 900 people, including roughly 110 police personnel, as of 2026.

citation.label: NIMHANS, WHO Collaborating Centre for Injury Prevention and Safety Promotion, nimhans.ac.in

key_individuals.frequency_of_engagement: Recurring, long-running institutional engagement rather than a one-off; no departure, retirement, or change in his NIMHANS/WHO Collaborating Centre role found as of September 2026.
key_individuals.background: DCP3 author; two-decade publication record on Indian road-traffic-injury epidemiology; WHO Collaborating Centre focus areas include road traffic injuries, traumatic brain injury, childhood injuries, workplace injuries, and violence/suicide prevention.
key_individuals.value_to_crashfree: Potentially the fastest way for Crashfree India to access credible Karnataka-specific crash and behavioural data; a technical partnership route, not a political one.
key_individuals.suggested_approach: Approach as a technical/research partner — propose a specific, narrow collaboration (e.g., a district or corridor this programme hasn't yet reached) rather than a general partnership pitch. Assessment (not fact): given the standing NIMHANS-Police-Johns Hopkins-Bloomberg partnership, a new NGO approaching Bengaluru independently may find the ground already occupied — the more useful ask may be how Crashfree India's model complements rather than duplicates this existing programme.
key_individuals.priorities_and_interests: His institution's stated priorities center on sustaining and expanding the WHO Collaborating Centre's mandate — international advisory work (Oman, Egypt, Iran, Indonesia), the long-running Johns Hopkins/Bloomberg Philanthropies partnership with Bengaluru Traffic Police, and continued grant-funded publication output, which are his career's institutional incentives as much as personal advocacy. The 2026 pivot toward training lay responders and police personnel in trauma first-response suggests a near-term programmatic priority on capacity-building/scale rather than new research alone. No documented tension with road safety — his institutional and personal incentives are already fully aligned with it by design, which is unusual among this list and worth noting explicitly rather than assuming.
key_individuals.caveats: No changes located; reconfirmed.

key_individuals.name: Prof. M. N. Sreehari
key_individuals.role: Long-serving traffic/transportation advisor associated with the Government of Karnataka; heads a private infrastructure/transport consultancy (CEO, Consortia of Infrastructure Engineers and Transportation Engineering Consultancy Services)
key_individuals.priority: Technical reviewer route
key_individuals.influence: One of the few people bridging four decades of continuous, hands-on Bengaluru traffic-engineering advisory work with an informal-advisor relationship to the state government.
key_individuals.road_safety_relevance: Has educated over 4.5 lakh road users on road safety; became an advisor to the Government of Karnataka on Traffic, Transportation and Infrastructure in 2004; has conducted road-safety audits on more than 25 National Highways and advised NHAI on road-safety initiatives.

track_record.text: Continues to be quoted and interviewed by local and national media (including a February 2026 video interview) offering engineering-led fixes for Bengaluru traffic problems, including commentary on the city's tunnel-road project.

citation.label: 101Reporters, Feb 2026, 'M N Sreehari talks on the condition of traffic in Bengaluru' (video interview)

key_individuals.frequency_of_engagement: Continuous since 2004; reconfirmed active in public commentary through February 2026, no evidence of a change in his informal-advisor status.
key_individuals.background: Over 42 years as a transportation-engineering professor and consultant; became Government of Karnataka advisor on Traffic, Transportation and Infrastructure in 2004.
key_individuals.value_to_crashfree: Useful as institutional memory and a possible technical reviewer for a specific corridor or junction, more than as a decision-maker.
key_individuals.suggested_approach: Not specified beyond his role as institutional memory/technical reviewer.
key_individuals.priorities_and_interests: His public statements consistently favour large infrastructure/engineering solutions (flyovers, tunnel roads, signal and audit fixes) over enforcement- or behaviour-change-led approaches — consistent with, though not provably driven by, his consultancy firms' commercial interest in infrastructure design and advisory contracts (inference, not a documented conflict). His institutional incentive as a 20-plus-year informal government advisor is likely to preserve continued relevance and visibility as Bengaluru's go-to traffic commentator. Not enough on record to say whether he sees CFI's likely behaviour-change/enforcement framing as complementary or competing with his engineering-first advocacy.
key_individuals.caveats: No changes located; reconfirmed.

track_record.text: KSHIP and the World Bank received an iRAP International Award for Excellence (2013) for building safety into new-road designs and major upgrades before construction, during Mahadevappa's tenure as PWD Minister.

track_record.text: As Social Welfare Minister in 2025-26, launched the 'Constitution is Light' civic-awareness campaign with Deccan Herald/Prajavani, said the government would consider a strict law against honour killings after a Hubballi incident, and vowed to upgrade government schools to match private ones.

citation.label: Deccan Herald, multiple 2025-26 reports on Minister Mahadevappa

key_individuals.frequency_of_engagement: No change found to his current Social Welfare portfolio; reconfirmed via multiple 2025-26-dated Deccan Herald reports as of this pass.
key_individuals.background: Former PWD Minister, 2013-2018; currently Social Welfare Minister since 2023, retained in the Shivakumar cabinet.
key_individuals.value_to_crashfree: Carries institutional memory of KSHIP's road-safety engineering legacy, at a moment when the current PWD minister (Satish Jarkiholi) is newly under active political and legal pressure.

key_individuals.frequency_of_engagement: Not established as a road-safety-specific engagement pattern; well-documented as a high-visibility, delivery-focused administrator generally.

Road safety is not something he has personally emphasised, but his infrastructure-delivery framing and appetite for high-visibility initiatives could make a well-packaged, growth-and-modernity-framed road-safety pitch (rather than a casualty-statistics one) more likely to land — an inference from his general communication style, not a documented preference.

key_individuals.background: Previously held Rural Development & Panchayat Raj and IT/BT in the outgoing Siddaramaiah government; three-time MLA from Chittapur.

focus_areas.relevance: Karnataka is not named in Crashfree India's own brief for this specific program — the Hit-and-Run Compensation Scheme pilot runs in Jaipur (Rajasthan), with Gurugram, Bihar and Delhi's DRSC work as feeders. That makes the state a genuine outreach gap rather than an active site. But the underlying need is real and volatile: MoRTH data (Lok Sabha Unstarred Question No. 6419, Annexure A) shows Karnataka recorded 2,193 (2020), 1,958 (2021), 3,017 (2022), 2,737 (2023) and 2,284 (2024, provisional) hit-and-run accidents — a sharp 2022 spike followed by a two-year decline, but still well above pre-2022 levels. The scheme exists precisely because victims of untraceable vehicles have no other fast route to compensation short of the multi-year MACT process (nationally ~10.46 lakh cases pending, ~₹80,455 crore, averaging 3.6 years to settle per Crashfree India's brief) — a burden Karnataka's own courts share. Karnataka's relative prominence for Crashfree India overall (as home to SATARK) makes the absence of a dedicated Hit-and-Run push here a visible strategic gap: a state with strong tech-enforcement ties but no compensation-side presence is an obvious next step for outreach, especially since claims processing (see progress) shows the administrative machinery already works better here than in most states. There is also a plausible operational link worth exploring for outreach: SATARK's ANPR infrastructure already captures vehicle-identification data at scale in Bengaluru, and in principle a state with mature ANPR deployment is better positioned than most to eventually trace hit-and-run vehicles — though no source found in this research draws that connection explicitly, so it remains a hypothesis rather than a documented fact.
focus_areas.progress: Karnataka's own claims data (Annexure B of the same Lok Sabha answer) shows a striking improvement curve: 0 claims registered/paid in FY2022-23, rising to 11 registered/3 paid in FY2023-24, then 193 registered/130 paid in FY2024-25, and 463 registered/385 paid in FY2025-26 as of 28 February 2026. The paid-to-registered ratio in the latest year (385/463, ~83%) is unusually healthy compared with the national picture Crashfree India cites — only ~205 claims filed nationally in FY2022-23 against ~25,000 hit-and-run crashes (~12% uptake), with 921 of a 1,026-claim sample sample stalled purely on documentation gaps. Karnataka's trajectory suggests the state's implementing machinery (police FIR-to-claim pipeline, Claims Settlement Commissioner processing) has scaled up faster than most states, even without any Crashfree India presence. Set against this improving claims picture, the near-total absence of Rah-Veer (Good Samaritan) recognitions is a stark counterpoint: Karnataka reported zero cumulative Good Samaritan awardees as of 12 February 2026 (Lok Sabha Unstarred Question No. 2178, Annexure I) — the state does not appear at all among states reporting any awards to MoRTH. This is a notable disconnect: a state that processes hit-and-run claims relatively well has apparently not operationalised the parallel scheme meant to encourage bystanders to help crash victims in the 'golden hour.'
focus_areas.policy_willpower: The clearest recent national-level policy signal is the Compensation to Victims of Hit and Run Motor Accidents (Amendment) Scheme, 2026, notified by MoRTH around March 2026, which formalises expanded roles for District Road Safety Committees (DRSCs) and the State Road Safety Council: districts now evaluate local implementation and escalate issues upward, an electronic portal (managed by the General Insurance Council) becomes mandatory for applications and sanctions, and the Claims Settlement Commissioner must sanction claims within 15 days of the enquiry report (SCC Online Blog coverage, tier-4 legal-analysis source, exact gazette notification URL not independently located). This applies to Karnataka's DRSCs by default, but no Karnataka-specific coverage of its implementation was found in this research. A Karnataka State Road Safety Authority (KSRSA) does exist (ksrsa.karnataka.gov.in), but its official page was inaccessible during research (repeated 503 errors), so its stated mandate on hit-and-run/DRSC coordination could not be independently confirmed. No Karnataka-specific budget line, ministerial statement, or legislative action singling out hit-and-run compensation was located; the state's improving claims numbers appear to be an administrative/execution story rather than a documented new-policy story. For a dashboard audience, the honest characterisation is that Karnataka's hit-and-run compensation trend line is a genuinely positive, verifiable data point (backed directly by MoRTH's own Lok Sabha answer), but the causal story behind the improvement — whether it reflects a specific state directive, a central push, or simply organic scale-up as awareness spreads post-2022 rate revision — could not be established from the sources located.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Karnataka is explicitly not named in Crashfree India's brief for the Hit-and-Run Compensation Scheme — the pilot is Jaipur, Rajasthan, with Gurugram, Bihar and Delhi as feeders. This is an honest gap: despite Karnataka being Crashfree India's flagship state for SATARK, there is no evidence the organisation has extended its compensation-side legal aid, Aasha AI companion, or compensation calculator work into a dedicated Karnataka push, even though the state's own claims data suggest fertile, receptive ground.

focus_areas.name: Gig Rider Safety
focus_areas.relevance: Bengaluru is one of India's largest gig-delivery hubs, making Karnataka self-evidently relevant to a national Gig Rider Safety programme that only began in February 2026 and remains thematic/national in scope on Crashfree India's own materials. The city's scale is documented independently: Bengaluru Traffic Police crackdowns in 2026 have targeted riders for Zomato, Swiggy, Instamart and Zepto specifically, and national coverage (including Al Jazeera, January 2026) documents fatalities and public-interest litigation that pushed a nationwide advisory curbing '10-minute delivery' guarantees. Karnataka is also distinctive on the policy side: it was the first major state to pass dedicated platform/gig-worker welfare legislation, the Karnataka Platform-Based Gig Workers (Social Security and Welfare) Act, 2025 (ordinance May 2025; detailed rules operationalised around November 2025), which includes explicit occupational-safety language — panic buttons, safety guidance, and mandatory information/training on occupational hazards and safe work practices — plus statutory accident and life insurance for registered gig workers. This is not a road-safety law per se, but it is the closest thing in India to a state-level legal hook connecting gig-worker welfare to on-road risk, and it predates Crashfree India's own programme launch, making Karnataka a natural policy-alignment target.
focus_areas.progress: On the enforcement side, Bengaluru Traffic Police in July 2026 rolled out a scheme replacing monetary fines with mandatory four-hour road-safety awareness sessions for delivery riders caught violating traffic rules (riding against traffic, using footpaths, jumping signals), extended across all 53 traffic police stations in the city, with nearly 4,000 cases registered in just the first three days (South Matters, 16 Jul 2026). This followed years of friction between the city administration and delivery platforms over rider safety and delivery-time pressure. Nationally, December 2025 saw large-scale gig-worker strikes (200,000+ workers across NCR, Mumbai and Bengaluru) partly over incentive cuts, and January 2026 brought government advisories curbing ultra-fast delivery commitments after fatalities and litigation (Al Jazeera). Platforms (Zomato, Swiggy) report offering accident insurance and mandatory safety training modules to active riders, with some training delivered at traffic-police training parks in Bengaluru. On the Crashfree India side specifically, the Gig Rider Safety programme page was marked 'Coming Soon' as of this research (September 2026) — partners named are Cars24, the Indian Road Safety Council, Bikes24 and TeamBHP, with no city-level rollout, pilot location, or Karnataka-specific plan yet published.
focus_areas.policy_willpower: Karnataka shows unusually strong independent policy willpower here relative to other states: the Platform-Based Gig Workers Act, 2025 was among the first state-level gig-worker welfare laws in India, moved from ordinance (May 2025) to substantive rules (around November 2025) in under a year, and created a standing Welfare Board and Fund financed by mandatory aggregator contributions — with accident and life insurance made a statutory entitlement rather than a voluntary platform perk. Separately, Bengaluru's traffic administration has shown it will act unilaterally on rider safety enforcement (the July 2026 fines-to-training pivot) without waiting for central or NGO programmes. Neither of these initiatives is coordinated with, or attributed to, Crashfree India, underscoring that Karnataka's gig-safety momentum is currently state- and city-driven rather than NGO-driven. For an outreach dashboard, this is a useful framing: Karnataka does not need convincing that gig-rider safety matters — it already has a functioning legal and enforcement apparatus moving in that direction — so any Crashfree India engagement here would be about complementing and connecting existing state/city initiatives (data, research, advocacy for enforcement of the Act's safety provisions) rather than initiating them from scratch, unlike some other states where the policy groundwork does not yet exist.
focus_areas.cfi_engagement: Crashfree India's Gig Rider Safety programme remains in a pre-launch, 'Coming Soon' state as of September 2026 with no city or state named yet, so there is no confirmed Karnataka engagement from Crashfree India specifically — despite Bengaluru being an obvious candidate given its gig-delivery scale and the state's own parallel legislative activity.
